title: Food Delivery - The $432B Industry That Benefits No One
note: Four-sided economic explainer (consumers, drivers, restaurants, apps) built on the opening claim that apps benefit no one; heavy on math and lists of numbers.
lines: Food delivery apps are a scam.
Do you want to get Chinese food?
Uber Eats.
Do you want to get Indian food?
Uber Eats.
Do you want to get burgers?
Uber Eats.
Do you want to get pizza?
Well, maybe DoorDash.
Food delivery has become a ubiquitous service that virtually everyone uses.
In fact, 86% of Americans use food delivery at least once a month.
31% use it at least twice a week and as for millennials, I mean this is basically their entire diet.
This is not too surprising given the extraordinary convenience of these food delivery apps.
You can order from virtually any restaurant in your vicinity and they have it delivered to your doorstep within an hour.
This is in stark contrast to food delivery just 10 years ago when your options were basically just pizza.
This unprecedented surge has allowed for the food delivery industry to thrive with several apps popping up from Uber Eats and DoorDash to Grubhub and Postmates.
But while these apps sure are convenient, they're not exactly a great deal for anyone.
The average American spends $37.28 every week on food delivery, which translates to $150 per month or over $1,800 per year.
And over a third of that amount is simply going towards service fees, delivery fees, and tips coming in at $13 per order or $650 per year.
But I'm sure you already knew that.
For most people, food delivery is more of a guilty pleasure than anything.
But unlike Netflix binging and singing in your car, this habit will cost you a lot more.
In fact, if young adults simply invested food delivery money into the S &P 500 between the ages of 20 and 65, they would end up with an extra $715,000 instead of a bunch of Panda Express boxes.
But that's not just end consumers who are getting a bad bargain either.
Food delivery is also not that great for restaurants, delivery drivers, or even the food delivery apps themselves.
Yet, the popularity of food delivery is only continuing to skyrocket.
it.
So, here's why food delivery apps are kind of a scam for everyone and why no one seems to care anyway.
We all know that food delivery is expensive, but just how expensive is it?
Well, let's do the math.
Single adults tend to spend between $59 and $91 every week at the grocery store, so about an average of $75 per week.
There's no stats about how much single adults spend on food delivery, but we do know how much Gen Zers spend on food delivery which should be pretty close.
The average Gen Zer spends about $30 per food delivery order.
So even ordering food delivery just once a week would increase the average person's food budget by almost 50%.
Twice a week would increase the budget by 80%, and 3 times a week would increase the budget by 120%.
For those of you who use food delivery every day, I know you're watching, you're increasing your food budget by nearly 300%, spending $210 every week on food delivery.
On the right side, your grocery bill is probably far lower than average, but that's not exactly a net positive.
To make things worse, this shortfall will only compound throughout your life.
Just one food delivery per week will set your retirement back $600,000, obviously assuming that you invest your money well instead.
This means that two deliveries per week is costing you $1.2 million, three deliveries is costing you $1.8 million, and a delivery every day is costing you $4.2 million.
At that point, that could literally be your entire retirement.
The only way that this is not a bad financial decision is if you're already investing $100,000 or more every year.
At that rate, you'd be worth $40 million by the time you're 65, so $4.2 million would still be a large amount, but percentage-wise, it's not terrible.
I suspect that most of you aren't investing $100,000 every year though, so probably best to cut back on the food delivery.
Now, I know what some of you are already saying.
What's the point of having so much money at retirement if you didn't even get to enjoy the journey there, and that is valid.
74% of people say that they would show up to an event if they knew the food was going to be good, so there's no doubt that food plays a big role in people's lives.
This brings us to exhibit B though, which is how much money is going towards the food itself and how much is going towards delivery.
It may seem like you're just paying a delivery fee and a tip, but that's just what's shown.
You see, restaurants know that people are willing to pay more for the same food when it's offered for delivery, and they've taken the liberty to increase prices across the board on delivery apps.
Take Panda Express for example.
A family feast costs $39 at the restaurant, but it costs between $45 and $47 on delivery apps.
It might not seem like a big difference, but when you combine this with the delivery fees and service fees, it becomes quite egregious.
The same Subway order cost 25% more on Grubhub, 46% more on DoorDash, 63% more on Postmates, and 91% more on Uber Eats, and that's not even accounting for a tip.
On average, people tip 15.7% for food deliveries, so really, you're spending an extra 40-100% over your meal price just for the delivery.
Let's call it an average of 70%.
Here's what this means long term.
247,000 of this is going to delivery.
494,000 of this is going to delivery.
$741,000 of this is going to delivery.
And a disgusting $1.7 million of this is going to delivery.
That's enough money to make a grown man cry, but all of that is just the consumer side of things.
YouTube has very much glamorized the life of delivery drivers.
Trying to make $500 in a day, trying to make $700 in a day, trying to make $10,000 in a month.
I mean, there's nothing wrong with these videos.
They're fun, entertaining challenges, but don't take them for anything more than just that.
While delivering food may be lucrative for pro college students and young adults, and it's not exactly as good as it sounds, especially as a career.
To reach numbers like $10,000 per month, delivery drivers have to work 12 to 15 hours every single day.
And when you do the math, it's not all that great.
Even calling it just 12 hours per day, delivery drivers have to work 360 hours per month to reach those numbers.
If delivery drivers worked a more reasonable 40 hours per week or 160 hours per month, they'd make about $53,000 per year, which doesn't sound too bad.
But that number is actually super misleading because most of us contextualize that number as a job.
I mean, that's how much teachers and police officers make, but the difference between making $53,000 on Uber Eats and making $53,000 on a job is day.
First of all, the job is infinitely more stable, but let's put that aside as there's plenty of other attributes to discuss.
For example, most of the numbers you see on YouTube are top-line numbers that don't account for gas or depreciation of the car, but let's even put that aside.
The real first obstacle that you'll face as a delivery driver is taxes.
As a delivery driver, your tax status will be self-employed, which means that you have to pay both sides of social security and medicare tax.
This adds up to an extra 7.65% every single year, so earning $53,000 on Uber Eats is effectively the same as earning $49,000 at a job, and that's just because of taxes.
Next, you have to deal with health insurance.
Most people making $49,000 per year have some sort of government job or low-end private job.
Either way though, the benefits are pretty strong in most cases.
The average teacher for example gets $10,500 in health insurance benefits.
As a delivery driver, you'll have to pay this amount out of pocket, which takes your salary down to $38,500.
After that, we have retirement benefits.
Police officers, for example, get as much as $29,000 towards retirement every year.
If you're trying to match this as a delivery driver, you'll be down to less than $10,000 in that income, but we can be more conservative.
Let's say you're missing out on $5,000 in retirement benefits.
That still knocks you down to $33,500.
dollars.
Most jobs will also have paid time off, sick days, and other perks.
But if you want these as a delivery driver, you'll have to pay it out of pocket, which will bring your net income to below $30,000.
But it gets even worse.
When you hear that police officers and teachers make $50,000 or $60,000, that's truly an average across the nation.
These jobs exist in every community and every city across the world really.
The opportunity to do Uber Eats full-time however, only exists in the highest cost of living cities like New York, San Francisco, London, Austin, etc.
I mean, you're not gonna be very busy if you're trying to do Uber Eats in Nebraska.
In many of these high cost of living cities, the minimum wage itself is $15 per hour, which translates to just over $30,000 per year.
So, while top line numbers on YouTube challenges may look appealing, driving for these food delivery apps is basically just an unstable minimum weight job.
It's not just consumers and drivers that are getting screwed over by these apps either.
Restaurants are also getting the short end of the stick.
Have you ever wondered why delivery prices are relatively affordable?
Of course, we've discussed how even these small $10- $15 fees can add up over time, but in terms of face value, it's not too big of a fee to have any restaurant delivered to your doorstep.
Well, the reason for this is that you're not the only one that's paying.
Restaurants have to pay exorbitant amounts to be listed on these food delivery apps, which was basically required during the pandemic.
On DoorDash, for example, restaurants have to pay 15%, 25%, or 30% depending on how much they want DoorDash to push their restaurant.
DoorDash also gets an additional 6% commission on pickup orders given that they can't charge you a delivery fee.
Uber Eats and all of the other delivery apps are virtually identical pricing plans.
And given that restaurants tend to have pretty meager profit margins of 3-5%, there's no question that these fees weigh down on these businesses quite a bit.
This is the main reason that restaurants mark up their food so heavily on these delivery apps in the first place.
Oftentimes, they have to charge that much more just to break even.
They also have no option to avoid these apps either because the pandemic transitioned much of their customer base to delivery.
But delivery apps aren't just hurting the bottom line of restaurants, they're also oftentimes hurting their reputation.
You see, first, these delivery apps use extremely aggressive salespeople to convince restaurant owners to list their restaurants.
But if they don't agree to do it voluntarily, these apps often just go ahead and list the restaurants.
Anyway, they figure that most owners don't have the time, money, or energy to take these corporations to court.
Maybe 1 in 1,000 or 1 in 10,000 will actually sue and win, but this doesn't really matter for these apps.
They're basically having to pay $300,000 or $500,000 for every 10,000 restaurants that they list.
So, listing these restaurants without the owner's permission is a no-brainer net positive.
The same, however, cannot be said for owners.
When these apps list menus without their permission, they often end up using outdated menus and prices.
So, customers end up ordering something and get mad when they realize that their food is no longer being offered or cost more than they thought.
customers will naturally get mad at the restaurant and think why don't these people even keep their menus up to date?
but in reality it wasn't even the restaurant's fault.
these frustrations don't just apply to wrongfully listed restaurants either.
correctly listed restaurants have their own set of headaches with the delivery drivers and angry customers.
for example drivers have the ability to drop an order up until they pick it up and this happens more often than you think.
The driver arrives at the store and sees that the line is super long or they find a more lucrative delivery or whatever the reason may be.
If another driver doesn't accept to do the delivery, the food is ready and the customers want the food.
But the food will never get to the customer.
The customer will want a refund and the restaurant will have lost out on the food and the money.
Little to say, there's not much for restaurants to get excited about when it comes to food delivery apps.

With customers getting screwed over, drivers getting screwed over, and restaurants getting screwed over, you would think that at least the food delivery apps must be coming out on top, but this is also not the case.
All food delivery apps lose money, and the most popular ones lose the most money.
Inflation is only making these losses even worse with most delivery apps posting record losses.
In the last 12 months, DoorDash lost a record $1.36 billion, but that's nothing in comparison to Uber's $9.1 billion loss.
For Uber, this isn't even a record as they've been casually losing $8-10 billion for 4 years now.
With all the fees they charge everyone, this might be a bit confusing, but when you think about it, it all makes sense.
The only food industry that has mastered delivery and is able to stay profitable is pizza chains, and they have to make a lot of sacrifices to achieve this.
Every restaurant only delivers to a very small radius, they have full-time delivery drivers, and they've refined their delivery process to be extremely efficient over decades of doing this.
Modern delivery apps are basically the exact opposite of this.
Drivers usually have to go to different restaurants for each delivery.
They have to deliver to a very big radius, and drivers generally choose deliveries based on how lucrative they are as opposed to how efficient they are for the overall platform.
Given this combination, it's no wonder why delivery apps are struggling to turn a profit.
The bottom line is that delivering from any restaurant to any doorstep is simply a logistical nightmare that requires a bunch of man hours which is not cost effective by any means and never will be.
In the meantime, everyone from drivers and consumers to restaurants and delivery apps will have to put up with the associated expenses.
And to think that all of this pain for everyone can be traced back to us being too lazy not just to cook, but even pick up cooked food.

title: Why Amazon Wants Their Employees To Resign
note: Hook-reversal explainer: Amazon deliberately churns staff, shown through vesting-schedule math and PIPs, then why people join and the looming warehouse labor shortage.
lines: The world's largest retailer, Amazon.
Amazon.
Amazon.
Amazon is now offering its employees money to quit.
Up to 18,000 employees are getting fired starting this year.
Amazon wants their employees to resign.
This might sound counterintuitive, but it's true.
It turns out that for Amazon, it's actually beneficial to constantly churn through employees.
This is actually one of the main reasons that Amazon treats their employees so poorly.

Whether it be exposing warehouse workers to safety hazards, making their drivers pee in bottles, or working tech staff to the bone, Amazon does it all, and it looks like their efforts of creating a terrible working environment are playing out perfectly.
In fact, Amazon's turnover rate is so high that they measure it on a weekly basis.
Amazon loses approximately 3% of their warehouse workers every single week.
This translates to an annual turnover rate of 150%.
In other words, Amazon's entire warehouse workforce is replaced basically every 8 months.
And considering the working conditions of these people, this rate is not too surprising.
But why in the world would Amazon want their employees to resign?
They likely spent thousands if not tens of thousands of dollars on recruiting each and every one of their employees.
And let's not forget all of the time and resources they spent on onboarding and training employees.
So, it doesn't really make sense to sign them on just for two thirds of warehouse workers to leave in 90 days and their tech workers to leave in two years, right?
Wrong.
It turns out that constantly churning through employees is not only cheaper for Amazon, but substantially more productive.
In fact, Jeff Bezos has gone as far as declaring that a tenured workforce is simply a march to mediocrity.
As employees become more tenured, they tend to also become more comfortable and more lazy, or at least that's what Amazon thinks.
So, over the years, Amazon has perfected how to attract employees and push them away at the same time.

Essentially, they want you to come in with big dreams, work your ass off for two years, realize that no one recognizes your efforts, and then leave so that the next sucker can come in and do the exact same thing.
They've basically mastered the art of running a cutthroat meat grinder.
So here's the twisted economics of Amazon and the downright putrid tactics they use to screw over their employees.
In terms of how Amazon pushes out blue-collar workers, it's not really rocket science.
They basically create a high-pressure, high-stress environment with lofty targets and no downtime.
But the way they handle their tech workers is a lot more interesting.
As you know, tech workers demand a pretty lofty salary, so Amazon has to employ some pretty clever yet disgusting strategies.
Likely the most notable of these strategies is screwing over their employees with wonky vesting periods.
If you're not familiar with vesting periods, and it's basically how much time you have to wait until you can cash in on your stock compensation.
Most tech companies operate under a 4-year vesting schedule with stock compensation being evenly split up across the years.
At Facebook for example, employees get 25% of their total stock rent every year, with 6.25% being unlocked every quarter.
Google actually takes it to another level in terms of vesting.
They not only front load their stock vesting, but they do vesting on a monthly basis, so it's almost like a monthly salary.
Amazon, however, does the exact opposite, as they backflow their vesting.
Engineers have to wait a full year just for 5% of their stock to vest, and another full year just for 15% to vest.
It's not until the third and fourth years that engineers actually receive 80% of their promised stock.
This might not sound like a big deal, but if you enter Amazon at a relatively senior level, it really screws you over.
For example, Let's say you have the option to enter Google as an L6 and Amazon as an L7, which are approximately equal positions in terms of work and responsibilities.
On paper, both companies pay approximately the same amount, just over $500,000.
Amazon actually pays $30,000 more.
But if you made your decision based on these top-line numbers, you'd be making a mistake, and here's why.
This stock grant number of $318,000 is not something that you receive every year.
It's just an average of what you'll receive over the next 4 years.
So, Amazon is basically offering you $1.27 million for the next 4 years and vests according to this schedule.
The same thing applies to Google, but given that they have a much more fair vesting schedule, it's not really to your disadvantage.
In fact, here's how both jobs break down over 4 years.
During year 1, Google pays $611,000, while Amazon pays $306,000.
$306,000 is obviously not a bad amount, but it's only half of Google despite Amazon's compensation seeming like it was actually higher than Google's.
During year 2, Google will pay another $611,000, while Amazon will pay $433,000.
During year 3, Google drops to $506,000 while Amazon rockets to $750,000.
And during the last year, Google drops further to $401,000 while Amazon stays constant at $750,000.
If you're wondering why Google's compensation drops over the years, it's because they're betting that the stock price will increase by the time you receive it.
So, when you account for stock growth, your compensation should be relatively stable at Google.
Amazon will of course also experience stock growth, so their compensation in the last two years will likely be over a million.
But you can bet that they're gonna do everything they can to push you out in the first two years.
Statistically speaking, neither the average Google nor the average Amazon tech worker reaches 2 years.
The average tenure at Google is 1.9 years, while the average tenure at Amazon is 1.84 years.
So, not a big difference in terms of employee retention, but the difference in compensation is night and day.
Given that Google has monthly vesting, an employee leaving at 1.9 years has actually vested over 60% of their stock.
An employee at Amazon leaving at 1.84 years, however, won't have even vested their year 2 stock as they have to finish the year.
So, they're left with just the 5% that was vested after year 1.
In other words, remember that massive $1.27 million stock grant that Amazon offered you when you joined?
Well, the average Amazonian will only end up receiving a mere $63,000 of this.
The average Googler would have received $571,000 worth of their stock compensation.

When you annualize these numbers along with the base salary and bonus, you'll see that the Googler was earning an effective salary of $611,000 while the Amazonian was only earning $274,000 or less than half of what the compensation appeared to be.
Again, you can't really complain with either of these salaries, but you can see just how misleading Amazon's top line number was.
Now, I should note that Amazon sometimes offers a large cash bonus during year 1 to make up for some of this gap, but that only goes so far and doesn't apply to everyone.
Why not just stick around for 4 years, then you'll get the full promised amount, right?
Well, the reality is that this is extremely difficult due to the axe aka PIPs.
PIPs stands for performance improvement plans and Amazon swears by these.
Through these plans, Amazon ranks all of their employees every single year and then they go ahead and fire the bottom 10% every single year.
And as you would guess, this policy disproportionately affects new hires and it creates an extremely toxic work culture.
Basically, all of your team members will be trying to backstab you so that they're not the ones who are put on these performance improvement plans.
Everyone is trying to survive the 2 year cliff and cash in on the stock compensation that's so close yet so far away.
The reality though is that the average employee doesn't even pass 2 years, but let's assume that you're part of the lucky few who make it through the full 4 years.
Congratulations, you got a big payday, but now Amazon still wants you to leave.
If you survive the first 4 years, it's unlikely that they'll put you on a performance improvement plan and force you out that way.
But what they will do is severely nerf your pay and hope that you either leave or stay and work for substantially lower pay.
Either option is okay with them.
How do they do this you ask?
Well, remember that massive stock grant that they offered you when you joined?
Well, let's just say you ain't getting that again.
If you're lucky, you may get stock refreshers, but that's usually nothing in comparison to your compensation in year 3 and 4.
If you were an L7 for example, your compensation will drop from nearly a million down to 300,000.
And you're expected to maintain the same level of output if you want to continue avoiding the pips.
By this point though, most remaining Amazonians don't want to put up with this anymore, so if the pips didn't get them, the nerfed pay usually does.
If things are so unfair at Amazon though, why do people still join?
Well, for delivery drivers and warehouse workers, it's often the only job they're able to find.
But what about the tech workers?
Surely, they're smart enough to see through these tricks and do their research, right?
Well, they are.
Most of them know all about this, but they choose to join anyway because Amazon is oftentimes the only fang job that they're able to land.
Of course, they could go ahead and join a respectable background company like Visa or Oracle.
But that won't make the same impact on their career trajectory that Amazon would.
You see, no tech worker is putting up with all this just to work on Amazon retail.
All the hype for tech workers is to get into AWS or Amazon Web Services.
If you're not familiar with AWS, they're the gold standard when it comes to cloud computing and infrastructure.
AWS holds a market share of 41.5% in the cloud computing market, which is more than their main competitors combined.
Microsoft comes in at 29.4% while Google comes in at a measly 2.6%.
As such, everyone in the cloud space is looking for ex-AWS employees.
In fact, many job postings will literally list AWS experience as a minimum qualification.
So, many tech workers figure that putting up with Amazon is their best shot at potentially lending a job at a non-abusive fan company.
And more times than not, this actually does work out.
Many of the people who leave Amazon after 1.84 years aren't actually getting fired through PIP.
Rather, they were offered an opportunity to join Apple or Google's cloud departments.
And if you want any proof regarding just how badly these people want to leave Amazon, just look at all the money they're leaving on the table in year 3 and 4.
Amazon doesn't take this as an insult though.
They're happy to be a springboard for other fan companies as at the end of the day, they're the ones who got the most labor for the cheapest price.
And within the tech side of Amazon, I don't think this will be changing anytime soon, but it may be changing on the blue collar side.
You see, when you're a small company and you're churning through a bunch of employees, it's not really a big deal.
But when you're at Amazon's size with over a million employees, you actually run the risk of running out of people to churn through.
And ironically, this is the exact crisis that Amazon has been facing since mid-2021.
According to leaked internal research, Amazon will run out of warehouse workers to churn through by 2024, which at this point is only 8 months away.
A looming recession may give Amazon some more time, but sooner or later, they'll have to confront the consequences of churning through so many people.
In the end, the reason Amazon wants their employees to resign simply comes down to productivity and financials.
They believe that the most productive employees are the ones that have just joined or have something to prove.
So, they structure all of their compensation plans and corporate performance policies around milking out these first few years of productivity for as cheap as possible.
Everything from their compensation policy and vesting schedule to their performance improvement plans and work culture is all designed to get engineers to join but not stay for long.
By this point, most engineers are well aware of the harsh reality of Amazon, but Amazon is able to leverage the reputation of AWS to continue recruiting engineers.

On the warehouse side of things though, they're up for a massive challenge not too long from now, but only time will tell how they handled this situation, and that's why Amazon wants their employees to resign.

title: Nvidia - The World's Next Largest Company
note: Company rise story told as a series of booms (gaming, mining, pandemic, AI) with a long-term-preparation thesis and a gold-rush shovels ending.
sections: Luck versus preparation and the shovels metaphor
lines: NVIDIA is going to be the world's largest company.
For years, haters have been saying that NVIDIA's time at the top is almost over.
As soon as the custom PC hype dies down, NVIDIA will get crushed.
As soon as the Bitcoin mining craze ends, Nvidia will get decimated.
As soon as the supply chain nightmare ends, Nvidia will be annihilated.
But time and time again, Nvidia has shown more resilience than any big tech stock on the market.
For example, just last year, Nvidia saw a 68% sell off due to the recession and general fears about tech.
But unlike Intel who stayed down, Nvidia has already rebounded 158%.
In fact, they're only 20% away from their all-time highs as we speak.
This makes Nvidia the 7th largest company in the world with a market cap of $650 billion.
But that's not to say that the haters don't have some valid concerns like Nvidia's valuation.
Nvidia is hands down the most richly valued big tech company, even more richly valued than Tesla.
Take their financials for example.
In the past 12 months, Nvidia has only pulled in $4.3 billion in net income.
For perspective, if Apple was the same size as Nvidia, they would be pulling in $25 billion or over 5 times more.
But just because Nvidia has a rich valuation doesn't mean that they won't continue growing in terms of fundamentals and market cap.
In fact, it's highly likely that this is the case.
They've got a foot in consumer grade products, a foot in enterprise grade products, and a ginormous foot in AI.
But it wasn't always like this.
Nvidia has been around since 1993, and up until 2016, this is how their stock graph looked.
So, here's how Nvidia went from being a no-name background company to being the world's largest semiconductor company all within a matter of 7 years and why all of this is just the beginning.
Taking a look back, Nvidia's exponential run can be traced back to early to mid-2016.
At the time, Nvidia primarily served a niche market of gamers.
They had a decent presence in enterprise.
Their most notable client was likely Tesla.
If you didn't know, it was Nvidia's GPUs that were initially powering Tesla's autonomous futures.
But Tesla itself wasn't exactly a big company.
In fact, they were simply fighting for their own survival, and they were actually the most shorted stock of all time.
So, really, Nvidia's main business was selling GPUs to gamers, but all of this would change with Bitcoin's Boruck.
You might be asking, what does Bitcoin have to do with the GPUs?
Well, the answer is actually everything.
The way that Bitcoins become available on the market is through a computationally intense process called mining.
And it turns out that Nvidia GPUs are often the most cost-effective way to mine various cryptocurrencies.
Since then, many of the top cryptos have actually become too computationally intense for Nvidia GPUs to handle, or they've switched to a proof-of-stake model, which eliminates the need for GPUs.
But despite this, the vast majority of the most profitable GPUs are still from Nvidia.
So, you can imagine how lucrative this was back in the day.
Miners would go out and buy dozens, hundreds, thousands of GPUs each.
As you would imagine, this led to an extraordinary amount of demand, and it wasn't long until Nvidia's supply started running out, leading to GPU prices skyrocketing.
Nvidia's GPUs were regularly selling for 50 to 100% more on the secondary market, and Nvidia actually got a bunch of flack from the gaming community.
Many of them felt that Nvidia was selling into this fad instead of supporting their main demographic.
They felt that Nvidia should be implementing quantity limits and nerfing the mining power of their cards to ensure that gamers could still get GPUs for MSRP.
But this didn't exactly happen.
Nvidia very much played into the mining craze and let the miners establish a new normal price for GPUs.
This did lead to a mini movement against Nvidia where a bunch of gamers switched to AMD.
AMD was crushing it against Intel with their Ryzen series, so many gamers were hopeful that they would also be able to take on Nvidia, but this never really materialized.
While AMD has been able to hold their own against Nvidia, Nvidia is still very much the GPU king.
But it wasn't all good news for Nvidia back in 2018.
Bitcoin's price would peak out at the end of 2017, and it would dramatically crash 83% right after.
This took out much of the appeal of crypto mining and it didn't take long for miners to leave the scene.
For gamers, this was Nvidia's judgment day.
They had to pay the price for siding with miners instead of gamers, and I guess they did pay some price.
Once the mining craze died down, Nvidia stock would drop 57%.
But with that being said, the mining boom allowed Nvidia to grow 11X in the prior 18 months, so I don't think they were exactly sad.
If anything, they were optimistic as they were determined to make the price increases due to mining permanent.
Everyone was expecting for GPU prices to plummet as soon as the miners left, but Nvidia had a different idea.
You see, just as the mining craze was dying down, Nvidia would come out with the 2000 series of GPUs.
Let's just say, it was substantially more expensive, especially when it came to high-end cards.
The GTX 1080 for example launched for $600.
The RTX 2080 though came in at $700 to $800.
The real difference was in the Ti series though.
The GTX 1080 Ti launched for $700.
The RTX 2080 Ti however came in at $1,000 to $1,100 or 50% more.
Nvidia's justification for these price increases were that they added ray tracing technology, which is a notable upgrade.
But it didn't exactly warrant a price hike and the proof can be seen in Nvidia's financials.
Between 2016 and 2018, Nvidia's net margin would nearly triple from 13% to 37%.
Clearly, the cost difference to add RTX was going straight to Nvidia's bottom line, but gamers were still hopeful.
They were optimistic that Nvidia would realize that these prices were unaffordable for most gamers and that they would eventually decrease prices.
But Nvidia would stubbornly hold on, and gamers would eventually compromise.
The ones that didn't would end up having to pay even more as Nvidia would experience yet another boom in 2020.
As everyone now knows, 2020 would bring with it the pandemic, which caused everyone to stay at home.
This led to an unprecedented number of people buying gaming PCs and getting into gaming.
But the pandemic didn't just bring more demand, it also brought less supply.
When China shut down every other week and there are new obstacles in every step of the production process from factories to logistics, it's no wonder why companies entered a supply chain crisis.
For companies that relied on volume of goods sold, this was devastating.
But for a company like Nvidia who could just jack up the prices, this was a gold rush, and don't even get me started on the secondary markets.
Remember how prices were hiked 50-100% during the mining boom?
Well, this time prices would be hiked 3, 5, 10x.
People were literally auctioning off GPUs as if it was some sort of antique product, and Nvidia would of course just fuel the fire with yet another series of cards, the 3000 series.
This time, Nvidia took the Apple approach.
They realized that they get a bunch of backlash when they increased the price of a given series.
So, they decided, why not just add another tier of GPUs like the iPhone Pro series?
And with that, we saw the launch of the RTX 3090 for $1500 and the RTX 3090 Ti for $2000.
But it didn't stop right there either.
If you're familiar with Bitcoin, you know that it usually follows a 4 year cycle, and it had already been 4 years since 2016.
So, yes, the miners were back, and this time, Nvidia was ready for them.
In early 2021, Nvidia would go ahead and nerf gaming GPUs with software so that they couldn't be used for mining.
Instead, they would go ahead and launch mining-specific GPUs that cost $4,700.
Originally, gamers were hoping that such a move would be beneficial for them, but now, they were paying a ludicrous amount and miners were paying an even more ludicrous amount.
If you thought gamers and miners were lucrative though, just wait till you hear what goldmine they tripped on next.
It turns out that GPUs aren't just capable of making your games look better.
They're also a requirement for machine learning and AI training.
I'm sure you know about ChatGPT by now.
ChatGPT was trained using a bunch of Nvidia GPUs called the H100.
The H100 runs between $10,000 and $20,000 depending on what specs you get.
We can call it $15,000 on average.
This is obviously an unreasonable amount for you and me, but surely that's nothing for a company, right?
Well, that would be the case until you realized that ChatGPT needed 10,000 of these suckers just for the initial training.
If you haven't done the math yet, that's $150 million.
Even accounting for a discount due to scale, we're talking about $100 million, and that That was just for phase 1 of development for one project.
Given the success of ChatGPT, you can bet that every tech company and their mothers want a piece of the pie.
The most notable example is probably Google Bard.
Over the past couple of years, Google has tried to develop their own computational devices called TPUs, but Google has by no means been able to replace NVIDIA.
In fact, I don't even think they're trying to replace NVIDIA as they're actually promoting NVIDIA products.
They're literally cloudifying NVIDIA GPUs and making that into its own business.
If buying this much computation power for your AI business is a bit too much, don't worry, you can just rent it from Google instead.
Most tech giants, however, are of course opting to just work with NVIDIA directly.
Tesla, for example, is using 5,760 NVIDIA A100 GPUs to train their self-driving.
Each of these GPUs costs a cold 10Gs, so Tesla's setup costs $57 million not including the setup, maintenance, and lease.
A similar story can be seen with Meta as well.
They've actually been using Nvidia GPUs since 2017 when they got access to 22,000 of their V100 GPUs.
As you can see, Nvidia is not just a monopoly in this sector, they're literally the only viable solution.
And that's not because of a lack of competition.
Companies like AMD, Intel, Qualcomm, TSMC, and AWS all see this opportunity.
It's just extraordinarily difficult to catch up to Nvidia when they have a lead of 20-30 years in the GPU scene.
So, let's just say, Nvidia isn't going anywhere anytime soon.
Hearing all this, you might be saying that Nvidia just got lucky with all these booms.
They just got lucky that there was a gaming boom, and then a mining boom, and then a machine boom, but that's completely untrue.
Luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity.
The reality is that Nvidia saw this vision 30 years ago in 1993.
It simply wasn't till 23 years later that the rest of the world realized how vital this technology really is.
First, it was the gaming community, then it was the mining community, then it was the enterprise community, and now it's the AI community.
But these are by no means the last to realize the potential of GPUs.
While it's unfortunate that it took so long for everyone else to get on the same page, this gave Nvidia an extraordinary amount of time to cement themselves as the undisputed king.
And unlike Intel who blundered their lead by stagnating, Nvidia is still innovating as fast as ever, which has made it impossible for anyone else to outdo them.
Now of course, all companies will eventually become like Intel, but that's not happening to Nvidia in the imminent future.
Here's what's happening instead.
Tech itself is a gold mine and you have all these companies, Google, Microsoft, Tesla, Apple, Facebook, all digging for gold.

So far, they've been pretty successful at finding gold, but whether they hit gold or not doesn't matter for Nvidia because they're the ones selling the shovels and that's why Nvidia will become the world's largest company.

title: Platforms Are Already Giving Up On Short Form Content
note: Argument essay opening on Meta's Reels losses, then three problems (creators, advertisers, audiences) and a Vine comparison.
lines: Companies are already giving up on short-form content.
Last month, Meta announced that they will stop offering bonuses to short-form creators.
Why, you ask?
Well, it turns out that pushing short-form content actually loses Meta money.
Here's the thing, while Instagram reels have exploded in popularity, they're not exactly stealing market share away from TikTok.
Rather, it's stealing market share away from themselves.
Instead of scrolling through pictures or the newsfeed on Instagram, people are now scrolling through Reels.
This doesn't sound like a big deal until you consider that Reels are substantially less profitable than Instagram's other products.
In fact, according to Zuckerberg himself, people switching to Reels is costing the company $500 million every single quarter or $2 billion every year.
And the most ironic part is that this entire time, Meta had been paying creators to make reels.
So really, they were paying to lose revenue.
No wonder they stopped.
But it's not just Meta who's pivoting away from short-form content either.
TikTok themselves are very much trying to move away.
In fact, they've been aggressively increasing their max video length.
What started at 15 seconds grew to 60 seconds, to 3 minutes, to now 10 minutes.
TikTok has even been experimenting with landscape mode on Android.
So TikTok is very much headed towards the direction of becoming the YouTube where people don't search.
Also, it's not like people search all that much on YouTube anyway.
Most of the time, you just use the homepage to find videos.
But what happened?
Why are all these companies pivoting away from Shorts?
Wasn't Shorts the new medium due to ever decreasing attention spans and the need for constant stimulation?
Well, it turns out that the answer is no.
While short-form content is great at garnering a lot of attention in the short term, it's not exactly the best model for companies or audiences long term.
Instagram and YouTube are starting to realize that they invested way too much money on a low ROI fad, and TikTok is fighting hard to not become the next line.
So, here's why companies got short-form content wrong and why they're already backing off.
All successful creator-driven platforms need a strong base of creators.
This is why platforms like YouTube and Spotify have even turned to offering exclusivity deals like it's NFL football or something.
So, it would be quite an issue if these platforms were struggling to grow a creator base, and that's very much the case with short-form content.
This isn't to say that TikTok and Reels aren't able to garner a bunch of creators because there's no shortage of that.
But what there is a shortage of is loyal short-form creators.
Here's the thing, 9 times out of 10, people don't start posting short-form content because that's what they truly want to do.
Rather, creators start posting short-form content because they see opportunity, they see a gold rush.
Most creators never find gold, but even those who do don't want to reinvest the profits into mining for more.
That's simply too risky.
Rather, what they want to do is sell the gold and start a stable business.
In other words, they want to switch to long-form content.
Much of this attitude can actually be explained by the algorithms used to promote short-form content.
Your follower count on short-form content really means nothing.
This is why it's such a gold rush.
If you start posting today, you have as good of a chance of posting a viral video as someone with 10 million followers.
Actually, I take that back.
If a creator has that many followers, they're probably pretty good at making viral content.
But the point is that the pivotal factor is the content itself, not the follower count.
While this is great for new creators, it's absolute garbage when it comes to longevity.
Creators are forced to always keep up with the latest trends and to put up something that can go viral instead of creating content that's actually impactful and meaningful.
This is why you see so many TikTok stars that rise out of nowhere and then disappear faster than they blew up.
Recently, I was watching an Iraq video where he trapped 25 tiktokers inside his house.
Many of these creators had millions if not tens of millions of followers.
So, I don't know if it's just me, but I had no idea who any of these people were.
Let me know down below if you were in the same boat.
But anyway, even creators who enjoy making short form content want to switch to long form because it's simply the smarter business decision.
That right there covers basically 90% of short form creators.
The other 10% are actually already long form creators.
Personally, I'm guilty of this as well.
A lot of creators have figured that they might as well try adapting their regular long form content to short form.
The mentality is usually, if it works, great.
If it doesn't, not a big deal.
So, little to say, no creator on TikTok, Instagram Reels, or YouTube Shorts is really loyal to said platform.
For all of them, short-form content is really just a springboard to garner attention or a medium to expand their existing long-form content.
So, when you're trying to run a creator driven platform with such people, well, let's just say it's difficult to say the least.
But building up a loyal creator base is just the first of these platform's worries.
Not only do these platforms have to deal with flaky creators, but they also have to deal with flaky advertisers.
The reality is that no advertiser really wants to advertise on short form content.
This isn't to say that short form advertising is always ineffective.
Beheza for example has shown time and time again that short form advertising is not only effective but can be super lucrative.
But with that being said, shorts just don't vibe with most brands.
I mean, can you imagine GE making a TikTok ad about the refrigerators or Intel making a TikTok ad about the new i9 processor?
It just doesn't feel right.
Now, some legacy companies are able to pull it off.
A notable example that comes to mind is Coca-Cola, but just because they're able to make effective ads doesn't mean that they want to advertise on these platforms.
The reality is that in most cases, these companies just don't want to associate with short form content because they see it as a risk.
I'm sure you're familiar with how companies don't want to associate with the following content on YouTube.
Well, newsflash, this is basically the entirety of TikTok.
But let's even put that aside.
Let's say you're okay with advertising next to this type of content.
You still have the challenge of running a successful ad campaign.
While TikTok can be great for promoting products like this, it's not exactly great when it comes to building general brand awareness and visibility.
Oftentimes, when companies like Apple or Coca-Cola put out an ad, they're not trying to get you to buy their product.
They don't even want you to click on the ad or buy on the spot.
Rather, they just want to build up their brand presence.
This is decently possible on YouTube given that viewers are forced to watch for 5 or 15 seconds.
But on TikTok, if an ad doesn't pique the viewer's interest within 0.2 seconds, they're gonna swipe up.
This means that advertisers are forced to include some sort of gimmicky hook which, again, just doesn't fit with their brand image.
And if you don't believe me, you can just look at the numbers.
For my usual videos, I generally get an ad rate of $4- $5 per thousand views.
For shorts, however, I generally get an ad rate of $0.05 per thousand views.
This basically indicates that advertisers are 100 times less likely to bet on short-form ad slots as opposed to long-form ad slots.
It also gives a lot more context as to why creators want to switch to long-form content so badly.
The reality is that if you want to make a living off short-form content, you have to pull in a brain-dead amount of views every single month.
To make just $5,000 per month for example, you have to pull in 100 million views.
Let me phrase that in a different way.
You have to reach 1 eighth of the entire world population every single year just to make 60 grand.
At least creators have the option to do direct brand deals or promote their own products.
For these platforms on the other hand, the only way they make money is through these ads.
So even with their ridiculous scale, it's just not all that profitable so it's no wonder why Meta is losing $2 billion every single year by pushing short form content.
While unloyal creators and hesitant advertisers are no doubt a pain in the neck, at least there's some hope with that.
As more modern companies start advertising on short form platforms, ad rates should go up which should make creating short form more worthwhile for platforms and creators.
But something that these platforms can't recover from is a waning audience.
The truth is that people are getting tired of predictable TikTok content, and the main reason for this is that these types of videos rarely have any substance.
Every single video is based around a thirst trap or some sort of gimmick, but rarely do they have any sort of real takeaway or message.
This is why people forget about most shorts within two minutes of watching it.
It feels good in the moment, but the feeling doesn't last long.
But wait a minute, isn't people's attention spans getting crushed by these platforms?
Well, to be honest, I think this effect is vastly overstated.
TikTok is basically like ice cream.
People like eating ice cream, they may even eat it on a daily basis.
But just because a person eats ice cream doesn't mean that they're suddenly going to stop eating steak or pizza or burgers or real food in general.
In fact, if you had the option of only consuming ice cream or pizza, I'm pretty sure that virtually everyone will choose pizza.
Looking back, the pandemic forced most people to stay at home, which led to them snacking way more than usual.
But as people return to their normal lives, their social media diet is also returning to real food, and this is already evident in the stats.
In 2021, TikTok rose to be the most popular domain in the entire world.
But in 2022, TikTok fell down to number 3 as Google and Facebook regained their leads.
And looking forward, it seems like this trend will only continue as TikTok is looking more and more like Vine.
I know that most of you just remember Vine as a big failure, but Vine was actually super popular for a period of time.
In fact, at the end of 2015, Vine had as many as 200 million users.
Why did Vine fail then, you ask?
Well, you can take it from the horse's mouth itself.
Twitter, the parent company of Vine, was unable and or unwilling to pay the creators that made the platform so popular in the first place.
This was actually Jack Dorsey's biggest regret.
But what is TikTok doing?
Well, they're unable and or unwilling to pay the creators that made their platform so big.
And as audiences and creators naturally shift back to Facebook and YouTube, these platforms see less of a reason to be so aggressive when it comes to promoting shorts.
In the end, it's not surprising why companies are backing away from short form content.
The reality is that creators are just using shorts as a springboard, advertisers don't want to get involved, and audiences are by no means ditching long form content.

This isn't to say that TikTok is going to die like Vine, but what has become abundantly clear is that short-form content is simply an addition to long-form content, not a replacement like the media often suggests.
So, Meta and YouTube no longer feel threatened by TikTok.
If anything, it's actually TikTok that strives to be more like Meta and YouTube so that they don't end up like Vine.
Combine this with the recession, and it simply makes no sense to bet so much on a historically flaky medium, and that's why companies are already giving up and pulling back on short-form content.

title: This Guy Stole $120M From Google & Meta (& Nearly Got Away)

lines: This guy stole $120 million from Google and Facebook and nearly got away with it.
Hearing this, you're probably thinking that this guy, Evaldus Remasaskas, was some sort of insane hacker or insider.
He must've breached through Google security systems or used insider knowledge to siphon money from Facebook.
But in reality, he was just an ordinary man from Lithuania and the scheme he used wasn't especially notable either.
He used a classic email phishing scheme, yet somehow he was able to trick some of the smartest people and companies in the world.
The craziest part was that these companies didn't even know they were being scammed and he could have easily gotten away with it if he didn't try to push his luck.
You see, Evaldus didn't just set out to hit a jackpot and retire.
He was looking to defraud as many companies for as much money as possible.
So, every time he hoodwinked a company, he would just do it again to the same company or the next company.
Originally, he stole $23 million from Google throughout 2013.
At that point, that's literally generational wealth, but our man Evaldis wasn't happy.
Just two years later, he would target Facebook and bag another $98 million.
dollars.
This greed, however, would eventually get him noticed, and these companies would notify the FBI, who would track him down to Lithuania.
They would of course arrest him, and he would be sentenced to five years in jail, but the same could not be said about his associates who were never found.
Apparently, Evoltis would wire the stolen funds all around the world as soon as he received them.
So, who knows how many people were involved and how much they were each able to get away with.
But all of this begs the question, how did he do it?
How was he able to outsmart the smartest companies in the world and get away with it for years?
And what does this mean regarding the security of the data that all of us have stored on these platforms?
Well, here's the story of Evaldus Remesascus, the guy who stole $120 million from tech companies and nearly got away.
Taking a look back, the story of Evaldus traces back to their early 2010s to Lithuania.
Like any country, Lithuania is mostly filled with awesome law-abiding people and great culture.
But unfortunately, they are notorious for one crime, car theft.
If you've ever heard of someone's car being stolen, it was probably dismantled within no time and shipped off to Lithuania.
From there, the car parts are listed on sites like eBay like nothing happened.
Their listings are usually way cheaper than everything else on the market for, well, obvious reasons.
But by the early 2010s, authorities were starting to catch on and they were busting these car rings left and right.
So, our man at Valtas needed a new strategy, something that wasn't so hot and risky, something that no one was even paying attention to.
One of the main problems with carjacking for criminals is that it basically always gets notified to the police.
I mean, who wouldn't report to the police that they had their car stolen.
Not to mention, carjacking wasn't even all that lucrative given how much risk was involved.
If you wanted to make a million dollars for example and you sold each car part for $500 on average, you would need 2,000 car parts.
This means that you would have to steal dozens of cars resulting in dozens of police reports.
Obviously, not a very good risk to reward ratio, so Evoldis decided to hatch up his own plan.
He first asked himself, where can I get a lot of money without the victim even noticing?
And the answer became clear pretty quickly, filthy rich tech companies.
There was only one problem, he was by no means the first or the last person to think of this idea.
Tech companies know all about how they're vulnerable to cyber attacks not just to steal money, but to steal personal data, top secret technology, and confidential information.
Just think about this, even the CIA stores their information on Amazon servers.
So, maintaining a secure public image is no doubt a top priority for these companies, and I don't think you'd be surprised here that these tech companies invest tens of billions into cybersecurity.
But this really only protects these companies against against cyber threats, people who are trying to directly hack into their systems to wreak havoc.
Evaldus wasn't even considering this option because, well, he didn't even stand a chance against the IT departments of these companies.
So, Evaldus looked to identify a weaker entry point, somewhere money was already exiting the company.
This left Evaldus with really only one option, the payroll department.
For most companies, paying employees and other businesses is by far their biggest expense, and Google and Facebook were no exception.
Google, for example, spent $56 billion on payroll last year.
But paying employees is a pretty streamlined and highly scrutinized process, so this wasn't exactly a great entry point.
Paying businesses, however, was highly custom and usually handled on a case-by-case basis.
So, if you posed as a business, you would only have to trick a handful of people who are approving a given invoice, not the entire company's IT department or security infrastructure.
And with that, Evaldis had his entry point.
Companies like Google and Facebook pay out money to thousands if not tens of thousands of different companies for all sorts of reasons from manufacturing and logistics to research and legal services.
While newer partners may get more scrutiny when it comes to billing, most established partners just send over invoices and these companies approve them without a second thought.
So, Evoltus decided to pose as one of these partners, a company called Quanta Computer.
Like me, most of y'all have probably never heard of this company, so here's what they do.
Quanta is a Taiwanese manufacturer that specializes in producing enterprise hardware like servers.
They're actually super reputable in the industry as they work with basically every tech company you can think of.
This includes Apple, Dell, HP, Amazon, Cisco, LG, Sony, Microsoft, Facebook, and so much more.
So, I don't think you'd be surprised to hear that they pull in over $40 billion worth of revenue and $1.5 billion worth of profit every year.
Similarly, Google and Facebook were also not surprised when they received tabs worth a couple million dollars from Quanta.
Evaldis went ahead and created fake invoices and contracts and signed them with the names of various leaders at Quanta.
He would then send over these documents to Google and Facebook from a Quanta domain email address.
You know those random emails that you get from Apple and Amazon stating that you've been charged X amount?
Well, this is exactly what Evaldis was doing, but instead of targeting elderly folks who didn't know better for a few hundred bucks, Evaldis was targeting tech giants for millions.
Same tactic, but completely different scale.
With all the articles that these companies put out about identifying and stopping phishing, you would think that the staff at these companies would know better, but it turns out they didn't.
You see, it's not like Evaldis charged Google $23 million and Facebook $98 million in one fell swoop.
According to the Department of Justice, Evaldis would regularly send multi-million dollar invoices to these companies.
If we assume that each invoice was worth $4-5 million, Evaldis trolled Google 5 times and Facebook a laughable 20 times.
So alright, whatever, people at these companies didn't put too much scrutiny on these invoices and they approve them.
They must have some sort of established payment system with these companies, right?
So, even if they accidentally made an unnecessary payment, it would be no problem getting the money back from the real company.
Surely, these companies weren't sending tens of millions to some random ass Latvian bank accounts detailed in the invoice.
They were sending tens of millions to some random ass Latvian bank accounts detailed in the invoice.
To be honest, I'm not gonna defend of all this, but you can't feel too bad for these companies either.
There's really no one to blame but themselves and their gross negligence.
In this situation, any normal person would have no chance of any recourse.
But given the power and status of these companies, you can bet they got justice.
Evaldus was smart enough to not hold on to the money in the same account that he received it.
He would instantly spread the money across the world into bank accounts in Latvia, Cyprus, Slovakia, Lithuania, Hungary, and Hong Kong.
Considering this, it's surprising that he didn't take more precautions to secure his own freedom, especially when he's scamming big tech companies.
With all this money, he could have easily moved to a non-extraditing country like the United Arab Emirates and lived it up in Dubai.
But he would stick to Lithuania.
I guess he must have felt that he was safe behind his computer screen, and as long as the money was dispersed and untrackable, he was good.
This was of course a blunder.
As soon as Google and Facebook noticed some discrepancies in their accounting, they would identify the fraudulent charges and notify the FBI.
For the FBI, tracking down someone like Evaldus was relatively easy, and they would have him cornered in no time.
And with no plausible deniability, Evaldus would just plead guilty and eventually he'd be sentenced to 5 years in prison.
If you're wondering what happened to the money, well, Evaldice would forfeit $49 million of it, and he was ordered to pay $27 million more in restitution.
Facebook and Google would claim this as a victory as they were technically able to recover the majority of the funds, at least on paper.
It's not clear if Evaldice has paid the restitution yet or if he ever will, so that still leaves $44 to $71 million worth of stolen funds unaccounted for.
But I don't really think Google or Facebook really cares about recovering these funds.
For Google, the total stolen funds are equivalent to 3.5 hours of profit.
For Facebook, the total stolen funds are equivalent to 37 hours of profit.
So, for these companies, catching Evaldis and putting him behind bars was more about the principle and making a statement as opposed to recovering the funds.
Spending even more effort on recovering the remaining funds is really just not worth it for these companies.
So Evaldus may very well have a fortune to return to when he eventually gets released around the end of 2024.
But all of this still leaves the question, how was he able to pull off something so simple against these companies?
Well, the bright side is that while this incident is truly quite embarrassing for these companies, it's not indicative of their IT or cybersecurity.
As far as we know, their systems are still as strong and secure as ever, and this incident has little to do with anything other than gross negligence and oversight.
In the end, this story shows us that no company is truly 100% secure.
I mean, a random person in Lithuania was literally able to pull a quick one on Google and Facebook with very little skills and resources.
All he had to do was attack them when they weren't looking.
He could have gotten away with it too if he played his cards just a little better.
But who's to say that he didn't come out on top anyway?
I'm sure there's a lot of people who'd be happy to do 5 years in jail for $40-70 million and the title of successfully scamming Google and Facebook.
And that's the story of the guy who stole $120 million from Google and Facebook and nearly got away with it.

lines: Just over 20 years ago, together they formed Cisco Systems.
I think I was very frustrated.
Len was as frustrated, but probably kind of quieter about it.
These two right here stole Cisco from Stanford University.
While immoral, this is nothing out of the ordinary within the business world.
For example, Mark stole Facebook from the Winklevoss twins and Divya Narendra.
Steve Jobs stole the Mac from Xerox, and Bill Gates stole Windows, also from Xerox.
Facebook, Apple, and Microsoft are all multi-hundred billion if not multi-trillion dollar companies today.
So clearly, the punishment for stealing ideas isn't all that high in the business this world.
Worst case scenario, you might have to pay $65 million to settle a lawsuit, but this wasn't the case with Cisco.
You see, like the other victims, Stanford wasn't really able to do anything about Cisco through the legal system.
They thought about filing criminal charges against the founders, but they figured that it would just be a better idea financially and stress-wise to just license the technology to Cisco themselves.
At this point, Cisco's founders probably thought that they were in the clear, but karma often works in weird ways.
Cisco's founders would end up losing the entire company to a predatory VC firm.
Normally, you might feel bad for these people, but in this case, they really just got a taste of their own medicine.
Not to mention, it was them who brought in these VC partners, so really, there's no one to blame but themselves.
By far the worst part about all of this is that Cisco actually ended up doing extraordinarily well under VC leadership.
In fact, in the 10 years after the founders were pushed out, Cisco would grow from being a couple hundred million dollar company to being the world's largest company.
At least, the founders must have gotten a massive payday thanks to their stake in the company, right?
Psych, they actually sold their entire stake for peanuts when they were pushed out of the company out of resentment.
Clearly, they didn't enjoy being on the victim side of having Cisco stolen.
So, here's the insane story of how this couple tried to pull a quick one on Stanford only to have a quick one pulled on themselves.
Taking a look back, the story of Cisco can be traced back to a couple named Leonard Bosak and Sandy Lerner.
Naturally, they were both highly educated individuals.
Leonard had a bachelor's in engineering from the University of Pennsylvania and a master's in computer science from Stanford.
It was while he was pursuing his master's that he got the opportunity to work on a special university project.
The project entailed connecting Stanford's computer science wing and business wing through a network so that data can easily be communicated between the two.
Hey, isn't that Cisco's entire business mod anyway?
It was also around this time that he met Sandy Lerner, who was also pursuing her own master's in statistics and computer science at Stanford.
The two would get married almost instantly, and they would both get jobs at Stanford after graduation.

Leonard would become the director of the computer science wing for Stanford's business school, and Sandy would become the director of the computer science wing for Stanford's computer science department.
Most couples would call it right here, but And that was easier said than done for Sandy and Leonard.
Due to their jobs, they were constantly coming across the smartest engineers in the world and their latest inventions, which created a lot of temptations.
One such temptation was the blue box created by Andy Bechtolsheim and William Yeager.
The blue box was a simple multi-protocol router, but back in the early 1980s, this was the voodoo magic that was connecting Stanford's various departments.
Imagine what you could do with this in the real world, but unfortunately, this wasn't possible.
Stanford had made it explicitly clear that the blue box was for internal use only.
This applied to even the original founders.
In fact, William Yeager claims that his request to commercialize the invention was outright denied.
But it doesn't seem like this denial put off Leonard all that much.
In 1985, Leonard would join forces with another Stanford employee named Kirk Lockheed, and the two would basically rip off Yeager Software to create Cisco IOS.
And with that, Cisco was born, but not everyone was happy with the company.
Stanford was naturally furious.
They had specifically told even a co-founder to not commercialize the product.
Yet, here they were dealing with a couple of hothead recent graduates trying to rip off the tech.
I don't think you'd be surprised to hear that Leonard didn't keep his job at Stanford for much longer.
Stanford would turn around and threaten to file criminal complaints against Cisco for theft of software, hardware, and other intellectual property.
But after thinking about it for some time, Stanford decided to not pursue this route.
The reality was that it would be Stanford who would have to deal with years of lawsuits to prove their case just to win a PD settlement from Cisco.
So Stanford made the smarter choice and decided to just license the tech to Cisco in 1987.
At this point, they couldn't stop Cisco from commercializing the tech, so they might as well profit from it.
Leonard and Sandy probably thought that they were in the clear, but they had yet to face the real predator.
By 1987, just two years after the company was founded, Cisco was pulling in nearly $2 million per month in revenue.
Originally, the people buying their network technology was research centers, government facilities, and universities.
But slowly, more and more companies became interested and they started making big orders.
While this was great news for the company, it was also terrible news because fulfilling these orders was much easier said than done.
Unlike startups today who can just scale to the entire world using insanely powerful cloud computers, Cisco had to scale the old-fashioned way.
After all, they were producing physical routers and networking gear, so they had to deal with suppliers, manufacturers, logistics, scaling, inventory, and all of that.
This is hard enough for a consumer company to deal with, so I think you can imagine how hard it was for a startup to fulfill orders of 10,000 or 30,000 routers.
So, Cisco really had no choice but to raise venture capital.
In 1988, they would approach the famous Sequoia Capital to give them some extra cash to grow the company.
Sequoia would happily give them cash the first time around, but this cash didn't even last 12 months.
And it wasn't long until Cisco was asking Sequoia for more, which Sequoia wasn't exactly comfortable with.
This was not long after Black Monday, so the stock market wasn't exactly performing great.
Not to mention, Sequoia had just given them money.
For Sequoia to get even more involved, they needed more assurance that this company would actually make it to the other side.
So, they proposed the deal.
Sequoia would continue funding Cisco if Cisco gave them controlling voting power and allowed for Sequoia's founder, Don Valentine, to become the chairman of the company.
Obviously, this was a pretty aggressive ask, but Cisco had no time to shop around for more money.
It was either take the deal with Sequoia or gamble with the company's life.
Leonard and Sandy of course chose to take the deal, and from a financial perspective, it worked out great.
By 1989, Cisco would expand to 3 products, 111 employees, and a cool $27 million in revenue.
But all of this, of course, came with a price.
They now had to deal with Don Valentine, who wasn't exactly a friend.
This isn't to say that Don didn't have Cisco's best interest in mind.
The problem was that that was the only interest he had in mind.
Frankly, he didn't care about Leonard or Sandy.
He had poured a lot of money into this startup and he was gonna make sure that it panned out.
To increase the chances of this happening, he would go ahead and hire a computer veteran named John Morgridge as the company's new CEO.
Leonard would be demoted to the role of chief scientist, which wasn't too bad.
Sandy though was demoted to the role of, wait for it, leading customer service.
At this point, Don Valentine was straight up insulting the founders and things would only get worse.
In February of 1990, Cisco would go public and enjoy a roaring IPO.
The company would close off the first day of trading with a market cap of $224 million, which made the founders centimillionaires.
Not a bad sum of money, but the company was just getting started.
They had just barely escaped the funding crunch, and the companies were just starting to leverage their tech.
So, they had a bright future ahead in the billions and tens of billions.
But it seems that Don may have had some ulterior motives when it came to taking Cisco public.
You see, Leonard and Sandy now had an easy way to sell their stakes, so it became that much easier for Don to push out the founders, and that's exactly what he would do.
On August 28, 1990, Don and John would straight up fire Sandy.
Leonard would instantly resign thinking that it would be some sort of protest, but Don didn't give a crap.
The reality was that Cisco didn't need Sandy or Leonard to be successful.
After all, they didn't even invent the technology.
To make things worse, Don and John felt that Sandy and Leonard were completely incompetent.
In fact, during Sandy's first meeting with John, he would tell her quote, I hear that you're everything that's wrong with Cisco.
Cisco.
This bad blood only increased over time as John felt that the founders had no clue about sales.
He felt that the only reason Cisco was even able to grow so far was thanks to companies that would go out of their way to have the latest and greatest.
Cisco was by no means appealing to the average company which is where the money really was.
And considering that Cisco would literally grow a thousand decks over the past 10 years under his leadership, it looks like he was right.
So, to be honest, when Leonard resigned, Don probably didn't think, oh no, I lost a co-founder.
Instead, he probably thought, great, two birds with one stone.
Leonard and Sandy should have taken the hint, stepped away, and just enjoyed their lives, but they wanted to send Don a message that they didn't need Cisco either.
And with that, they would go ahead and sell their entire 66% stake for $170 million.
That may have felt good at the time, but it was objectively a brain-dead decision.
I mean, it's not like they needed the money or that they didn't believe in the future of the company.
There was literally nothing to the sale other than ego and resentment, and they would be the ones who ended up paying the price.
Ten years later, Cisco would become the world's largest company with a market cap of $569 billion.
This means that their 66% stake would have been worth $375 billion.
Even if we assume that they sold off 46% of their stake, the remaining 20% would be worth over $100 billion.
Yup, they done diddly do screwed up.
Shortly after the whole Cisco fiasco, Sandy and Leonard's marriage would also fall apart, and this was really the rock bottom for these two.
But I do gotta say, they did pull themselves back up and focused on giving away the money that they did receive.
They would donate 70% of the proceeds to charities focused on promoting animal welfare and science projects.
If you ask the duo about Cisco today, they have some pretty diverse answers.
Leonard plays it off pretty cool and simply says that they walked away with a bunch of money anyways, so there's nothing to regret.
As for For Sandy however, she's understandably still pretty triggered about the situation.
Len and I underestimated our skills.
I certainly could have run that business.
I had my hands on the reins.
If you're wondering what happened to the original founders of the blue box, well, Andy Bechtelsheim would go on to found Sun Microsystems and he now boasts in that worth of over $10 billion.
So looks like he didn't need the blue box to make it big.
The only ones regretting their choices today is the ones who tried stealing.
