The hole in this plan is that when it comes to social highways, people are always moving cities.
What Mark really wanted was to control something like the internet, but it was obviously impossible for Facebook to take over the internet itself in the late 2010s.
If they wanted to control something so large, the only option was to get in early into the next internet.
And this brings us into Mark's obsession with virtual reality or the metaverse.
Things didn't start off hopeless for the metaverse.
In fact, they started off pretty bright actually.
Oculus was by far the most respected player within the VR scene and hardcore gamers loved their products, but there was one major limiting factor, cost.
Oculus headsets were simply unaffordable for the masses.
The Oculus Rift came in at $600, which in itself isn't cheap, but that was by no means the only expense.
The Rift was a tethered headset, meaning that it had to be connected to a PC to function.

Of course, you could connect the headset to your beaten up laptop, but if you wanted any sort of meaningful VR experience, you had to buy a multi-thousand dollar PC, which just wasn't practical for the average Joe.
So, Zuckerberg decided to address this concern head on with the Meta Quest 2, which came in at a mere $300- $400, no PC required.
Suddenly, the price of VR was comparable to that of a gaming console.
In fact, it was cheaper than most gaming consoles.
The main reason for this was that Meta was taking massive losses on these units, but that was okay.
They just wanted everyone to buy and use the darn thing, and they could figure out how to monetize later.
Initially, it seemed like their plan was playing out perfectly.
Given the hype around VR and the relatively affordable price of the MetaQuest 2, people were buying it in the masses.
In fact, Meta has sold nearly 20 million of these headsets.
But there was just one teensy tiny problem.
No one was using the headsets.
People would buy it, try it out for a few days, and then use it as a dust collector indefinitely.
Why, you ask?
Well, the biggest reason is simply that the experience just sucks.
The entire point of VR is to have an immersive, almost real-life experience.
And the only way to do that is to use powerful NVIDIA GPUs paired with airplane jet engines as coolers.
When you try to do the same thing with an iPhone chip for $400, well, a 360-degree Mi world is what you get.
The hardware was so limited that Meta couldn't even produce legs for your avatars, much less make them look realistic.
In fact, they couldn't even produce legs for demonstration purposes.
They would end up cheating using pre-rendered animations.
And don't even get me started on the enterprise side of things.
Mark was selling the metaverse as a way for business professionals to conduct more authentic virtual meetings that felt like real life.
Not a bad idea in theory, but with graphics like this, these meetings by no means felt professional and genuine.
If anything, they felt childish and out of place in a corporate setting, not to mention expensive.
Unsurprisingly, virtually every company has decided to stick with Teams and Zoom.
We should mention that after receiving all this negative feedback about lackluster immersion, Meta would come out with a higher-end headset called the MetaQuest Pro for $1,500.
But by the time this headset came out, the pros were already out and the reputation of the metaverse had already been tarnished.
Not to mention, the Pro wasn't all that much better to begin with.
So, let's just say, the MetaQuest Pro wasn't received very well and Meta would end up slashing the price by $500 just 5 months after release, marking the beginning of the end.
There's really no way to sugarcoat it.
Meta is pulling back on the metaverse hard, and it's no wonder why.
They're far from producing the tech and experience they want to.
Developing the metaverse is taking a massive toll on the company's bottom line and stock price, and the reputation of the metaverse is beyond repair.
Now, of course, if you ask Zuckerberg, he'll tell you that they're by no means ditching the metaverse, but all of the evidence is against this.
For starters, Meta has laid off a quarter of their workforce.
With a median salary of $300,000, this is saving Facebook roughly $6.3 billion every year.
Seems counterintuitive for someone who's planning on investing $100 billion into the metaverse.
But likely the best evidence that Meta is indeed moving away from the metaverse is the fact that Zuckerberg has become obsessed with something else, AI.
According to Meta's CTO Andrew Bosworth, Mark, Meta's chief product officer Chris Cox, and him are all spending most of their time working on AI, and more specifically, generative AI.
It seems that Mark has very much gotten caught up with the chat GPT hype, and he wants to get a piece of the action.
Meta has even announced their own large language model called LAMA and they're currently working on releasing this to researchers.
Bosworth has also confirmed that they're working on releasing a commercial AI product by the end of this year.
All of this may seem a bit confusing.
It seemed like Zuckerberg was super gung-ho about the metaverse.
So, how did he pivot so quickly?
Well, the reality is simply that Meta's commitment to the metaverse was simply overhyped by the media.
In fact, the metaverse wasn't even Zuckerberg's first attempt to pivot Facebook away from social media.
Before he got obsessed with VR, Zuckerberg was actually trying to build a space business.
He was launching a bunch of solar-powered drones and atmospheric satellites with the goal of trying to create satellite-based internet similar to Starlink today.
But as he saw that this wasn't picking up any steam and that SpaceX was going to do it themselves, Zuckerberg didn't hesitate to kill off the program completely and switch to the metaverse.
So, who's to say that Zuckerberg isn't willing to do the same thing with the metaverse?
Given that the metaverse was much more consumer oriented and futuristic than their space plan, it garnered a lot more media attention.
But for Facebook, it was just another attempt to break free from social media.
By now though, it's become clear that this path is not so viable and they're accordingly pulling back substantially.
This isn't to say that Meta is completely ditching the metaverse quite yet.
They're still pouring resources into the idea, but they're by no means adamant to sticking to just that.
If they can get something else to work instead, like AI, even better.
The bottom line is that Meta has become a mature social media company, meaning that they only have two paths moving forward.
They can either go all in on social media, optimize their operations, and become a dividend giant.
Or they can try to hit the next big thing.
With his performance over the past six months, Zuckerberg has made it clear that he can achieve the former at any time within a matter of 12 months if he wants to.
But what he really wants is the latter.
He wants to grow meta to the next magnitude and the only way to do that is to hit a grand slam.

He took a few swings at the metaverse and looks like he struck out, but being only 38 years old with majority control over the 8th largest company in the world, I assure you, He has a lot of swings left.
So, while people love mocking the metaverse, it's Zuckerberg that's getting the last laugh.

title: How Founders Became Tyrants
note: Opens with a Jobs anecdote and present-day examples, defines dual-class stock, then tells a historical ban-and-revival story through the NYSE and NASDAQ.
sections: Cold open: Jobs fired and modern founder control
Early dual-class history and Dodge IPO ban
NASDAQ's struggle and pivot to dual class
lines: Founders have dictatorized companies.
Back on September 16th, 1985, Steve Jobs was fired from his own company, Apple.
Fans like to argue that this was completely unjust and unfair, and from a moral perspective, they may be right.
It is unfair to kick out a founder from their own company, but it was also the right decision.
While Apple did get destroyed over the next decade, Steve Jobs had the opportunity to grow as a leader, a family man, and as a visionary.
And when he returned 12 years later, he was able to make Apple into the world's largest company.
Looking back, even Jobs himself has agreed that getting fired was the medicine that he needed.
This isn't to say that all founders should be fired from their companies to be grounded and put in their place.
But what it does show is that even the smartest minds in the world are just straight up wrong from time to time.
And this is precisely why large public companies have boards, chairmen, shareholders, and an entire executive team.
The idea is that there is a system of checks and balances that ensures that no single person becomes too powerful, but this is no longer the case.
Modern companies still have boards and investors and executive teams, but all of that is just for show.
At the end of the day, the person who has all the power is the founder or founders.
Now, this is no problem if we're talking about a private company or the given founders have a stake of over 50%.
But with modern tech giants, neither of these are the case.
Take Mark Zuckerberg for example.
Over the past few years, he's been gambling tens tens of billions on the metaverse, something that investors haven't exactly been excited about.
To make things worse, much of the launched metaverse products have flopped beyond belief, boasting as little as just 38 users.
All of this has given Zuckerberg a favorability rating of just 22% or only half of even Donald Trump.
This is precisely the type of situation in which a CEO would be fired, but Mark doesn't have to worry about that.
You see, Mark only owns 13.6% of Meta, not much more than Steve Jobs' stake of 11% when he was fired.
So, nowhere near a majority, but see, modern founders have learned from their predecessors.
They know what can happen if they give away majority control.
So, while they may give away a majority stake in their company, they never give away majority control.
How, you ask?
Well, they've brilliantly made a distinction between equity and voting power.
While Zuckerberg only owns 13% of Meta, he controls 54% of its voting power.
A similar story can be seen with Google.
At this point, Larry Page only owns 6.1% and Sergey Brin only owns 5.7%.
But together, they control 51.2% of Google's voting power.

This means that despite having single-digit stakes, this duo has ultimate control of a $1.3 trillion company with 180,000 employees, tens of millions of investors, and billions of users, as this is the story of how founders abused their power.
This is the story of how founders dictatorized companies.
The root of modern-day founders power is thanks to multiple classes of stock with different voting power.
Class A stock might come along with one vote per share, while class B stock comes along with 10 votes per share.
The average investor doesn't even realize this, but many companies actually have different classes of stock on the public market itself.
Likely the best example of this is none other than Google.
If you look up Google on your brokerage, you may come across the following listing, Alphabet Inc.
Class C, ticker symbol GOOG.
At first glance, it looks like Google stock.
The market cap checks out, the PE ratio checks out, the price looks about right, and that's because it is technically Google stock.
But what it isn't is Google stock with voting rights.
This means that you can buy a billion of these shares and invest $100 billion, but you wouldn't even get a single vote.
If you want voting power, you need to buy Alphabet Inc.
Class A stock or ticker symbol GOOGL.
Basically, everything about this share is identical to the Class C shares, except you'll get one vote for every share that you own.
But the shares that you really want are Class B shares.
With Class B shares, you get 10 votes for every share you own.
But you can look all you want on any brokerage you can find, but you'll never find Class B Google shares.
This is because Class B shares are reserved for founders, VC firms, and other close insiders.
Most investors don't look into this too much.
They figure that their 1,000 or even 100,000 votes won't really make a difference at Google.
And they're right, as an individual, they can't really make a difference at these companies.
But the fact that one or two people have all the votes that everyone else gives up does make a difference.
And that's why multi-class stock structures were banned for over 50 years.
You see, dual class and multi-class stock or DCS are by no means a new invention.
It's actually been around for well over 100 years, but it was a frowned upon invention.
The first American company to issue multi-class stock was the International Silver Company back in 1898.
Originally, this wasn't considered to be a big deal.
Founders wanted a bit more control over their companies.
And given that information wasn't nearly as accessible as it is today, it made sense for investors to be more passive.
But over time, founders started becoming more more and more aggressive.
What started off as 1 extra vote became 5 extra votes, and then 10 extra votes, and then 20 extra votes.
This practice only became worse with the roaring 1920s as everyday people started buying stocks.
They didn't care about voting shares or earnings reports, they just wanted to be a part of the Rockefeller fortune or the Ford fortune.
This gave companies plenty of room to test the boundaries until one company pushed it way too far, Dodge Motor Company.
In 1925, Dodge would have one of the most infamous IPOs of all time.
They would exclusively issue shares with absolutely no voting power.
This meant that insiders could own just a single share of stock and retain 100% voting power, and that's pretty much what they did too.
The insiders owned just 1.7% of the company, but they had absolute control over the company.
Investors were obviously pissed and this led to an uproar on Wall Street.
The New York Stock Exchange would end up siding with investors and in 1926, they would officially ban dual class stock.
This is where the story should have ended, but this practice has not only been revived, but it has taken over the market once again.
Throughout the next 54 years, the stock market operated perfectly fine.
Billionaire founders were made, millionaire investors were made, and everyone had completely forgotten that dual class stock was even a thing.
But this would all change on February 8th, 1971.
This was the day that the NASDAQ was created.
If you're not familiar with the NASDAQ, you should check out our video about them, but long story short, they technolify the stock market.
Before the NASDAQ, investors had to call stockbrokers at the NYSE to place buy and sell orders, and everything would be done manually.
But with the NASDAQ, the entire stock market was slowly made electronic, paving the road for how it is today.
This was obviously the superior technology, but investors weren't impressed.
They couldn't care less if quotes and trades were electronic or not.
In fact, they preferred to call a broker that they knew and trusted for 20 or 30 years.
So, despite offering great tech, the NASDAQ struggled to get investors throughout the 1970s.
To make things worse, the NYSE had started ripping off NASDAQ's tech, and they were rapidly modernizing their own systems.
So, things looked pretty bleak for the NASDAQ.
investors weren't using the exchange and their main advantage was rapidly disappearing.
So, in the early 1980s, they would decide to pivot their strategy.
Instead of trying to attract investors, they started going after companies.
If companies were exclusively listed on the Nasdaq, investors had no choice but to buy through the Nasdaq.
With that, the Nasdaq started charging far lower fees than the NYSE for companies, and they still do this to this day, but this too didn't work.
You see, there was a certain prestige and heritage to the NYSE.
JPMorgan Chase wasn't gonna switch exchanges just because you charged less.
So, the NASDAQ was back to ground zero.
They were worse off actually as they were now earning lower fees as well.
Throughout all of this, the NASDAQ couldn't help but notice that one exchange was actually succeeding at taking on the NYSE, the Amex, not American Express, but the American Stock Exchange.
One of the main factors that distinguished the Amex from the NYSE was their policy on dual class stock.
The Amex allowed for DCS with a voting ratio of up to 10 to 1.
The Nasdaq didn't have any DCS restrictions to begin with, but now they knew that this was precisely what they needed to lean into.
There were two target markets with this strategy.
The first was tech companies who were fearful that investors weren't really informed on tech, which was very much true at the time.
The second was companies that were targets of corporate ratings.
If these companies were able to distinguish between ownership and voting power, they could protect themselves from corporate raters.
Given that corporate rating was at its peak throughout the 80s and that tech stocks would go vertical in the 90s, the NASDAQ would also go vertical.
Seeing this, companies listed on the NYSE would threaten to switch to the NASDAQ if they didn't allow for DCS.
And with that, the NYSE had no choice but to unban DCS in 1986.
With that being said though, companies were pretty reasonable in the early days.
In fact, some notable NASDAQ companies didn't even opt for dual class shares like Apple and Microsoft.
But there's always someone who ruins it for everyone else, and in the case of dual-class stock, it was our good old friends Google and Facebook.
Nowadays, most tech companies opt for a dual-class structure because, I mean, why wouldn't they?
The average investor isn't even aware of it.
The practice has been normalized, and it gives founders ultimate control.
It's one of those things where it's like, If no one is opposing it, why would you not do it?
Some notable tech companies who have adopted this practice are Snapchat, Dropbox, Lyft, Kayak, Robinhood, Coinbase, Zoom, Roku, and TripAdvisor.
But this practice is by no means limited to tech companies.
Some legacy companies leveraging DCS include Coca-Cola, Ford, Nike, Levi, and Hyatt Hotels.
Also, don't bet on media companies to report on this issue, as the most notable ones leverage it themselves including the New York Times, Fox News, CBS, and Comcast.
And there are of course extreme examples as well.
The Ford family, for example, owns 4% of the stock but controls 40% of the voting power.
Similarly, EchoStar CEO Charlie Ergen owns 5% of the company but controls 90% of the vote.
So, let's just say, things have gotten pretty bad, but I do want to point out some notable exceptions, starting with Amazon.
While Jeff Bezos gets a bunch of critique for his practices, this is not one of them.
It turns out that he's actually pretty loyal to shareholders.
Another exception is Elon Musk and Tesla.
In fact, this is why Elon was able to be forced to give up his chairman position back in 2018.
And as for a startup that's going against the trend, we have Uber.
So, the good news is that some companies are doing the right thing.
Also, the S &P 500 is putting up some resistance as well.
Starting in 2017, they ruled that companies with multi-class stock will no longer be added to the S &P 500.
This is the main reason that many notable startups like Snapchat have been unable to join the index despite their size.
And given that index fund investing is on the rise, newer companies will very much be losing out if they're not part of the index.
Will this be enough to stop their practice altogether?
Probably not, but it is a step in the right direction.

title: Apple’s $573 Billion Bet (& Are They Going Private)
note: Guessing-game hook about Apple's spend, then a historical explainer of buybacks (ban and legalization) before returning to Apple and the going-private myth.
sections: Great Depression origins and the ban
lines: Apple has invested $573 billion into this over the past 10 years.
Can you guess what this is?
Maybe R &D?
Well, Apple spends about $6-7 billion per quarter on R &D.
So, while that adds up to about $250 billion over a 10-year period, that's less than half of this other investment.
Maybe they spent it on acquisitions?
Well, Apple only has two acquisitions that even cross the billion dollar mark, Beats, and Intel smartphone modem business, so nowhere near $573 billion.
Maybe they've just been hoarding a crap ton of cash, while Apple has actually been decreasing their cash reserves consistently from over $100 billion down to just over $50 billion.
Okay, then maybe it's the total value of all of Apple's assets?
Well, while Apple's assets do tower at an impressive $350 billion, it still falls over $200 billion short of $573 billion.
But then, if Apple didn't spend this money on R &D, acquisitions, cash reserves, or investments, where the hell did such a ginormous amount of money go?
Well, it turns out that Apple's biggest bet over the past 10 years is actually stock buybacks.
That's right, Apple has spent $573 billion over the past 10 years on stock buybacks.
For perspective, that's enough money to buy a fortune 10 company cash.
In second place, we have Microsoft who comes in at a measly $170 billion over the past 10 years or over $400 billion less.
It looks like this disparity is only going to grow larger as Apple is simply doubling down.
In fact, nowadays, Apple is spending nearly $100 billion on stock buybacks every single year.
Assuming that this continues to increase, Apple will spend over a trillion dollars on buybacks over the next 10 years.
This has sparked rumors regarding whether Apple is trying to go private.
But more importantly, it has raised concerns about whether this is healthy for the economy.

Instead of investing this money into creating new products, creating new jobs, or even just storing it in cash or bonds where it can be lent out, Apple has decided to spend half a trillion dollars on inflating their stock price.
So, here's the story of how a once-banned practice became so popular and why companies are throwing trillions at buybacks every single year.
The reasoning behind why companies love stock buybacks is not rocket science.
By purchasing shares from the market and burning them, companies are not only adding demand to the market, but they're also reducing supply.
So, thanks to basic supply and demand economics, this dynamic leads to stock prices going up.
Aside from boosting the stock price, buybacks also boost the benefits of being a shareholder.
For example, let's say that Apple had a total of 100 shares of stock and that you owned 10 of them.
This means that you own 10% of the company, but what if Apple came in and eliminated 20 of these shares by buying them back.
Well, you still only own 10 shares, but since the total number of shares has decreased to 80, you now own 12.5% of Apple.
This means that you'll now get 12.5% of the dividends, 12.5% of the voting power, and so on and so forth.
So, it's no wonder why companies and shareholders love buybacks, but the impact of buybacks on the economy is not so bright.
This is why stock buybacks were banned for over 50 years up until 1981.
You see, the idea of companies buying back their own stock is by no means a new one.
It's only natural that once a company runs out of external places to invest, they turn to investing in themselves.
But ironically, the roots of buybacks actually trace back to times of despair as opposed to times of prosperity to the Great Depression.
A lot of activists who are not a fan of buybacks like to claim that stock buybacks are what led to the Great Depression in the first place, but this is not true.
The primary reasons for the Great Depression were simply excessive speculation paired with excessive levels of debt.
But while buybacks did not cause the depression, the depression did cause buybacks, and buybacks only made the depression worse.
For obvious reasons, investors became frantic when the Dow Jones crashed 90% within a matter of three years.
They demanded that executives put up strong quarterly reports, increase dividends, and basically defy the economic situation.
Understandably, this was simply not possible for most companies given the economic landscape.
But what they were able to do was provide investors some solace through buybacks.
While this did not change the fact that most investors were down a ridiculous amount, it did ensure that they could maximize the wealth that they did still have.
So, buybacks quickly became the go-to way to pander to shareholders during the depths of the Great Depression.
But this was terrible for the economy.
To escape the depression, America needed corporations to invest in employees, factories, and R &D.
But instead, companies were spending the little money they did have on superficial avenue.
This went on for a couple of years until the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
This legislation wasn't targeted at stock buybacks specifically.
In fact, it doesn't even mention buybacks.
Rather, it was designed to prevent the depression from happening again by putting some checks and balances in place.
One of these checks and balances was that companies were not allowed to manipulate their own stock price.
Technically, there was no mention of stock buybacks, so that was more of a gray area, but no company was brave enough to test the SEC.
So, the practice of stock buybacks simply disappeared into oblivion.
It would've been great if it stayed that way, but that obviously wasn't the case.
For the next few decades, no one even mentioned the idea of stock buybacks.
The entire world was in recovery mode both from the Great Depression and World War II.
America was also super focused on showing up the USSR with capitalism, up.
So, allowing corporations to inefficiently spend their reserves on buybacks was out of the question.
But as the stock market blew past its pre-depression highs and America landed people on the moon, Congress became a lot more relaxed.
They were no longer out to prove something, they had already come out on top.
So, now they were able to focus on personal gain.
And what's the easiest way to make money as a politician?
Well, the answer is to align yourself with the richest business people and corporations around the world.
This coincided with yet another economic disaster, the inflation crisis of the 1970s.
In the early 1970s, President Nixon would end the gold standard, meaning that US dollars were no longer backed by gold.
This led to inflation spiraling out of control, the stock market stagnating, and interest rates rising to a painful 19%.
So, when President Ronald Reagan stepped in and suggested doubling down on capitalism, people were more receptive than ever.
The logic was that capitalism is what saved America from the Great Depression and made America into a world power.
So if we wanted to get back on track, we should just let capitalism do its magic.
With that, President Reagan would enact a slew of pro-capitalist legislation, now known as Reaganomics.
This included things like slashing personal income tax from 70% down to 28%, reducing corporate tax from 48% down to 34%, and easing regulations substantially.
One of these regulation reducing moves was rule 10b-18, introduced by the SEC in 1982.
As you may have already guessed, this rule created a safe harbor for stock buybacks as long as companies abided by four stipulations.
These stipulations governed when, where, and how companies were allowed to buy back stock, but complying with these rules is actually completely voluntary.
As we previously touched on, the SEC never actually outright banned stock buybacks.
So, companies could still try to push the limits and buy back stock without following these stipulations.
But given that they're pretty easy stipulations to follow, no one has really ever pushed the boundaries.
And with that, stock buybacks were officially legal once again, but the practice didn't catch on as quickly as you might expect.
You see, back in the 1980s, value investing was way more popular than growth investing.
And one of the key attributes that value investors were looking for was a strong and increasing dividend.
So, whenever companies had extra cash lying around, they far preferred to just pay out larger dividends than buyback stock.
Not to mention, companies used to have much more modest profit margins of 10-20%.
So they couldn't meaningfully buy back a substantial portion of the company anyway, but all of this would change with the rise of tech.
Over time, the mentality of corporations and shareholders slowly shifted, and this is beautifully documented by statements from the Business Roundtable which is a coalition of top CEOs.
In 1981, this was the purpose of corporations as defined by these CEOs.

Corporations have a responsibility, first of all, to make available to the public quality goods and services at fair prices, thereby earning a profit that attracts investments to continue and enhance the enterprise, provide jobs, and build the economy.
But by 1997, this was the new purpose of corporations as defined by these CEOs.
The principal objective of a business enterprise is to generate economic returns to its owners.
If the CEO and the directors are not focused on shareholder value, it may be less likely the corporation will realize that value.
This probably sounds familiar as this is how companies are run today.
The sole purpose of most companies and executives today is to serve shareholders as best as possible.
So, stock buyback started looking more and more favorable.
But again, no company could afford to spend tens if not hundreds of billions on stock buybacks until Apple, or actually more specifically, the iPhone.
Apple didn't instantly turn to stock buybacks either though.
For the first five years after the launch of the iPhone, they had plenty of expenses regarding scaling production, marketing, and R &D.
But by 2013, Apple had achieved a pretty strong financial position leading to their first stock buyback.
Apple was by no means shy.
They didn't start off with a modest $1 or $2 billion buyback.
They went straight for a $10 billion stock buyback in 2012.
And less than 12 months later, they would announce a record-breaking stock buyback of $60 billion.
And that was it.
From then on out, Apple has been the undisputed king of stock buybacks, pouring in tens of billions into buybacks every single year.
All of this brings up the question, is Apple trying to go private and is that even possible?
Well, with Apple's market cap ballooning to $2-3 trillion, it's becoming less and less possible.
But in the late 2010s, it was very much possible.
In fact, in 2017, Apple was on track to buy back 50% of itself by 2020.
So, going private was not out of reach per se, but this was never part of the plan.
You see, when Apple buys back shares, they're not putting these shares in some sort of company treasury.
Rather, they're burning the shares and removing it from the supply.
So, the shares that Apple is buying back are basically being donated to all shareholders in proportion to their ownership.
So, with that being said, Apple is by no means going private and that is just a myth.
People are often critical of stock buybacks, but the reality is that stock buybacks are just the tip of the iceberg.
The bigger underlying trend is that the entire purpose of corporations is shifting.
Originally, the purpose of corporations was to create value in the marketplace while generating a respectable profit.
But nowadays, the sole purpose of corporations is to serve shareholders no matter the cost.
Stock buybacks are just one example of this trend, but they're by no means the only issue.
With that being said though, it doesn't seem like this trend will be changing anytime soon because that's not in the executives' best interest.
You see, as companies engage in stock buybacks, lobby for lower taxes, lobby for less regulation, and maximize profits, shareholders are much more willing to pay executives more and more.
Back in 1965, the average CEO was paid 20 times the average worker at the company.
Today, the average CEO is paid 399 times the average worker at the same company.
So, as long as this ratio keeps increasing, you can bet that Apple and every other company will continue betting big on stock buybacks.

title: Why Microsoft Has Willingly Given Up On Trying To Innovate
note: Paradox hook, then a strategic history in phases: penetration, domination, failed innovation, Nadella's acquisitions, concluding with the holding-company answer.
sections: Cold open: Microsoft stopped innovating but thrives
Phase two: market domination (Internet Explorer, bundling)
Decade of failure: Zune and Windows Phone
Satya Nadella and the acquisition era
lines: Microsoft has given up on trying to innovate.
This is usually a terrible sign for companies.
We've seen countless examples of juggernauts being toppled over due to a lack of innovation, from Nokia and Xerox to Blockbuster and Yahoo.
But this doesn't seem to be hurting Microsoft.
In fact, at this point, they haven't been innovating for quite some time.
Microsoft is the only tech giant that hasn't created a revolutionary product within the past 10 to 20 years.
Apple has the iPhone, Google has Chrome, Amazon has AWS, Tesla has electric self-driving cars, and even Meta is trying with the Metaverse.
But what about Microsoft?
Microsoft is still really only known for two products, Windows and Microsoft Office.
And it's been nearly 40 years since Windows was released and over 30 years since Office was released.
For those of you commenting that they created ChatGPT, they didn't create that.
They bought it.
And this is really the secret behind their success over the past 15 years.
They've been trying to buy themselves to the top.
Historically speaking though, on innovative companies, buying innovative companies doesn't usually work out.
Likely the most notable example of this in recent history is GE.
Back in the late 2000s, they did everything from jet engine manufacturing and financing to producing appliances and pumping gas.
But eventually, this became way too much to handle, and GE would end up shrinking their investments from $781 billion to $164 billion.
dollars.
They've even spun off into three different companies to try to lower the burden.
So, little to say, you can't just buy yourself to the top.
But Microsoft seems to be the exception as they've been doing better than ever.
In the past 5 years alone, their revenue has doubled, their net income has tripled, and their stock?
Well, their stock has grown 10x within the past 10 years.
For perspective, that's the same amount that Apple has grown and they've had the mobile revolution on their side.
So, has Microsoft cracked the code to eternal life or are they going to end up like GE?
Taking a look back, the reality is that Microsoft has never been innovated with their products.
The key to their success has always been brilliant business strategies and marketing, as opposed to actually creating the next big thing.
This is true for even Windows and Office.
Windows was ripped off from the Mac, which was ripped off from Xerox.
So, the product itself wasn't all that innovative, but what was innovative was Microsoft's go-to-market strategy.
Instead of limiting their software to a specific piece of hardware, they made it compatible with basically everything.
Not only did they make Windows compatible with everything, they also made Windows accessible to everyone by actively encouraging piracy.
And if you don't believe me, here's Bill Gates on the topic.
Sort of a, as long as they're going to steal it, we want them to steal ours.
I sort of get addicted and then we somehow figure out how to collect sometime in the next the next decade.
So, you know, it's a great, great place to be involved in.
And it was a lot of fun, which was, I guess, the key.
As you can see, the key to Microsoft's early success was simply extraordinary market penetration.

While not everyone was paying off the bat, this strategy gave Microsoft unbelievable market control, which they were eventually able to monetize by licensing to PC makers, corporations, universities, and governments.
This was really phase one of Microsoft's rise, they were able to successfully substitute market penetration for innovation.
Moving on to phase 2, we would see Microsoft substitute market domination for innovation.
The first notable example of this was Internet Explorer.
Microsoft saw the explosive success of the internet back in the early 90s with AOL and Netscape, and they decided they wanted a piece the pie.
So, in 1995, Microsoft would go ahead and launch IE, but again, there was nothing particularly special about IE.
It was just a run-of-the-mill browser with an even less inspiring name.
I mean, it was literally named Internet Explorer.
At least, there's no confusion about what it does, I guess.
But none of this mattered because Microsoft once again had an effective strategy to get the product to people.
The strategy was to simply bundle in IE with Windows.
Sure, people could go out and download whatever browser they wanted after they buy the computer.
But back in the late 1990s, people were just then getting their first computers, so most people had no baseline or prior expectations.
Everything was new to them, so they might as well stick with the browser that's already there.
This would lead to IE's market share rising to 95% by 2003 and a slew of antitrust lawsuits, but that's a whole other story.
The takeaway here is that IE wasn't successful because it was innovative.
IE was successful because Microsoft was able to leverage their domination with Windows.
Microsoft would use this same strategy on a few more products throughout the late 90s and early 2000s.
MSN Search for example was decently popular because it was pushed by IE which was pushed by Windows.
The same thing could be said about Hotmail and MSN Messenger and basically all of Microsoft's other products during this time period.
But if you read the news at the time, you would see headlines that yes, Microsoft was a monopoly, but also that they were the most innovative tech company in the world.
And let's just say, Microsoft would let this go to their ahead.
By the end of the 1990s, Microsoft had become the world's largest company and they were synonymous with tech.
Fun fact, Microsoft is the only top 10 company from the year 2000 that's still a top 10 company today.
But maintaining this level of success was by no means an easy feat.
In fact, the next 10 years would be the decade of failure for Microsoft as they would try to innovate, and their inability to innovate would really shine through.
The first notable example of this came in 2006 with the Microsoft Zune.
Most of you have probably never even heard about the Zune, and the main reason for this was that it was such a massive flop.
The Zune was essentially Microsoft's answer to the iPod, but there were a lot of fundamental issues with the Zune, starting with timing.
For starters, the Zune came out 5 years after the original iPod, meaning that the iPod was already the go-to product for most people.
So, Microsoft was fighting an uphill battle from day one, but that doesn't necessarily have to be a bad thing.
Plenty of successful products came out super late like Chrome, Gmail, and Zoom.
But the reason that these products were able to take over was because they were categorically better than the competition.
The same could not be said about the Zune.
The Zune was by no means a bad product.
In fact, users liked it just as much as the iPod, and it costed the same as the iPod.
But this was also the biggest problem.
If it's identical to the iPod, who would buy it over the iPod, which was already the popular thing?
Well, the answer is no one, and Microsoft would cancel the Zune just a few years later.
Microsoft should have learned from this and approached smartphones from a different strategy, but Microsoft would go ahead and make a fool of themselves not much later.
I mean, just listen to former Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer's reaction to the iPhone.
$500 fully subsidized with a plan?
I said, that is the most expensive phone in the world, and it doesn't appeal to business customers because it doesn't have a keyboard, which makes it not a very good email machine.
Now, to his credit, he did clarify that it might sell really well.
But if that's the case, you probably shouldn't be laughing at it.
It may sell very well or not.
We have our strategy.
We've got great Windows Mobile devices in the market today.
You can get a Motorola Q phone now for $99.
It's a very capable machine.
Instead, you should be looking at why it might sell well, who will be buying the product, and how you can get a piece of the pie.
Microsoft was in the perfect position to become the Windows of the smartphone world, but instead they would let Google take the spot.
In the meantime, Microsoft would sit around for 3 years and come out with the Windows phone in 2010.
The worst part though was the OS.
The reason the iPhone was so successful was not because it was a small computer, but because it was a reimagined small computer.
Every single application, interaction, and gesture were reimagined to work on a smaller screen with fingers instead of a mouse.
You could say that Apple was indeed innovating.
With the Windows phone on the other hand, we basically got a beta version of Windows 8 on a smaller screen.

unsurprisingly the windows phone would not only be a humiliating failure but also an expensive one but unlike with the zoon microsoft would actually learn from the windows phone and let's just say they've turned things around big time Usually, companies have quite an ego when it comes to acknowledging or acquiring a competitor.
They usually want to do everything themselves.
This was very much the case with Microsoft as well.
Instead of working with AOL and Netscape, Microsoft decided to compete against them.
Instead of working with the iPod and iPhone, Microsoft decided to compete against Apple.
But all of this would change in early 2014 when Satya Nadella took over the company.
Satya was very different from his peer CEOs.
Most tech CEOs are world class in specific fields.
Tim Cook, for example, is world class at supply chain and operations.
Similarly, Sundar Pichai is the technical genius behind Chrome.
home.
Satya, on the other hand, wasn't an expert in any one field, nor did he go to IIT in India or Stanford and Harvard.
This is by no means to say that Satya was incompetent, but the biggest characteristic he brought to the table was not a technical skill.
Rather, it was humility.
He had the humility to accept that younger, newer companies were simply doing things better.
And instead of trying to resist like his predecessors, he was going to embrace leading to Microsoft's era of acquisitions.
He started off relatively small with Mojang in 2014 for $2.5 billion.
These are the guys behind Microsoft, but it didn't take him long to scale up.
In 2016, Microsoft would go ahead and buy LinkedIn for $26.2 billion.
He followed this up with GitHub for $7.5 billion.
ZeniMax Media also for $7.5 billion.
Nuance Communications for $19.7 billion, Activision Blizzard for $68.7 billion, and of course, $10 billion into chat GPT.
Those are just a few of Microsoft's most notable investments and acquisitions.
Here's a full list of all of Microsoft's known purchases.
This is in stark contrast to every other tech giant.
Apple, for example, just avoids high-profile acquisitions altogether.
Their last big purchase was Beats, and that was almost 10 years ago.
Google, on the other hand, does do a crap ton of acquisitions, but almost all of them are in the tens of millions or hundreds of millions.
They're not in the billions or tens of billions.
They clearly prefer to play an active role in building up brands as opposed to buying out established businesses.
The only other tech company that has engaged in such massive deals is Facebook, but there's a key difference between Facebook's purchases and Microsoft's purchases.
Facebook buys products to integrate into their own ecosystem.
Microsoft buys companies as passive investments and keeps them as separate from their original business as possible.
And if you don't believe me, check this out.
It's been 7 years since Microsoft acquired LinkedIn, but to this day, there is no sign in with Microsoft or Outlook option, though there is a sign in with Google or Apple option.
The same thing can be said about GitHub.
To create a GitHub account, you have to do it the old-fashioned way by entering an email address.
You can't just log in with Microsoft.
And it's not just signing in either.
Users of these services wouldn't even know that these companies are owned by Microsoft unless they were explicitly told.
This goes much deeper than just superficial things as well.
If you ask the CEOs of these acquired companies, they have nothing but good things to say about Microsoft.
Microsoft has not forgotten why we did the deal in the first place and what the important pillars of the deal are.
The first and foremost principle is to put developers first, and that is what we do every day.
In stark contrast, all of WhatsApp's and Instagram's founders have left Facebook on negative terms.
Clearly, Microsoft is not just acquiring a bunch of companies for a bunch of money, they're also maintaining them in the right way.
In the beginning of this video, we talked about how Microsoft is the only tech giant that hasn't created a revolutionary product in the past 10-20 years.
But they're also the only tech giant that isn't dependent on one revolutionary product.
To this day, over 50% of all of Google's revenue comes from Google search.
Over 50% of Apple's revenue comes from the iPhone.
The only reason Amazon is even profitable is because of AWS.
And the entire business of Meta can be summed up by Facebook, WhatsApp, and Instagram.
Microsoft, on the other hand, isn't tied down by one or even a handful of products.
They are truly a diversified business with hundreds and hundreds of products, each operating on independent terms.
Before, the sentiment around Microsoft was that they were able to transition from being a consumer business to being an enterprise business.
But this doesn't tell the full story as they have since transitioned from being an enterprise business to being a full-on holding company.
And that is the state of Microsoft today and why they're able to get away without innovating themselves.

title: The Man Who Nearly Bought Netflix Is Now Wanted For Running A Ponzi
note: Hook on Icahn and Netflix, flashback biography, raiding era anecdotes (TWA), then the defenses and why the whole practice died, closing with the Hindenburg accusation.

T. Boone Pickens, Gulf Oil and mega takeovers

lines: The most feared corporate raider in the world.
One of the truest investors on the planet.
He moves markets by the mere mention of his name.
You have a bombshell today from short seller Hindenburg Research, which is revealing a new short position against Carl Icahn's IEP.
Fortune magazine says he may be making more money for shareholders than anyone else on the planet.

This was really a Halloween spook for Netflix, as Icon was someone that you didn't want anywhere near your company.
People like Icon constantly assure you that, oh, it's just a passive investment, I'm not trying to take over the company.
And then, boom, you get sued for depicting Cleopatra as black.
Wait, never mind, wrong result.

With a net worth of $21 billion, he could literally buy out Netflix with a personal loan, and that was probably what he was planning on doing despite his hollow promises.
Netflix's executive team would scramble trying to find a way to fend off this bully, and they would end up implementing a defense called the poison pill.

Had the poison pill really worked?

The reality is that Icon had lost his mojo.
While his net worth had gone up over the years, his days in power toying with fortune 10 companies were long gone.
It wasn't just Icon who was in this situation either.
Corporate raiders as a whole had lost their power.
Back in the days, these guys were the worst nightmares of small companies and their shareholders.
With financing from Wall Street, raiders would march into random companies where they were not welcome and buy out a large portion of the company if not the entire company.
After that, they would go on to fire a large portion of the workforce, increase efficiency no matter the cost, and bolster the stock price through any means possible.
Once the company has been milked, raiders will happily sell off the remaining pulp to some random sucker before moving on to their next victim.
This was the brash and ruthless job of being a corporate raider, but while this was no doubt a nasty job, it was also lucrative.

Till recently, Icon was worth over 20 billion dollars, but today he's fighting against accusations that he's been running a Ponzi, which has crushed his net worth down to just under 8 billion dollars.
So, here's the insane story of how Icon went from playing with fortune 10 companies to being accused of fraud.
Taking a look back, corporate raiding does not have an extensive history like stock buybacks or dual class stock.
It rose in popularity during an era and then disappeared shortly after.
There were a few instances of corporate raiding throughout the late 1960s, but corporate raiding didn't really become a thing until Carl Icahn.
Icahn started off as nothing more than an average kid born in 1946 to a Jewish family in Brooklyn, New York.
His family was squarely in the middle class with both of Icahn's parents being school teachers.
But this didn't hold him back from getting into Princeton University and graduating with a degree in philosophy in 1957.
At first, it seems that he wanted to be a doctor as he would enroll in the NYU School of Medicine, but he would end up dropping out and joining the military reserve forces.
He would follow this up with a traditional job on Wall Street as a stockbroker in 1961.
Here, he would learn the ins and outs of stocks, options, bonds, warrants, and other financial products before opening his own company called Icon & Company in 1968.
From the very beginning, Icon was especially interested in leveraging market inefficiencies, but he was by no means buying out entire companies.
Rather, his company was focused on something called arbitrage trading.
This is basically when you make money by leveraging discrepancies in market pricing between different markets and exchanges.
For example, Tesla stock might be worth $100 on TD Ameritrade but be worth $101 on Robinhood.
In this case, it would make sense to buy Tesla stock on TD and then instantly sell the stake on Robinhood.
You would only make $1 per share, but if you did this with 100,000 shares, well then you're making serious money.
That's just an example though as it's not nearly that easy.
Such blatant pricing discrepancies are extremely rare.
You'd be lucky to find a 5 or 10 cent discrepancy on popular stocks, but you'll have a much better chance if you look deeper than just common stock.
For example, you could look at the debt market.
Many companies issue bonds that can be converted to stock at a set ratio.
So, theoretically, you could buy a Tesla convertible bond and convert it into 10 shares of Tesla stock.
If your all-in cost for the bond is less than the current price of 10 Tesla shares, well then you're golden.
You can just sell the 10 shares and make money.
This is precisely how Icahn made his initial money.
He was constantly looking for discrepancies between options, preferred stock, common stock, bonds, warrants, and mutual funds.
He was constantly converting between these assets to generate a profit.
Many people aren't big fans of market arbitrage as they see people like Icon as bottom feeders.
They basically scrape by and make a bunch of money without adding any real value to the world.
The argument against this would be that arbitragers make markets more efficient.
But I don't think Icon was too concerned about justifying his means to anyone as it wasn't long until he jumped into something much more controversial.
Much of the popularity of corporate rating throughout the 70s and 80s can be explained by the economic environment.
Interest rates were extraordinarily high at up to 19%.
At first glance, this might sound like a great thing as you can just store your cash in a savings account and earn a Warren Buffett level returns until you consider inflation.
Inflation also reached up to 15%, so rarely were you making any sort of real return.
This didn't just apply to savings accounts either.
Whether you were looking at real estate or stocks or gold or index funds, chances were high that there was no real return.
This made investors especially desperate and risk-tolerant.
They were willing to do just about anything, including piling into junk bonds.
In fact, between 1979 and 1989, the junk bond market exploded from $10 billion to $189 billion.
But our man Icahn had a much better pitch for investors.
Given that people were shying away from stocks, the market had stagnated for about 10 years, and many blue chip stocks were heavily discounted.
This was a great opportunity for value investors like Warren Buffett, but Icahn didn't stop at just investing in these value companies.
Icon would purchase a controlling share or the entire company and he would quote-unquote optimize the company.
By optimize, he would basically strip these companies down to their bare bones and eliminate anything that wasn't generating a profit.
This might not sound too bad until you realize just what he was eliminating.
For example, he might go in and kill a company's R &D department or their safety department.
This would make the company more profitable than ever for the next 3-5 years, but after that, they're absolutely screwed.
This was none of Icon's concern though as he would have already flipped the business by this point.
So essentially, Icon and his fellow corporate raiders were basically going around and ruining companies for personal gain.
Icon's first target was an appliance company called Tappan.
He would acquire a controlling stake in the company in 1978 and do some gutting.
He would then force the company to be sold to Electrolux, netting him a gross profit of $2.7 million or a 100% return.
With a taste of success, Icahn would quickly jump up to playing with the tens of millions.
In 1983, for example, he would acquire ACF Industries and flip it to Philips Petroleum in 1985 for a $50 million profit.
At least with these two instances, Icahn was simply flipping these companies.
In other instances, he would straight up blackmail these companies as was the case with Saxon Industries.
Icon bought a stake in Saxon in 1980 and threatened that he was going to find someone to buy the entire company.
This forced the company to buy out Icon shares which netted him a quick 2 million.
Seeing this, there was no doubt that Icon was wreaking havoc quite early on but no one really fought him.
The companies that he was going after were no-name brands with not much support.
Surely, he couldn't pull this off with a true giant, or at least that's what they thought until he did.
In 1985, Icahn would pull together all of his investors funds and max out his bank credit lines to purchase a 20% stake in Transworld Airlines for approximately $70 million.
dollars.
Most of you probably aren't familiar with Transworld Airlines or TWA, well, because Icon would run it to the ground, but we'll get to that.
When Icon purchased his stake, TWA was the fourth largest airline in the US.
In fact, their planes alone were worth over a billion dollars, which was massive stuff for 1985.
This isn't to say that they were perfect though, they were dealing with issues with unions and trying to stage a turnaround.
But Icon's presence ensured that this turnaround never came.
Just a few months after his initial purchase, Icon would up his stake to just over 50% which gave him control of TWA.
And a few years later, Icon would take TWA completely private upping his stake to 90%.
During a normal corporate turnaround, businesses would focus on eliminating the bad parts of the business and doubling down on the good parts but Icahn would do the exact opposite.
He would eliminate the good parts of the business by selling them off.
For example, he would sell off their popular London routes to American Airlines for $445 million.
Pretty soon, TWA had nothing left but losses, and they would unsurprisingly file for bankruptcy in early 1992 with $540 million in debt.
This didn't really matter for Icon though as he had already secured $469 million worth of profit for himself.
The story of TWA definitely made some waves on the news cycles back in the 80s, but it wasn't Icon that really turned everyone against corporate raiders.
That honor actually goes to one of Icon's biggest rivals, T.
Boone Pickens.
In the early 1980s, Pickens would launch a hostile takeover against Gulf Oil.
This was absolutely unprecedented because Gulf Oil wasn't just a massive company, they were straight up a fortune 10 company.
Fortunately, the Standard Oil Company of California or Chevron was able to step in and buy out the entire company for $13 billion, which prevented Pickens from wreaking any havoc.
But while this did salvage Gulf Oil, it also gave Pickens a profit of $760 million.
Pretty soon, Icahn was also playing with mega billion dollar companies.
In 1986, for example, he launched an $8 billion takeover of US Steel.
He never succeeded in taking over the entire company, but that didn't stop him from making a cool $200 million.
His biggest profit, however, came in 1989 when he sold his $2 billion stake Texaco for a $700 million profit.
Things had gone way too far, and enough was enough.
These tycoons were playing around with Fortune 10 and Fortune 100 companies as if they were lemonade stands.
Companies were understandably not just annoyed, but triggered, and pretty soon they would start fighting back.
One of the first defenses that came about against corporate raiders was the poison pill defense.
You may have heard about this with Twitter as they were indeed using this defense.
This defense basically consists of diluting the corporate raider into oblivion by issuing a crap ton of shares.
This way, the corporate raider is never able to acquire majority control of the company through the public markets.
This is actually how Netflix defended themselves against Icon.
Right after Icon purchased a 10% stake in Netflix, Netflix would adopt a poison pill defense.
This may have been successful at preventing Icon from buying out Netflix, but this didn't stop Icon from making $800 million nonetheless.
Though he would have made $40 billion if he just held on.
Anyway, another popular strategy that companies adopted was golden parachutes.
This doesn't actually do anything to save the company or shareholders, but it does save the executives.
Essentially, golden parachutes allow for executives to walk away with massive payouts if the company gets acquired.
Twitter's executives, for example, walked away with over $100 million in severance.
To be honest, I wouldn't call this a defense.
This is more of a case of executives saving their asses.
A more traditional defense though is the white knight defense.
We briefly touched on this actually with Gulf Oil and T-Boone Pickens.
Remember how Gulf Oil sold themselves to Chevron to avoid pickens?
That's a white knight defense, selling yourself to a friendly party to avoid a takeover from a hostile party.

There are a bunch of other defenses as well like the green male defense and the employee stock ownership defense, and many of these have been used to successfully defend companies from Texaco and Gucci to Netflix and Twitter.
But none of these strategies really took down corporate rating.
Sure, they made corporate rating harder, but they by no means made it impossible or non-lucrative.
Heck, the richest man in the world today, Bernard Arnault, made most of his fortune by rating the fashion industry throughout the 80s and 90s.
and Elon literally just did one with Twitter, so it's definitely still possible.
But then, why has corporate rating become so rare?
Well, the primary reason is because investors walked away.
Back in the late 1900s, making a 100% return within 3 or 4 years was unheard of.
But thanks to tech stocks, it's been largely normalized.
This isn't to say that a 100% return within 3 to four years isn't a phenomenal return.
It is a phenomenal return, but there's simply far more opportunities to make such returns.
Meta, for example, has recovered nearly 200% within the past six months itself.
So why be the villain, destroy companies, and take on so much risk when you can just bet on up-and-coming blue-chip companies and make the same or even better returns with far less stress?
The answer is no reason at all.
All of the people who would have backed someone like Icon in the 80s have simply turned to backing someone like Zuckerberg or Pitche or Bitcoin.
And that right there is what truly killed corporate rating.
Today, Icon is being plagued with a completely new controversy.
At the beginning of May, Hindenburg Research accused that ICON has been paying out dividends using funds from new investors.

And given that Hindenburg has a pretty good track record from taking down Nikola Motors to taking down the Adani Group, it's very possible that these accusations are legitimate, but only time will tell.
In the end, corporate raiding was an invention that came from an investor's desire for outsized returns over everything else.
This allowed for several raiders to rise to prominence who played with billion dollar companies on regular basis as they made billions for themselves and their investors.
Eventually though, companies started catching on and started fighting back with varying levels of success.
There's also an argument to be made that banks became more reluctant to lend to corporate raiders as a lot of raiders simply failed.
But really, the bigger trend that killed off corporate raiding was the rise of tech.
Investors simply found a new shiny thing to invest in.
Why flip appliance and oil companies when you can bet on tech companies that reach billions of people?
And that is what marked the end of the hunt for Carl Icahn, the infamous legend who tried to buy Netflix.

title: Bottled Water Is Literally A Scam
note: Topical explainer with an opening data-heavy argument, then a historical arc of bottled water's rise, collapse and marketing-driven revival.
sections: Cold open: bottled water is a scam
Struggling to cut costs: glass to plastic
Pepsi and Coca-Cola pivot from soda to water
Weak regulation and the health facade
lines: In 2016, bottled water outsold soda for the first time in US history.
From one perspective, this is a great thing, people are choosing to drink water instead of soda.
But from another perspective, it's brain dead that Americans are spending so much money on bottled water.
It's one thing if you don't have access to clean drinking water, but this only applies to 0.6% of Americans, most of whom live in rural areas.
Despite this, 96% of Americans continue to buy bottled water, resulting in the average American consuming 47 gallons of bottled water every year.
And much of this consumption isn't on hiking trips or vacations.
No, Americans literally buy cases of bottled water and drink it on a regular basis even at home instead of tap water.
Families who do this spend on average, wait for it, $1,350 per year on bottled water.
If you ask them why, they'll point to the taste or the filtration or the mineral content, but there's no evidence to back this up.
In fact, a 2010 study found that the majority of participants could not even distinguish between bottled water and tap water.
Also, bottled water is not healthier than tap water.
If anything, bottled water is actually worse because 93% of bottled water tends to be contaminated by microplastics.
And speaking of plastics, 86% of bottled water gets thrown away, resulting in 4 billion pounds of plastic trash and 2.5 million tons of carbon dioxide every single year.
So objectively speaking, bottled water provides no health benefit for 99.4% of Americans, and it's expensive financially and environmentally.
But then, why do people still buy bottled water?
Well, the answer is brilliant marketing.
You see, the soda industry isn't crying over the fact that people are moving away from soda, because they're the ones who engineered this transition in the first place.
Take a look at this lineup of bottled water.
At first glance, it looks like a good assortment of different bottled water.
But many of these brands are owned and or distributed by none other than Coca-Cola and Pepsi.
Coca-Cola is involved with Dasani, Seal, and Smartwater, while Pepsi is involved with Aquafina, Schweppes, Lifewater, Sobe, Sparkling O, and Evian.
And if a bottled water brand isn't owned by these two, it's probably owned by Nestle who owns 67 water brands around the world.
So here's how these three behemoths brainwashed America into paying $16 billion for bottled water every single year.
Taking a look back, bottled water is by no means a new invention.
The first bottled water plant can be traced back to 1622 to the United Kingdom.
From the very beginning, the premise of bottled water wasn't exactly scientifically sound.
I mean, the first bottling plant in the UK was literally called the Holy Well Bottling Plant.
As you may have guessed, the water promised to offer medicinal value especially when it came to healing and rejuvenation.
Despite its shaky scientific roots, this idea quickly spread across Europe and we saw bottling plants popping up next to every natural spring across the continent.
This trend was simply accelerated by European colonization and imperialism.
As these superpowers traveled to new areas, they were exposed to nature that was completely untampered with.
And this simply got them more obsessed with the idea of getting their hands on the most natural water possible.
But while this idea was quickly spreading across Europe, it took quite some time for it to catch on in America.
In fact, the first commercially produced bottled water in America didn't come about till 1767 or nearly 150 years after the UK.
Americans also didn't buy bottled water for some sort of miracle reason.
Rather, they were just trying to get access to the cleanest drinking water they could which was actually a serious concern.
Back in Europe however, bottling plants were simply leaning more and more into the marketing aspect.
In 1783 for example, a Swiss clockmaker named Johann Jacob Schwepp would discover a way to carbonate water.
Suddenly, bottling plants had another way to market water.
Not only was their water holy but now it was holy and sparkling.
Surprisingly, this also took quite some time to catch on in America.
It wasn't until 1809 or 26 years later that the first patent for carbonated water was filed in America.
It seems that Americans were surprisingly grounded when it came to bottled water.
Gimmicks like holy water and sparkling water didn't really push them to buy bottled water, but disease did as was the case in the 1850s.
Typhoid and cholera outbreaks were becoming increasingly common, which made bottled water highly appealing.
And given that the supply of bottled water was somewhat limited, did, pricing went through the roof.
A single pint of water cost as much as $1.75.
Adjusting for inflation, we're looking at $63 for a pint of water.
This was the first time that bottled water started carrying a certain prestige in America.
Only the rich were able to spend $63 on bottled water, so bottled water naturally started being associated with a high social status.
This was the case for quite some time as in the next 50 years, but in 1905, the entire industry would be disrupted.
This year, English doctors would convince authorities to implement public chlorination plants.
A few years later in 1908, New Jersey would also implement water chlorination, and this marked the end of bottled water at least for quite some time.
The impact of water chlorination cannot be understated.
Water chlorination is considered to be one of the 10 greatest public health achievements of the 20th century, and looking at the numbers, it's not surprising why.
Water chlorination destroyed diseases like cholera and typhoid well before vaccines were developed.
In 1900, there were 100 cases of typhoid fever per 100,000 people.
By 1920, this number dropped to 33.8 cases per 100,000 people.
And by 2006, this number dropped to just 0.1 cases per 100,000 people.
And even amongst these cases, 75% of them occurred amongst international travelers.
But not only was chlorination extremely effective, it was also extremely cheap.
In fact, you can treat a million gallons of water with just a single dollar.
This made it easy for municipalities across the US to implement water chlorination, and within no time, most Americans had access to clean drinking water from their taps.
This quickly put an end to the popularity of bottled water.
The reality was that bottled water was simply too expensive for the average American, and the only reason that it was so popular was because drinking tap water was an actual health risk.
But now that tap water was safe to drink, people were quick to forget about bottled water.
This isn't to say that bottling plants quit trying to sell bottled water though.
From their perspective, the biggest obstacle was price.
If they could just make bottled water cheap enough, maybe they could convince people to buy it once again.
The biggest factor making bottled water so expensive wasn't actually the water itself, it was actually the bottling.
Water was traditionally bottled in glass, so no wonder it was expensive.
This was only made worse by the Great Depression as the average person had less money than ever.
This was really the rock bottom for the water bottle industry, but things did slowly get better.
In the 1940s, bottlers would start experimenting with plastic bottles.
These were indeed cheaper than glass bottles, but only marginally so.
It wasn't until the 1950s and the introduction of high-density polyethylene that bottlers were really able to bring down the price, but this didn't help sales like they expected.
While bottled water was indeed affordable, it was still significantly more expensive than tap water which made it kind of a stupid purchase especially when there was no objective benefit.
This is very much the case to this day.
In fact, bottled water is one of the most highly marked up items in the world.
Producing bottled water only costs 5 cents on average, so if you're paying a dollar for it, you're looking at a 2000% markup.
For perspective, even movie theater popcorn is only marked up 1300%.
This is because somewhere along the line, bottlers finally realized that they simply couldn't compete against tap water in terms of price.

Tap water was simply always going to be cheaper, and if bottlers couldn't convince customers based on price, they had to convince them based on perceived quality, and that's exactly what they would do.
The extraordinary resurgence of bottled water can be traced back to a single marketing campaign from a company called Perrier.
Perrier was already doing quite well back in France.
They were very much the exception when it came to bottled water as they were not only doing well, but they were exploding in popularity.
In fact, between 1946 and 1952, Perrier was able to grow their sales 50 next from 10 million bottles per year to 150 million bottles per year.
What made their popularity even more perplexing was that they were seemingly doing everything wrong.
They had stuck to glass bottles and they were unapologetically expensive at over $2 per bottle.
But the truth was that this was their secret.
Perrier marketed themselves as the premium water meant for premium customers.
And in 1977, Perrier would bring this same marketing strategy to America.
They would spend $5 million advertising Perrier as Earth's first soft drink.
They claimed that Perrier was more quenching, more refreshing, and most importantly, more natural.
This tapped into our natural desire to live longer and healthier and find the oh-so-elusive fountain of youth.
Perrier would pair this marketing with brilliant positioning.
They would place their water in the most elite restaurants and hotels in New York and Los Angeles.
This solidified the idea that the rich were living longer and better due to the water they were drinking.
This completely redefined how Americans perceived bottled water.
They started to believe that bottled water was indeed better than tap water, but it wasn't quite enough to get the average Joe to switch over.
You see, Americans were addicted to something else, soda.
But over time, awareness about just how unhealthy soda really is started to spread, and the people would start cutting back in the late 1990s.
Pepsi and Coca-Cola were witnessing the stagnation firsthand as they saw their empire slowly melt away.
But that didn't last for long as both of these guys would swiftly pivot to water.
These guys already had decades of experience advertising sugar water.
All they had to do now was market the water without the sugar.
Perrier had already created a premium image around bottled water, so all Pepsi and Coca-Cola had to do was double down.
Pepsi would launch Aquafina and Coca-Cola would launch Dasani, and they would both strategically priced bottled water to be more expensive than soda.
Why was water more expensive than soda?
Well, obviously because it was healthier.
These two also had connections with basically every retailer on the planet, so getting their miracle water into stores was no problem at all.
Once their product was on shelves and their commercials about youth and nature were airing, all they had to do was wait.
During the first 8 years of the 2000s, bottled water would rocket in sales while soda stagnated.
During the next eight years, bottled water continued to rocket while soda actually declined, leading us to where we are today.
In the end, the only reason that bottled water is so popular today is because of a brilliant pivot from Pepsi and Coca-Cola.
They saw that their core market was declining due to health concerns, so they created new brands centered on health.
The reality though is that bottled water has nothing to do with health.
In fact, bottled water is less heavily regulated than tap water.
The FDA does not require bottlers to disclose water sources, treatment processes, or even containment reports.
Municipalities, on the other hand, are required to send you this information on an annual basis, though of course no one looks at these, but at least they're there.
This means that there's usually a lot more variation regarding cleanliness when it comes to bottled water.
One study found that top water is pretty consistent, generally having between 0.2 to 2.7 bacterial colonies per milliliter.
Bottled water, on the other hand, had anywhere between 0.01 to 4,900 colonies per milliliter.
In fact, 6 of the tested brands had 1,500 to 4,900 colonies per milliliter.

So, the idea that bottled water is healthier or cleaner is just a brilliantly constructed facade and all the extra money you're spending on bottled water is just going to the pockets of our favorite bottlers, Coca Cola and Pepsi.
And that's how America got brainwashed into drinking bottled water.

title: YouTube Has Become Pay To Win
note: Opinion essay with a thesis up front, then supporting examples; no single protagonist. Ends restating the hook.
lines: YouTube has become paid to win.
Gone are the days that random Joes could pick up cameras and record themselves playing games or discussing a topic.
Nowadays, everyone from MKBHD and Mr.
Who's the Boss to Airack and Mr.
Beast spend tens of thousands if not hundreds of thousands on each and every video.
They also all have millions of dollars worth of equipment, dedicated studios, and dozens of employees.
At this point, they're pretty much just full-on production studios, and that's on the personality side of YouTube itself.
Then, you have the whole company side as well, with channels like Brightside, the Infographics Show, T-Series, and Cocomelon Nursery Rhymes.
There are a few outliers who have stuck to a reasonable level of production like Sniper Wolf and Penguin, but these are very much the exception, not the rule.
Also, most of these guys were OGs to YouTube.
Trying to replicate their formula today from scratch probably wouldn't work all that well.
This is quite a shame as raw authenticity is what made YouTube different from traditional media platforms in the first place.
People liked that they could see their favorite creators without censorship, without filters, and without advertiser influence.
People liked the genuine and vulnerable nature of YouTube, but modern creators shy away from these characteristics as much as possible.
These attributes simply lead to drama, controversy, and potentially getting cancelled.
So, the best solution is to just stay as vanilla as possible.
Never have an opinion, never push the boundaries, and never ever piss off the people on Twitter.
Larger creators are simply leaning into these attributes as it allows them to outsource more work, create a better distinction between their personal lives and their online personas.
us.
And it gives them a larger moat against aspiring up and coming creators.
So, a pretty smart strategy from their end, but this is arguably destroying the essence of YouTube.
So, here's how YouTube became paid to win and the upsetting future of the platform.
Taking a look back, the roots of this evolution can be traced back to the mid-2010s to creators.
By this point, most niches had already become saturated with tons of creators.
People were starting to understand that YouTube could not only be a viable career, but a lucrative one that came with popularity, fame, and influence.
So, it's no wonder why people were jumping at every opportunity they saw, but this brought along with it quite a few challenges.
Larger creators often struggled to keep up with the quantity of content from smaller creators.
It was also super difficult to think of original ideas as every topic you can think of had already been covered from every aspect you can think of.
The saying, there are no original ideas, was truer than ever.
But despite this, creators attempted to keep up with the YouTube machine, leading to burnout and high levels of stress and depression.
A few notable creators, however, were able to find an escape from this vicious hamster wheel.
These guys accepted that they would never be able to keep up with the firehose of content that was being put up on YouTube.
If they were a tech YouTuber, there were simply too many smartphones, laptops, and gadgets coming out to cover them all.
If they were a vlogger, it was simply impossible to make their lives interesting every single day of the year.
This was simply not sustainable, so these creators decided to take another path.
Instead of trying to cover every single topic, they decided to simply cover one topic better than anyone.
The idea is that people would tune in not because the ideas or concepts were unique, but because the delivery was exceptional.
