A perfect example of this is Marcus Brownlee.
Somewhere along the line, Marcus decided to drop a quarter million dollars on a robotic camera.
Let me just say, there is no way to quantifiably justify this investment.
You can't be like, oh, this camera is going to increase my viewership by 6.2%, so in 42 months the ROI will be net positive.
It simply does not work, because it's unlikely that this camera led to any sort of noticeable increase in viewership, at least not in the short term, but that's okay.
This camera was not purchased to boost viewership.
This camera was purchased to build a brand, a perception.
Whenever you see a crazy camera shot on tech YouTube, you know it's Marcus, and this association gets him one step closer to being the undisputed king of tech YouTubers.
So the next time an iPhone drops, it doesn't matter if a hundred people post reviews about it before Marcus.
You can bet that millions of people are waiting to see Marcus's take, specifically because he provides an experience that they can't get anywhere else on YouTube.
Marcus is by no means the only one leveraging this strategy either.
This strategy has become very prevalent with Mr.
B's channel as well.
Take a few of his recent videos for example, $1 vs $500,000 plane ticket and $1 vs $1 million hotel room.
These are by no means groundbreaking video ideas.
BuzzFeed made identical videos 6 years ago.
In fact, they had a full-on series called Worth It comparing cheap options to expensive options.
Yet, Mr.
Beast's plain video got 150 million views and his hotel video got 217 million views.
Why?
Simple, his scale and production.
Those are just two examples, but I could name dozens.
Mr.
Who's the Boss, Air Rack, Magnate's Media, Good Mythical Morning, Mark Rober, Stuff Made Here, Film Theory, Jin Hao Tan, Wong Fu Productions, and basically every other large channel you can think of.
While their initial success may have been fueled by down-to-earth Mortal videos, it's their production quality that's kept them at the top.
It's not just the creators who have evolved either.
Audiences have also very much evolved.
Back in 2007 and 2008, let me just be real here, the people who watched YouTube were a bunch of anti-social nerds and gamers.
But nowadays, everyone watches YouTube, and with that comes along a vastly different set of expectations.
Most people are used to TV, Netflix, and movies, and to them, that level of production is normal.
So naturally, these people flock to channels that are able to live up to these standards.
Also, let me say, this is not a trend that's unique to YouTube.
In general, people flock to high production value content.
Take Avatar 2 for example.
The storyline was at best mundane, but this has proved to be completely irrelevant as Avatar 2 ended up as the third highest grossing film of all time.
The same thing could be said about the original Avatar as well.
While the storyline was more substantial than Avatar 2, critics argued that it was just a ripoff of Dances with Wolves.
This is very much true, and even James Cameron himself has admitted this.
But that didn't stop Avatar 2 from becoming the highest grossing film of all time.
Why, you ask?
Well, the visuals are stunning, the world building is unbelievable, and you forget that it's even CGI.
die.
Now, this isn't to say that Cameron or creators should come up with crappy storylines and buff it up with visuals.
Not a good strategy.
Ideally, the story is good and the production is good.
That would obviously lead to the best results, but the thing to note is that a good production can make up for a bad story.
A good story, however, doesn't always make up for a bad production, at least with the general audience.
Another great example of this is the Grand Theft auto series.
The GTA series has been around for 25 years at this point, and while there are some differences between the games like the city that it's based in, it all boils down to the same thing.
You're a bad guy doing bad things to make money and earn respect.
Simple as that, but despite milking the same plot for so long, GTA 5 ended up becoming the highest grossing piece of media of all time, pulling in $7.7 billion.
And we can only imagine how well GTA 6 will perform.
The reasoning is simple, Rockstar Games is constantly creating an unmatchable experience with each and every iteration.
So when audiences are constantly being fed this level of content by movies, TV shows, and games, it's only natural that they come to expect the same from YouTube.
The creators that are able to keep up do exceptionally well.
The others, well, the others are left behind.
Creators often like to blame the algorithm when it comes to a video not performing well or the channel being killed off.
Audiences also like to complain that platforms are recommending thirst traps and low productivity content.
But the truth is that both of these parties are just shifting the blame.
The algorithms of social media platforms are nothing but audience psychology.
So if a video isn't performing well or a channel is receiving less views, it's not because the algorithm doesn't like the content.
It's because the audience doesn't like the content, at least not a broad audience.
The opposite is true as well.
If a channel is performing really well, it's not because YouTube is biased or something.
It's because that's what the audience wants to see.
And based on who the biggest creators are today, it's clear that what the audience wants is fast-paced, high production value content, which brings us to our main question.
Where does that leave small creators?
Well, not in a good place.
Also, when I say small creators, I don't mean people with hundreds of thousands of subscribers or even tens of thousands.
I'm talking about people who are trying to get their first thousand or their first 5,000 subscribers.
As Casey Neistat once said, 10,000 subs is the hardest thing to do on YouTube because at zero, nobody's tuning in, nobody cares.
And this is harder than ever today because top creators have simply set the bar for entry so high.
Now, there's no point in blaming these creators.
Not only do they produce awesome content that's enjoyed by hundreds of millions of people, but they're just doing what's best for their brands and their businesses.
That's only reasonable, but with that being said, this trend has largely shifted the tide against new creators.
In fact, 97% of YouTubers don't make it, which is not that different from Hollywood where only 2% of actors make it.
Most small creators today are hoping for that one viral video that will explode their channel, but this is not that different from actors and musicians hoping for that one lucky break.
The reality is that this break will never come for most people.
Now, a lot of creators will have you believe that it's not a lock-in that it comes down to one's understanding of YouTube and the audience.
MrBeast has even claimed that he could get to 1 million subscribers from zero within 3 to 4 months.
How long would it take you to get to 1 million subscribers?
Probably 3 months, maybe 4.
From zero, easily 3 or 4 months.
Like, if that's all that guy was doing.
And they're right.
Succeeding on YouTube is not necessarily luck, but the thing to note is that creators that are starting off also don't have the same skills or mindset.
It's like those shows where millionaires try to start from zero and become millionaires again.
Admittedly, these are super interesting to watch, but to think that a homeless guy could do it just because a millionaire could is absurd.
Similarly, thinking that an average joke could get to a million subscribers in 3 months or even a year just because Mr.
Beast could is also absurd.
Of course, there will be exceptions, but that's what they are, exceptions.
The harsh reality is that making it on YouTube is becoming harder and harder every day, because the bar for entry is also becoming higher and higher.
In the end, the state of YouTube today is not out of the ordinary by any means.
That's how every other artistic industry has always been whether that be games, movies, TVs, writing, or art itself.
The reason that this is upsetting with YouTube though is because YouTube used to be the exception.
They started off like Be Real, but expecting them to stay this way is simply unrealistic.
Be Real is already dying and if YouTube chose this path, they too would probably be dead.
The reason that YouTube is so successful today is because they evolved.
They became more like traditional media and the creators followed suit.
With all that being said though, if you are able to make it to the other side, the opportunity on YouTube is insane.
But getting to the other side is harder than ever because YouTube has become pay to win.

title: Why Does Walmart Pay So Much?
note: Company origin story told through two founders who become the bridge; the cause of high pay is the Cosmix acquisition. Pay hook paid off by the humility pivot.
sections: Venki and Anand: Jungli to Amazon
lines: Salaries at Walmart have become insane.
Software engineers for example can expect to earn as much as half a million dollars per year.
Now, such salaries aren't too crazy at big tech companies and VC funded startups, but Walmart isn't either of those.
They're a retailer, a legacy retailer.
For perspective, the top engineers at Target earn over $200,000 less at $278,000.
And at Costco, the average software engineer is barely able to cross $100,000.
This doesn't just apply for software engineers either.
For product managers, Walmart is offering up to $500,000.
For engineering managers, they're offering up to $600,000.
And even for data scientists, they're offering up to $400,000.
In fact, Walmart is paying so much that for certain tech job titles, they're literally on the leaderboard for paying the highest compensation.
Take Solution Architect for For example, Walmart comes in as the 24th highest paying company for this position with a median of $223,000.
This places them just $2,000 behind Apple and $3,000 behind Facebook.
This also places them ahead of some of the largest tech companies out there including Cisco, Salesforce, Oracle, and Dell.
We should also note that Walmart is the only retailer that makes the leaderboard other than Amazon of course, but they're more of a tech company than a retailer.
Walmart, on the other hand, is definitely still more of a retailer, but they're leaning into tech more than ever.
In fact, they have a full-on subsidiary called Walmart Global Tech, formerly known as Walmart Labs with 8,000 employees.
Why does a retailer need this many tech employees?
Well, it's because Walmart doesn't treat tech as an addition to their retail business, they treat tech as the basis of their retail business.
But it wasn't always like this.
In fact, for nearly 16 years, Walmart had stalled out.
But since 2015, the retailer has tripled their market cap, growing to a valuation of just under $400 billion, making them the 19th largest company in the world.
So, here's the story of how Walmart saved their stagnating business with tech.
Taking a look back, Walmart's transition into tech can be traced back to the late 1990s, when Walmart was very much the boomer of the retail industry.
By this point, they were already the largest retailer in the US and the world's largest private employer.
In fact, Walmart still holds this title to this day with a whopping 2.3 million employees.
But while things were going great at Walmart, they were starting to see a little thorn pop-up called Amazon.
You may have heard of them.
At first, they started off as a no-name online bookstore, but every year they were growing by hundreds if not thousands of percent.
They were expanding into new categories all the time, and it seemed like they wanted to be the Walmart of the online world.
In fact, they were starting to coach a bunch of Walmart employees by luring them with sky-high stock compensation.
This made it easy for Amazon to steal Walmart's world-class logistics and supply chain secrets.
Usually, when an up-and-coming competitor is able to steal your employees and perform extraordinarily well, it's usually a sign that they're doing something that you're not.
With the case of Amazon, the X Factor was obviously their online presence.
So, the best idea for Walmart would have probably been to poach some tech employees from Amazon and double down on their online presence.
In fact, this is precisely what they've been doing over the past several years.
But back in the day, Walmart would take the boomer approach and try to bog down Amazon by suing them.
While that fiasco was playing out at Walmart, a story jumps over to two tech entrepreneurs named Venki Harinarayan and Anand Raj Rahman.
These guys were your classic tech guys from India, having both completed degrees at IIT in India and Stanford in America.
They had gone on to create an online company called Jungli Corporation, which allowed shoppers to easily compare prices and features of various online products.
This is nothing crazy today, but back in the 1990s, this was revolutionary stuff, and Jeff Bezos would take interest in the company.
In 1998, he would buy out Jungli for 1.6 million shares of Amazon, which at the time was worth $250 million.
Today, it's worth $22 billion, so safe to say that these two had scored a pretty lucrative deal, but they were by no means ready to retire.
Both Venki and Anand would join Amazon as high-level directors and closely work with Jeff Bezos himself.
These two would actually end up being instrumental in the launch of Amazon Marketplace.
You may not be familiar with this brand, but I'm sure you know what they do.
This is the part of Amazon that allows for third-party sellers to list products on Amazon.
As you know, this is basically the bread and butter of Amazon today, so it looks like Bezos definitely got his money's worth with this duo.
While that's cool and all, you're probably wondering, what in the world do these guys have to do with Walmart?
Well, these two are the ones that would create what would eventually become Walmart Global Tech.
After helping Bezos launch Amazon Marketplace, our duo would help him launch Amazon Mechanical Turk.
This is basically the fiver of the corporate world.
Companies can outsource brute force work like data validation and content moderation through Amazon.
By the time Mechanical Turk came out though, Venki and Anand had spent the better part of a decade at Amazon, and they started to feel that it was time to move on.
They didn't directly switch over to Walmart though.
They would actually lean back into entrepreneurship and start another company together called Cosmix.
Cosmix was a rather niche company, but it was extremely valuable for the enterprise customers that were in that niche.
What did Cosmix do, you ask?
Well, they specialized in search engine optimization.
More specifically, they aimed to transform vertical search engines into horizontal search engines.
Vertical searching is the most rudimentary type of searching.
It's when people enter a keyword and the engine searches a given database for matches.
Horizontal searching, on the other hand, is more like the YouTube algorithm.

It uses the keyword that you entered along with your previous searches and purchases to display the products that you would be most likely to buy as opposed to the products that are the closest match to the keyword that you entered.
Again, standard stuff nowadays, but a novel concept back in the 2000s.
Venki and Anand would go on to build an encyclopedia for nearly 5 million categories with hundreds and hundreds of parameters.
For example, they accounted for where customers were searching from, what cars they drove, what music they listened to, and even what type of cheese they liked.
You could use all these parameters to display the products that would be the most likely to convert into sales.
So, for obvious reasons, this technology was extremely valuable for retailers and they would eat it up.
Cosmix would end up growing hundreds of percent per year, partnering with several organizations, and even acquiring smaller companies.
So, Cosmix was no doubt killing it, but the same could not be said about Walmart.
Walmart wasn't exactly doing bad, but they weren't exactly doing well either.
You see, maturity had hit Walmart like a ton of bricks, and they were feeling the pain.
During the 80s and 90s, Walmart had grown a ridiculous 60x, putting all other retailers to shame.
But for 10 years now, Walmart had gone nowhere.
If the industry as a whole had stagnated, this wouldn't be too big of a problem, but e-commerce was still growing exponentially, and Walmart was simply missing out.
They did have an online presence, but compared to Amazon, this was largely a joke.
In fact, if you navigate back to their 2010 website, you're hit with a Adobe Flash Player is no longer supported warning.
Amazon, on the other hand, already had a recommended section and was already evolving into its current form.
Walmart clearly needed to pivot, but if they wanted to stage such a large turnaround, they needed the help of experts.
And what better experts to hire than the former Amazon directors that helped launch Amazon Marketplace and were now working on a highly valuable search engine.
And with that, Walmart would acquire Cosmix for $300 million in cash in early 2011.
It's easy to say that Walmart just bought their way into tech, but that's not really the case.
Yes, they had a lot of help from Cosmix, but Walmart deserves a bunch of credit as well.
Usually with acquisitions, companies try to integrate the child company into the parent company.
They want the child company to adopt the same culture, the same philosophies, the same salary bans, and so on.
Walmart, on the other hand, decided to take a much different approach.
They could clearly tell that what they were already doing wasn't working, so it didn't make a whole lot of sense to force this up and coming company to also do the same thing.
Instead, they would decide to adapt Walmart to what Cosmix was doing.
This takes an insane amount of humility and most companies would never make such a pivot, but Walmart did.
While all of their peers were paying legacy company tech salaries like AT &T and IBM, Walmart was paying FANG level salaries, or at least as close as they could get.
Obviously, they would never be able to pay as much as actual tech companies as they simply don't have the same margins.
But for a physical retailer, they were paying extraordinary amounts.
This allowed them to recruit some of the best talent out there, including a bunch of Amazon employees who were trying to escape the toxic work culture at Amazon.
Suddenly, Walmart had all the resources they needed to build a modern online platform, and that's exactly what they would do.
But they didn't just blindly copy Amazon, they did indeed add their own twist.
One of the biggest bottlenecks for Amazon is their fulfillment centers.
To continue driving down delivery times, Amazon has to keep opening up fulfillment centers that are increasingly omnipresent.
I mean, if you want to deliver within 24 hours to any address, you need fulfillment centers within 24 hours of every address.
That's kind of how that works, but the problem with opening so many fulfillment centers is that you quickly reach the point of diminishing returns.
Opening more centers becomes more expensive than it's worth, but if you want to keep driving down delivery times to 2 hours and 1 hour, that's the only way.
But see, this isn't nearly as big of an issue for Walmart because, well, they're already omnipresent, at least within the US.
In fact, the average American lives within 4.2 miles of a Walmart.
So, forget one hour delivery, Walmart could do 15 minute delivery.
All they had to do was convert their thousands of stores into high tech warehouses, and that's exactly what they've been doing.
Walmart Global Tech could handle all of the AI and machine learning involved in running such a large retail operation.
What products needed to be carried by which stores and when?
What routes do their trucks need to make to ensure that every store has what they need at all times and so on and so forth?
Meanwhile, Walmart's legacy business could focus on logistics, fulfillment, and customer satisfaction.
This strategy was already working out well in the late 2010s, but the pandemic changed things up big time.
You see, Walmart had one thing that Amazon is still struggling to offer, fresh groceries for pickup and delivery.
And this was exactly the advantage that Walmart needed to cement themselves as an e-commerce juggernaut.
Today, Walmart has been able to regain the momentum that they had lost in the 2000s.
Over the past 7 years, their stock has tripled and their fundamentals have led the way.
In fact, Walmart is the number one revenue driver in the entire world, pulling in a crazy $600 billion per year.
Now, I do want to note that their earnings have not kept up with the revenue growth, but this isn't really a concern.
The main reason for this is simply that Walmart has been investing much of their profits into the tech side of the business and revenue growth.
And for modern companies, growth is simply way more valuable than the bottom line.
Amazon, for example, is still not profitable, but they're worth over a trillion dollars.
So, it looks like Walmart has not only adapted to modern tech, but they've adapted to the modern business landscape.
And that is why Walmart is so successful to this day.

title: YouTube Should Feel Stupid For Banning AdBlock
note: Opinion essay arguing one position in steps (reputation, bans fail, competition, better alternative), using Netflix, prohibition and Chrome as analogies.
sections: Bans don't work: prohibition and workarounds
The right strategy and slippery slope
lines: YouTube is stupid for blocking ad block.
Not just from some sort of, information should be free and screw big corporations mindset, but from a grounded, fundamental perspective.
This might be confusing to hear.
Wouldn't blocking ad block lead to more people viewing ads and or upgrading to YouTube premium?
That would lead to more revenue for YouTube, not less, right?
Well, while that argument may seem true at first glance, it doesn't hold up against scrutiny, and here's why.
First of all, let's establish just how popular Adblock really is.
As of 2021, 42.7% of internet users worldwide use Adblock.
This number is likely a good amount lower on YouTube because people tend to watch YouTube on mobile devices and TVs where Adblock doesn't work, but the point still stands.
Adblock is extraordinarily popular.
And when you combine this with the scale of YouTube, we're talking about hundreds of millions of people.
YouTube literally has 2 billion monthly active users, so even something that affects only 10% of users adds up to 200 million people, much less 42.7%.
So, safe to say, we're talking about a lot of people, which opens up YouTube to substantial reputational risk.
You might be asking why?
After all, YouTube isn't doing anything wrong by forcing ads.
It's their platform, and they're providing billions of people with value, whether that be educational value or entertainment value.
So, it's only fair that YouTube expects to gain some value in return, whether that's directly through YouTube Premium or indirectly through ads.
That only makes sense, but the reality is that what's fair is mostly irrelevant.
You see, people often like to get mad at big corporations and say that all these companies care about is maximizing profits over everything else.
And that's completely true.
But here's the thing, it's the same way with like 90% of people.
The only thing that the vast majority of people care about is what value they get from a business.
They don't give a crap about the business making money.
They might have some sympathy towards a mom and pop shop or local restaurant, but with a megacorporation like Google, that sympathy is non-existent.
In fact, most people are happy when these companies lose money or embarrass themselves.
How do I know that?
Well, those are usually my most viewed videos.
So, with that being said, the average person simply does not care if Adblock is losing Google money.
And this is extremely important to note because it lays the foundation for how people will react to an ad block ban.
Hundreds of millions of people have been conditioned for over a decade to watch YouTube for free without any ads.
When you change that, they're naturally gonna get mad.
When hundreds of millions of users get mad, you start seeing substantial backlash against the company.
But this doesn't manifest in the way that you might expect.
It's not like people are gonna go throw fits on Twitter and make a scene.
Wait, never mind, people are already doing that.
But that isn't most people.
Most people will never argue that adblock is good or that YouTube is wrong for banning adblock because, well, they know that it's mostly fair.
But what people will do is hold a grudge that they express in several different ways, and the perfect example of this is Netflix.
You've probably noticed that over the past 12 to 18 months, people have suddenly started to hate Netflix.
If you read through YouTube comments about Netflix, you'd be convinced that the company is on the brink of collapse or something, which is absolutely not true.
Yes, they lost subscribers for a quarter or two, but they're already gaining subscribers once again.
Also, even if they did stagnate, over 200 million paying subscribers is nothing to complain about.
But then why are people so pessimistic about Netflix, even rooting for its demise?
Well, it really just comes down to this.
Netflix is increasing prices, they're implementing ads, they're cracking down on password sharing, and they're losing content to competitors.
That's the bottom line, but most people will never admit this.
Instead, they'll point their finger at some BS reasons, some of which may have even been advantages previously.
Take Netflix's content catalog for example.
Nowadays, it's popular to say that there's a lot of stuff on Netflix, but none of it's good.
When you were sharing passwords with four friends and only paying $4 per month, having too much content doesn't seem like a negative.
In fact, I bet most people viewed it as, Yo, this is awesome.
I'm never gonna watch most of this stuff, but the fact that I can get all of this for $4 per month, that's insane.
But when you have to pay full price, the attitude suddenly switches to, Bro, I'm paying $20 per month and they can't even show me something that I want to watch.
What is this?
It's the same Netflix in both scenarios.
Even the pricing is the same.
The only difference is password sharing, but now it's the platform that sucks.
The same sort of thing will happen on YouTube.
Most people will never blame YouTube directly for blocking Adblock.
But they'll take out their anger on every other shortcoming of the platform, like the algorithm.
them.
It's no secret that YouTube recommends some random stuff from time to time.
Normally, people take this pretty jokingly.
They might go on to these random videos and comment, yo, the algorithm is drunk again.
But when they're forced into buying YouTube premium and the same thing happens, the attitude shifts to, dude, Google is a trillion dollar platform and they can't even figure out recommendations?
This is unacceptable.
People are naturally really good at finding justifications for their grudges.
In fact, that's probably why many of you are watching this video right now.
You want justification for using Adblock.
Whether this is fair or not is besides the point.
It's simply basic human nature, and as a company, it's in YouTube's best interest to be cognizant of this bias and act accordingly.
Otherwise, it may not be long until they end up with a brand favorability like Netflix at a staggering 11%.
Putting the whole branding aspect of blocking ad block to this side, the reality of such bans is that they don't even work.
The most classic example of a ban not working is prohibition.
Back in the 1920s, the US decided that it would be a great idea to ban alcohol, but But this didn't stop people from drinking.
It simply led to illegal production and black markets, not to mention, it also led to a rise in gang violence and organized crime.
Congress would eventually repeal this law 13 years later, but we don't even have to look that far.
We can just look at Adblock itself.
The fact that there are multiple adblocks on the Chrome Web Store itself with hundreds of millions of downloads each show that people will work around rules that they don't like.
If Adblock is no longer the bypass for ads, they'll find a new bypass.
Maybe that means downloading an app that streams YouTube videos without ads or downloading the videos through some sort of third-party application.
YouTube may be able to stop funny business from happening directly on the platform, but they can't stop it from happening just outside the platform.
This could easily lead to a situation in which people still watch YouTube videos, but just not on YouTube itself.
This is a massive problem for YouTube because as Bill Gates said, as long as they're gonna steal it, we want them to steal ours.
Similarly, if people are gonna watch YouTube videos without ads, it's in YouTube's best interest that they still watch it on YouTube itself.
Sure, they may not make money off these viewers, but they still have control and influence over these viewers which could be monetized later down the road.
If people migrate over to some bootlegged version of YouTube though, that's no longer the case.
But it's not just these viewers that YouTube risks losing, YouTube also risks losing the casual viewer.
The casual viewer probably isn't gonna go out of their way to pirate YouTube videos, but if they start feeling that watching ads is annoying, they'll likely just watch YouTube less.
And in an era where attention is the most valuable currency, YouTube is actively trading long-term attention and even addiction for short-term cash.
Simply not a great trade.
Also, this trade may open up YouTube to competition.
For the longest time, YouTube was impossible to compete against because it was universally accessible and completely free.
But as Google cracks down on ads, competitors now have the ability to say, come to our platform, we don't have ads.
This is exactly what Netflix did with cable TV.
Before, viewers didn't care about such temptations because, well, they could get the same experience on YouTube itself with ad blockers.
But as Google cracks down, such alternatives may seem more and more enticing.
So if YouTube wants to protect their monopoly, well then, allowing ad block is ironically their best move.
If people are gonna steal, you want them to steal from you.
Okay, all of this makes sense from a theoretical standpoint.
A lot of people use adblock, so clamping down so hard will no doubt piss off a bunch of people and threaten the monopoly.
But then, what is the alternative?
How do you go about monetizing viewers who don't want to pay for YouTube premium and use adblock?
Well, the answer is simply what Google was already doing.
Google had it right the first time.
You may not know this, but Google actually has their own ad block that's built into Chrome, and this is automatically enabled.
This likely seems super counterintuitive for an ad company, but this is the way.
For any sort of sales effort, the number one priority is to get eyeballs.
Only after that can you sell or monetize or whatever.
Google understood this perfectly.
Their number one priority was to get people to use Chrome.
They didn't want ads to be the reason that someone chose Safari or Edge over Chrome.
And this strategy worked out perfectly.
Basically, everyone started using Chrome.
And once everyone was on the platform, Google focused on monetization.
But with this new ad block crackdown on YouTube, and it seems like Google may have their priorities mixed up.
Now, you may be asking, if Google never cracks down, how will they ever be able to monetize?
Well, for that, we can just look at Google search once again.
There's plenty of ad blocks for Google search ads as well, but Google didn't ban these or take them off the Chrome Web Store.
Instead, they straight up just partnered with them.
That's right, Google pays ad blocking services to whitelist Google-specific ads.
This is why most ad blockers do not work with Google search ads.
These ad blockers are literally getting paid to show them, but they won't just show any ad.
They only show ads that they feel are discreet and don't take away from the user experience because their reputation is on the line.
If the ads are too annoying, people will simply blame the ad block for not being effective, not Google, and that's the genius behind the strategy.
For a small fee, Google is able to run their ads without being the bad guy, and if people do get annoyed, it's the ad blocker that takes the heat.
I think Google should have taken this same approach on YouTube.
Now, you might be saying that this is misleading, and it is, but that's not the goal.
The goal is not to trick people.
The goal is to make the ad experience so good that it's not actually a negative.
Ideally, people shouldn't even notice that the ad block isn't working.
As such, the right strategy isn't to force people to watch ads by banning ad block.
The right strategy is to make the ad experience so pleasant that people don't even feel the need to use ad block in the first place.
Google understood this perfectly for the longest time, and they still definitely do.
Though with the recent crackdown, it looks like they're willing to take a gamble.
They're essentially betting that people are so addicted to YouTube that they can force ads and get away with it.
And they might be able to with this move specifically, but that's a slippery slope.
If they can force us to watch one ad, why not make it two, three, four, five ads?
And before you know it, YouTube will be indistinguishable from cable TV.
Is that where YouTube's heading?
Only time will tell, but this is not a great first step, and that's why YouTube should feel stupid for blocking adblock.

title: How To Make $300,000,000,000 By Getting The CCP Drunk
note: Business case study built on debunking the origin myth, then tracing political storytelling to the status brand; thesis is branding power.
sections: Mao, Nixon and the elite drink
lines: How do you make $300 billion by selling liquor?
Well, the answer is by getting the CCP or the Chinese Communist Party addicted to it and then charging them a fortune.
This probably sounds quite daunting and borderline impossible, but that's precisely what a company called Quechomotai has managed to do.
That name probably doesn't ring a bell, but Quechomotai is actually the 25th largest company in the world with a market cap of $307 billion.
That's more than Pepsi and Coca-Cola, which means that Quechua Motai is the largest beverage company in the world.
In fact, they're almost the largest food company in the world as well, only beaten out by Nestle.
They're also the second largest Chinese company, only beaten out by Tencent themselves.
This is no doubt quite impressive, but when you take a look at how much Motai costs, It all makes sense.
A single bottle of Muay Thai costs anywhere between $300 to $44,000 depending on the age.
For a 500ml bottle, this translates to $0.60 to $88 per milliliter.
For perspective, even human blood only costs $0.39 per milliliter.
And that's just normal Muay Thai.
It's not uncommon to hear about vintage Muay Thai selling for more than a million dollars.
This has allowed Quechou to grow to $20 billion in revenue and $13 billion in net profit every single year with a net margin of 53%.
But it wasn't always like this.
In fact, just 20 years ago, the entire company was barely pulling in $200 million worth of revenue and $75 million worth of profit.
This means that within a matter of 20 years, Quechou has managed to grow 100 to 200x.
And this is very much reflected in the stock price, which has run up as much as 290x.
Even if you bought Google at IPO, you would have only gotten a 50x return.
So, how did Quechamotay go from being a boutique distillery to being the world's largest beverage company with a drink that tastes like rotten cabbage?
Well, the answer is a bit of deception, some powerful connections, and a lot of brilliant marketing.
story of Kuecho Motai.
Taking a look back, Kuecho is by no means a heritage company.
In fact, the current version wasn't even created till the end of 1999, but the same cannot be said about Motai, which according to some sources dates back over 2000 years to 135 BC.
This was during the rise of the Han Dynasty, not to be confused with the Hans from Mulan.
The Han Dynasty is one of the strongest dynasties in China's history, having ruled over much of modern-day China for over four centuries.
Many of the traditions and cultures that we now associate with China today can be traced back to the Hans, so it wouldn't be surprising if Muay Thai was also popularized by the Hans.
The story goes that a diplomat from the Western Han Dynasty named Tang Meng would travel to an independent kingdom named Nan Yu back in 135 BC.
During this trip, Tang would apparently enjoy a drink which he brought back to the Han Dynasty.
And according to legends and Quechou's own history page, this is the roots of Muay Thai.
But what if I told you that all of that was just a facade, a legend popularized by Quechou for marketing purposes?
You see, according to historical scholars and records, there was indeed a man named Tang Ming who traveled to Nan Yu back in 135 BC.
There's even evidence that he did enjoy a drink there, but this drink was not Mu Tai, it was Zhu Jing.
So the reality is that Mu Tai is nowhere near that ancient, but it's in Kuei Cho's best interest to convince people that it is.
A lot of the appeal of Mu Tai is that it's what the greatest Chinese people of history drank and it's the drink of China.
This ideology and Chinese pride is what really sells the drink because the drink itself is vile and putrid, and I can't understate that.
In fact, here are some reviews.
Imagine rotten cabbage, ethyl alcohol, and paint thinner blended and strained.
The first time I tried Mo Tai, it tasted like engine oil.
I've never met anybody even at the heights of alcoholic derangement prepared to admit that they actually liked the taste.
None of these reviews are that surprising though when you consider that Mu Tai is 53% alcohol.
So yeah, Mu Tai is a terrible tasting drink that has nothing to do with the Han Dynasty.
The real roots of Mu Tai actually go back to the much more modern Qing Dynasty who were in power between 1644 and 1911.
Sometime during this period, some northern Chinese distillerists would apparently introduce some advanced techniques to create a distinctive type of Baiju known as Mo Tai.
But again, this is mostly just fluff.
The reality is that the invention of Mo Tai was unceremonious and largely unknown because it wasn't really an invention to begin with.
These northern Chinese distillers were simply making classic liquor using the climate and ingredients they had access to.
It just so happened that this climate and these ingredients gave the liquor a unique taste which has since become the iconic taste of Motai.
So while Kweicho likes to claim that Motai is some sort of magic juice with the 2000 year history, Motai is actually just some random local drink with a terrible taste.
But none of this would hold back Motai in the 1900s.
Like with many popular products, the popularity of Muay Thai has more to do with optics than intrinsic value.
And the optics of Muay Thai can be traced back to 1915 to the Panama Pacific International Exposition.
This exposition was held in San Francisco and is one of the most monumental events in American history.
Nine years before the exposition, San Francisco experienced the worst earthquake in its history, estimated to be a magnitude of 7.9.
This exposition was designed to show that not just San Francisco, but all of America was willing to fight through and recover from anything.
As such, this exposition would be marketed like never before and attracted a whopping 18 million people.
The exposition showcased some of the most advanced tech of the time like America's first transcontinental telephone call.
In one corner of this grand exposition though, there was an exhibit for Chinese Muay Thai.
While nowhere near as impressive as a transcontinental telephone call, Muay Thai was no doubt a heavyweight when it came to hard liquor.
The aroma and taste was something that the rest of the world hadn't never experienced.
This not only made them popular at the exposition, but allowed them to straight up win a gold medal establishing China's presence on the world stage.
This was the first time that Muay Thai was linked to Chinese pride, but it was by no means the last.
The event that would certify Muay Thai as a hood classic was the Chinese Civil War between 1927 and 1949.
This war was fought between the Republic of China backed by the United States and the Chinese Communist Party backed by the Soviet Union.
The army of the CCP is referred to as the People's Liberation Army, and the story goes that Muay Thai is what led this army to victory.
Apparently, the Red Army soldiers drank Muay Thai to lift their spirits and disinfect their wounds during the Battle of Chishwai River.
This battle turned out to be the turning point of the bloody 22-year-long war, leading to the CCP's victory.
And as this battle became legendary, so did Muay Thai.
Now, to be clear, we don't even know if these soldiers actually used Muay Thai, but that's the story that's propagated by Quechua Muay Thai and the CCP.
After the war, the CCP would double down on this image advertising that Muay Thai was the favorite drink of the Chinese leader, Mao Zedong.
But it wasn't just Mao who enjoyed this drink either.
Pretty soon, Muay Thai became quite popular with foreign leaders as well.
Likely the most notable instance of this was with President Richard Nixon in 1972.
Thanks to the Cold War, China and the US were basically sworn enemies up until this point.
So, this meeting between Richard Nixon and Chinese leaders out in Lai was very much unprecedented.
And to celebrate this monumental event in Beijing, the CCP would of course serve Muay Thai.
We don't know what President Nixon thought about the drink, but his Secretary of State Henry Kissinger was much more vocal.
He said, I think if we drink enough Muay Thai, we can solve anything.
This event cemented Muay Thai as not just the drink of the CCP, but the drink of the elite, leading us to the modern day Kweja Muay Thai.
Over the next few decades, Muay Thai transitioned from being a pride thing to being a status symbol.
It was the drink of millionaires and billionaires, and if you were hosting someone important, serving them Muay Thai was the standard, but there was no standard brand.
While all Muay Thai came from the city of Muay Thai, there were several brands that you could choose from up until 1999.
In 1999, the CCP would consolidate all of the most notable Muay Thai distilleries into one state-owned enterprise called Kwechomotai.
While this did create a monopoly, it wasn't a very big deal.
It's not like Apple and Google were merging.
Rather, it was a bunch of local distilleries who barely had a combined revenue of $200 million.
But then, how did such a small operation become the world's largest beverage company?
Well, the answer isn't rocket science.
One look at China's GDP graph will explain a lot.
Back in 1999, China's GDP stood at $1 trillion.
Today, China's GDP stands at $17.7 trillion, meaning that China's GDP has grown 17x.
For perspective, America's GDP has only grown about 2.5x during the same time period.
So, Kuechou Muay Thai has acted as a sort of index for Chinese wealth and the power of the CCP.
In fact, the vast majority of Muay Thai is consumed by government officials.
In 2012, it was estimated that half of all sales came from government-related customers.
President Xi has tried to fight against this.
One of the first things he did after coming to power in 2012 was crack down on the spending of CCP officials.
This did momentarily reduce the price of Muay Thai, but it has since recovered, which just goes to show how powerful the brand really is.
but it's not all good news.
For one, Muay Thai is only relevant within China.
In fact, 97% of all Kui Chou's revenue comes from China alone.
While Westerners do often try to drink when visiting China, they rarely pick it up as a habit because it tastes like drinking liquid razor blades.
Not to mention the price.
But it's not just Westerners who are shying away from Muay either.
China's youth is also not so fond of the drink, primarily because of the taste and association with older generations.
Currently, the core demographic for the liquor is 40 to 60 year old men.
So, only time will tell if Muay Thai will survive through generations, but as for the imminent future, it's not going anywhere.
In fact, in late 2022, Guaichou briefly overtook tension to become China's largest company, period.
So, there's really no question that Kuei Chou Muay Thai has basically become the expensive alcoholic Coca-Cola of China, and that won't be changing anytime soon.
In the end, it's easy to dismiss Kuei Chou Muay Thai as some sort of bougie company that sells ridiculously priced liquor to China's elite.
But when we peel back the layers, it's clear that Quechua Muay Thai and more specifically Muay Thai itself is much more than just that.
It's really a testament to the power of branding.
Objectively speaking, Muay Thai has virtually nothing going for it.
It's a byproduct of a random Chinese city's climate and resources.
But through the power of narrative, storytelling, and branding, Quichu Muay Thai has made Muay Thai into a Chinese icon.
They were able to tie together random events from over 2000 years ago to modern events that hit close to home like the Chinese Civil War and Mao Zedong.
And while there may be a longer term trend away from Muay Thai, just like there is with soda, Muay Thai is by no means going anywhere but up anytime soon.
And that is how you make $300 billion by getting the CCP drunk.

title: Goodwill? More Like Ill Will - The Ugly Truth
note: Exposé in escalating sections (money, wages, deaths) with one anecdote, Dave Goody, as the emotional peak.
lines: Goodwill, more like ill will.
On the surface, Goodwill seems like the friendly neighborhood thrift store focused on giving back to the community and fighting inequality.
On paper, they're a non-profit that isn't owned by anyone which means no shareholders, no stock, and hopefully no anti-consumer behavior.
Their board of directors is actually filled with a bunch of volunteers, so theoretically, their only goal would be to give back to the community which they do do in several ways.
They have a bunch of career programs that help underprivileged people make some cash and learn new skills.
They're also one of the only organizations out there that will hire people with disabilities aside from the government.

They've also been around for quite some time, as Goodwill has been around for over 120 years, which means that they've donated tens of billions, if not hundreds of billions of dollars to charitable services.
In fact, in 2018 alone, they pulled in $6.1 billion in revenue, out of which $5.27 billion was spent on charitable services.
So, they're doing a great job, right?
Well, yes and no.
There are definitely commendable portions of Goodwill, and I don't want to take away from that.
But there's also a lot of reprehensible portions as well.
For one, Goodwill isn't even all that charitable in the first place.
Goodwill claims that 82% of their revenue goes towards programs and services for people in need.
Some regions even have percentages as high as 90%.
But this is largely misleading as this does not mean that 82% or 90% of the money that you spend at Goodwill actually goes to charity.
In fact, there's evidence that as little as 1 eighth of their profit actually goes to the main programs that they advertise.
Also, you know how goodwill employs disabled people?
Well, this may be more exploitative than generous.
You see, there are special laws that allow organizations to pay disabled people as little as 22 to 41 cents per hour, which is already quite bad, but it doesn't stop there.
Disabled employees also don't have the same protections that everyone else does, which makes them the perfect scapegoats to hand off dangerous tasks to.
And when it comes to whistleblowers and employees fighting back, Goodwill may as well just be a private corporation as that's how they behave.
They usually threaten, fire, and publicly discredit people that fight back.
So here's the truth about Goodwill and why you should think twice before donating to or purchasing from Goodwill.
Jumping straight into their donations, Goodwill claims that they spend between 80 and 90% of their revenue on charitable services, and technically speaking, this is probably accurate.
As we touched on, in 2018, Goodwill pulled in $6.1 billion worth of revenue and donated $5.27 billion.
So, that falls right in line with about 86% of the revenue being donated, but this doesn't mean what you think it means.
Any normal person would probably think that this means that for every dollar you spend at Goodwill, 86 cents gets donated.
Or at least maybe for every dollar they profit, they donate 86 cents, but neither of these are true.
The reality is that much of Goodwill's charitable spending isn't even funded by us, the customers.
It's actually funded by various government organizations.
Take Goodwill Omaha for instance.
They have a bunch of job training and assistance programs, but nearly all of these activities were funded by government grants and contracts.
And you know their program to employ disabled people?
Well, that was primarily funded by school districts.
It turns out that out of the $4 million worth of profit generated by the region, only $557,000 or a little more than an eighth was spent on these flagship job programs.
And keep in mind, that's profit, not revenue.
Only 1 eighth of the profit is being spent on these programs.
So imagine how little of the consumer-based revenue ends up at these programs.
But then where are all these profits going instead?
People are literally donating items for free, so surely Goodwill shouldn't have too many manufacturing or shipping or sourcing expenses.
Well, the official destination is administrative overhead, but that's just a fancy term for large executive compensation.
Goodwill actually has a history of paying executives super large salaries.
In 2014, for example, they paid their CEO Frank McGree $933,000.
This actually won him so much criticism and backlash that he would end up resigning, but things haven't exactly gotten better.
His successors were paid a base salary of $434,000, and there are rumors that total compensation reached as high as $1.1 million.
Though, Goodwill does dispute the total compensation numbers.
Either way though, executives and high-level managers are being paid multiple six figures.
In fact, Change.org claims that the top managers at 150 Goodwill locations are being paid more than $30 million.
Also, some of these people don't seem to have any issue charging a bunch of personal expenses onto corporate cards.
Former CFO Tim Liggett, for example, charged over $75,000 worth of personal purchases onto a Goodwill corporate card.
So yeah, that's where much of the profit is going.
Also, for the record, I have no issue with people making a lot of money.
If you want to make a lot of money, go to a private company or start your own business.
Don't leech off of a non-profit.
Also, one more thing about these executives is that many of them are politicians by trade.
The current CEO Steve Preston for example was the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development under President George Bush.
And the former CEO Jim Kibbins was part of the White House Council for Community Solutions under President Barack Obama, so take that for what you will.
But it's not just your donations that Goodwill is exploiting, they're also exploiting the people who work there.
One of the trademarks of goodwill is providing jobs to underprivileged people, and especially people with disabilities.
But once again, this isn't as great as it sounds.
It's actually really bad.
You see, goodwill leverages an archaic role found in the Fair Labor Standards Act which was passed way back in 1938.
Section 14c of the act basically allows companies to legally pay disabled workers wages that are lower than minimum wage.
This has resulted in disabled people in Pennsylvania earning as little as $0.22, $0.38, and $0.41 per hour.
Goodwill claims that these are outlier cases and they're probably right about that.
But just because the average disabled worker isn't making these absurdly low wages doesn't mean that they're making good wages either.
Also, I wanted to point out that it's not just Goodwill that's exploiting these rules either.
Basically, every organization that hires disabled workers other than the government leverages tactic.
Disabled workers at Applebee's for example were making $397 to $596 per hour, and disabled workers at Barnes and Noble were making $380 to $485 per hour.
So, it's kind of an industry-wide problem, and it doesn't seem like it will be fixed anytime soon either.
Goodwill has actually fought against proposals that suggest raising the minimum wage.
Their reasoning is that they simply can't afford to pay employees anymore, which doesn't really make sense when you consider how much their executives make and how little actually gets donated.
But not only does Goodwill pay disabled workers low wages, they also expect a lot of work.
In fact, disabled workers are straight up tested for their effectiveness.
Disabled employees have to take a time test to see how quickly they can sort and hang clothes.
The ideal rate is 100 garments within 32 minutes.
For most people, this is a pretty reasonable target, but if you're blind for example, this becomes exponentially harder.
And if you don't reach this target, your hourly wage gets deducted proportionately.
This is how you end up with employees making ridiculously low wages.
One blind Goodwill employee named Shayla Legland for example was already only making $3.99 per hour, but Goodwill wanted to reduce this to $2.75 an hour.
Shayla would just end up quitting, but this is not a luxury that most disabled workers have, so they're just stuck making $2.75 an hour.
Goodwill claims that they're not exploiting workers and that they're actually providing opportunity as 80% of disabled people in the US don't have any opportunity at all.
But pity jobs that milk these people for the lowest wages possible isn't the same as truly uplifting and supporting the disabled community.
As Alice put it, at least we gave them jobs is not a progressive socially responsible move.
If you didn't think that exploiting disabled workers was bad enough, well, it gets even worse as Goodwill has been linked with several workplace deaths.
Goodwill's PR and legal team loved to write off these deaths as tragic incidents that were not their fault.
But when you take a look at the evidence, that story becomes a lot harder to believe.
Take former Goodwill employee Dave Goody for example.
Dave only worked at Goodwill for a mere six months as a waste management driver, but let's just say that he went to hell and back during this short tenure.
One day during his shift, he noticed that the trailer brakes weren't working when activated from the cab.
So, as a responsible driver, he would pull over, shut down the truck, and call management.
He was hoping that Goodwill would send out a technician who could fix the issue.
But instead, they just sent out another driver that was willing to drive the truck despite the issue.
This was no doubt jarring for Dave, and he would of course go ahead and file complaints to Goodwill regarding this incident.
But this was by no means the only safety hazard that he noticed.
He also noticed a major safety hazard regarding Goodwill's trash compactors.
He reported, quote, based on my personal observations, most employees now operating compactors at each plant have not received the required training.
He would go on to warn that this could result in injuries, deaths, and fines, which could all be completely avoided if proper training was implemented.
But as fate would have it, Goodwill would take no action, and a 26-year-old employee named Abraham Garza would be killed by a trash compactor just a few weeks later.
This would have been a good time for Goodwill to apologize to Dave for not taking his complaints more seriously.
But instead, they would fire Dave and blame the incident on Abraham.
Kalosha would eventually step in and fine Goodwill $106,000, but even after that, Goodwill would continue to maintain that they were not liable.
If this was a one-off incident, they would have some plausible deniability, but Goodwill actually has a history of on-site injuries.
In 2008, a 27-year-old was crushed to death by a trash compactor lift.
In 2014, a 69-year-old was crushed by a forklift.
And in 2017, a 54-year-old was killed by another forklift.
And the worst part is that many of these deaths are amongst disabled workers.
You see, employers aren't as liable for disabled workers because the disability may increase the chances of a workplace injury.
So, goodwill is literally incentivized to place disabled workers in dangerous jobs, and it seems like that is exactly what they're doing, leading to many disabled workers literally being killed.
Those are just a few of the most notable issues at Goodwill, but they're by no means the only issues.
For example, another major critique against Goodwill is that they send clothes that they can't sell in western countries to developing countries.
And given that these were donated items, they can sell these clothes for super cheap which screws up the local clothing industries.
And the only reason that Goodwill is able to get away with so much is because they're a non-profit.
If a for-profit company like Amazon was exploring disabled workers by paying them ridiculously low wages and exposing them to significant workplace risk, they would be crucified by public opinion.
But since Goodwill is a non-profit slash charity, these issues often get glossed over.
Now again, this isn't to say that Goodwill is completely evil like Big Pharma or something.
They do do some awesome things, but they've also got some major issues that have been ignored for way too long.
And just maybe, if we bring enough attention to these issues, we can actually get them to change, but that's just what I think.

title: 171,849 "Self Offings" - Is Eli Lilly Involved? (Allegedly)
note: Corporate history told chronologically with an alleged-wrongdoing frame; opens on a sensational Prozac claim, flashes back to the founder, then a list of harmful drugs culminating in Prozac.
lines: Since 2000, the self-offing rate in the United States has increased by 50%, from 11 per 100,000 people to 16 per 100,000 people.
Many would blame modern tech for much of this increase.
People are more glued to their phones and computers than ever before, leading to less human interactions and more isolation, resulting in higher levels of depression and thus more self-offings.
Now, that could very well be a factor, but something that has a much more concrete connection is a medication called fluoxetine or Prozac.
Prozac is a medication that is supposed to treat depression, OCD, panic disorders, and bulimia.
Theoretically, it is supposed to accomplish this by increasing serotonin levels inside the brain, which seem to have a positive correlation with mood, emotion, and sleep.
Today, Prozac is the 25th most prescribed medication with an estimated 23 million patients within the US alone.
So, at first glance, Prozac seems like a miracle medication that has helped hundreds of millions of people overcome the darkest parts of their lives.
But what if I told you that Prozac was actually doing the exact opposite?
You see, while Prozac may be successful at giving patients a surge of joy or excitement, over the long term, it can actually make patients more likely to end it all.
Surely, such a severe side effect was an unintended consequence, and something that Eli Lilly, the creators of Prozac, simply didn't discover during their initial studies.

Well, actually, there's reports from the British Medical Journal suggesting that Eli Lilly not only knew about these side effects, but that they went as far as concealing the evidence that was suggesting this.
One of their own studies found that 38% of patients taking Prozac displayed symptoms of agitation and aggression, while only 19% of patients taking the placebo displayed the same symptoms.
And this was way back in 1988, but Eli Lilly, allegedly, never handed over these findings to the FDA clinical reviewer who was responsible for approving the medication.
Now, this could have been an honest mistake, but when coincidence aligns with opportunity, that's rarely the case.
Not to mention, this is just one of Eli Lilly's many allegations and settlements.
But despite the shady history, Eli Lilly is not only doing well, they're doing phenomenal.
In fact, their stock is up 5x within the past 5 years alone, which has given them a market cap of just over $400 billion.
At this point, they're often trading spots with J &J for the title of world's largest pharmaceutical company.
So, here's how Eli Lilly managed to make $400 billion worth of blood money.
Taking a look back, the story of Eli Lilly dates back to the late 1800s to a man named Eli Lilly.
Eli was a Civil War veteran, having served as a colonel during the war.
He wanted to transfer the altruistic ambitions of the Civil War into a company of his own, only instead of fighting slavery, he would be fighting disease.
And with that, Eli would open up a small laboratory in Indianapolis in 1876.
Eli wasn't creating anything groundbreaking per se.
He was simply producing and selling medications that were already on the market.
But thanks to his war legacy and a lack of big pharma, it didn't take Eli very long to get the people of Indianapolis behind him.
One of the first medicines that Eli sold was quinine which is used to treat malaria.
This alone allowed him to reach over $4,000 worth of sales by the end of the first year loan.
That's over $120,000 today.
Within just three years, he would over 10x that amount, growing to $49,000 in sales or over $1.3 million today.
All of this extra revenue gave Eli plenty of headroom to expand and invest back into the business, and that's exactly what he would do.
In 1878, Eli would hire his brother James as his first full-time salesman, and James would start marketing the product across the nation.
Back at home, Eli was also heavily investing into research and development.
One of their first inventions was adding fruity flavors and sugar to their pills which made them much more palatable and thus far more popular.
As their medicines gained popularity across the nation, Eli would go ahead and formally incorporate the company in 1881 and this marked the beginning of Eli Lilly's monumental rise.
Within the next 20 years, Eli Lilly would grow to over 2,000 product lines, more than $300,000 in annual sales, and nationwide relevance, but Eli never let the success get to his head.
He strongly believed that the industry needed ethical reform, that miracle medicine needed to be replaced by medications that had strong scientific backgrounds and mountains of evidence.
These are the only types of medication that Eli carried up until his death in 1898, and his son Josiah would uphold this legacy after he took over.
During the early 1900s, Eli Lilly would become masters of manufacturing, which was really the secret behind their extraordinary reach and scale.
In fact, Eli Lilly was so good at manufacturing that they would often have excess capacity that they would sell off to their competitors.
By 1917, they were operating the largest capsule factory in the world, producing more than 2.5 million capsules per day.

But with Eli's son at the helm, it seems that this success did get to his head, as it wasn't long until we saw the first inklings of monopolistic anti-consumer practices, and this started with none other than insulin.
In 1921, three scientists from the University of Toronto began working on a treatment for diabetes, which at the time was deadly.
These guys would end up developing a commercially producible insulin, which ended up winning them a Nobel Prize.
Eli Lilly was watching all of this unfold from the sidelines, and they were extremely interested in this project from the very beginning.
But to their disappointment, the researchers were extremely hesitant in regards to working with a commercial firm.
They had much more altruistic motives and were more concerned about insulin helping people as opposed to generating a profit.
But despite this, the researchers would eventually team up with Eli Lilly when they realized that this was the only way to reach the scale they dreamed of.
And with that, Eli Lilly began selling insulin in 1923, and they've had a monopoly over insulin ever since.
In fact, to this day, Eli Lilly, Sanofi, and Novo Nordisk control 90% of the US insulin market.
For the first time, Eli Lilly had a medication that people would buy regardless of their financial situation, and this would quickly showed during the Great Depression.
While people were losing their life savings, companies were going bankrupt, and investors were losing millions, Eli Lilly would actually reach record high sales of $13 million in 1932.
That's the same as $287 million today.
As you can see, with insulin, Eli was starting to veer off their altruistic roots, but they had yet to turn to the dark side completely.
In fact, throughout the next few decades, they would be involved in a few commendable efforts starting with World War II.
During the war, Eli would partner with the American Red Cross to process plasma for wounded soldiers.
And by the end of the war, they would process over 2 million pints of blood, which was about 20% of all of the plasma that was processed in the United States.
But their contribution to World War II was nothing in comparison to their contribution to polio.
If you pay attention in history class, the name Jonas Salk may ring a bell.
Salk is the legend that created the polio vaccine, but not only did he create the vaccine, but he also actively chose to not patent it so that it could reach as many people as possible.
Obvious reasons, Sok is often described as a hero and rightfully so, but he didn't do it alone.
While he had created the vaccine, it still had to be distributed to people around the world, and the first person to step up to the plate was of course, Eli Lilly.
But this was also one of the last universally good activities that Eli would participate in.
Since then, most of their philanthropic efforts have had an undertone of branding and marketing, which isn't the worst thing but also not ideal.
But what has really given Eli a bad rep since then is their medications themselves.
One of Eli's first controversial medications was Darvon, which came out in the late 1950s.
The medication was advertised as a mild painkiller, which it was not very effective at, but what it was effective at was getting people addicted.
And this is not too surprising when you consider that it falls into the opioid category.
By the early 1970s, these dangerous side effects were starting to become clear, and that non-profits like Public Citizen were starting to advocate for a ban.
Eli would of course try to defend Darvon, claiming that it was safer and less addictive than morphine.
But the allegations claim that Darvon was actually even less effective than aspirin in terms of pain relief, but even more effective than the white stuff in terms of killing people.
Despite this, it wasn't till 2010 that the FDA would finally ban Darvon, meaning that Eli was able to profit off Darvon for decades.
At least, Darvon was just addictive.
Some of Eli's other medications were straight up harmful like an antibiotic called erythromycin.
In the 1970s, evidence emerged that this antibiotic was toxic for the liver, often resulting in jaundice.
The FDA would initially ask Eli to discontinue the product, but after another review at Eli's request, the FDA would somehow change their mind.
Another Eli medication that was straight up deadly was their synthetic estrogen, DES.
Apparently, the medication was supposed to prevent miscarriages, but it actually just led to women developing cancer.
Worse, it led to their daughters developing cancer as well.
A couple of class action lawsuits were filed against Eli, but none of these really went anywhere as Eli would just pay these people off by settling outside of court.
You would think that Eli would be more careful after these lawsuits, but they would actually become more risk-on with an arthritis medication called Oroflex.
In the early 1980s, dozens of people taking Oroflex would end up dying due to liver and kidney failure.
Any moral pharmaceutical company would pause the sale of Oroflex and conduct more testing or at least include a warning label.
But what Eli did was try to cover up the fact that people were dying from regulators.
And this is not an allegation.
This is actually a fact as Eli would end up pleading guilty.
But do you know what the fine for this heinous crime was?
A pitiful $25,000.
Usually we talk about how such fines are nothing in comparison to what these companies earn.
I mean, that's literally something that a lot of everyday people can afford.
Diabetes patients literally have to pay more than this to Eli for insulin over a 5 year period.
So yeah, you can take that for what you will.
All of this brings us into Eli's worst offense, which is of course, Prozac.
In the late 1980s, Eli would launch an antidepressant called Prozac, despite allegedly having evidence that Prozac increased the likelihood of people self-offing.
When third party evidence came out against Prozac, Eli would launch a full-on campaign to defend Prozac.
It appears that Eli was successful at defending Prozac, but that also means that humanity was unsuccessful at defending our most vulnerable.
And the results speak for themselves.
People ending it all has increased by 50% over the past 20 years as hundreds of millions of people took Prozac.
Since then, Eli has battled with hundreds of lawsuits and dozens of fines.
But while this has created some friction for their business, it has by no means stopped the damage.
None of this is to say that Eli Lilly is evil just because they put out medications with side effects.
The reality is that no clinical testing is perfect and some side effects only show up at scale, so that's not a problem.
The reason that Eli Lilly is evil is because they do not respond to this damage.
In fact, they actively try to get away with it.

They deny that their medications are causing the damage, they insist on keeping their medications available despite mounting evidence against them, and they even conceal evidence that makes their medications look bad.
Not to mention, they also exercise monopolistic control over much of the pharmaceutical market.
All for what?
Well, to sell as many medications as possible and to maximize profits over human lives.
And looking at the numbers, this is one thing that Eli is extraordinarily good at as they're headed towards becoming a fortune 10 company.
But while they may still have an empire, it doesn't change that their empire was built on blood.

title: TikTokers Are Getting A Harsh Reality Check
note: Analytical explainer built on a pay-gap hook; stacks causes (advertisers, short-form math, rivals) before the weigh-up of possible fixes. Vine is the comparison case.
sections: YouTube and Instagram face it too
Silver lining: ByteDance and the CCP
lines: Pay on TikTok is horrendous.
Now, before you go to the comment section and leave angry remarks, let me explain.
TikTok only pays about 2 to 4 cents per 1,000 views, so even if you get a ridiculous amount of views, you're not making much.
Take Kaby Lame for example, he's the most followed TikToker on the planet with a whopping 159 million followers and nearly 18 billion views.
But in terms of ad revenue from TikTok, these 18 billion views only translates to $540,000.
Now, that's not a bad amount by any means, but keep in mind, we're talking about the most followed TikToker in the world.
For perspective, if you got the same number of views on YouTube, your total earnings would be closer to $54 million, assuming a $3 RPM.
Now, of course, these TikTokers don't just rely on TikTok ads.
They also do brand deals and sponsorships and affiliate marketing and all that stuff, which pulls in a whole lot of money.
But the disparity between TikTok ads and YouTube ads is still staggering.
I mean, we're talking about a 100x difference.
And it's not just creators who are feeling the pain.
TikTok is also very much feeling the pain, having lost $7 billion last year alone.
And it's only getting worse.
Vine was facing this same challenge 10 years ago, and this is the main reason that they eventually shut down.
All of their most popular viners would translate their audiences over to YouTube.
This included Drew Gooden, David Dobrik, Danny Gonzalez, Cody Ko, and of course Logan Paul and Jake Paul.
We're starting to see the exact same thing happen with TikTokers as well.
Notable examples are Charli D'Amelio, Bella Porsche, Addison Rae, and Call Me Chris.
this.
Kami Kris, for example, has likely earned about $350,000 on TikTok, but she's already made millions on YouTube.

This is not a great sign for TikTok in terms of longevity, as this is hard evidence that people are simply using TikTok as a springboard for YouTube or to jumpstart their music career, while the platform is burning billions.
So here's TikTok's monetization crisis and the uncertain future of the platform.
By far the largest shortcoming for TikTok is advertisers.
Advertisers simply do not want to advertise on TikTok.
It's easy to blame the medium for this reluctance.
Most advertisers aren't used to making short formats in portrait mode.
And this is true to a certain degree, but it's not the main reason.
I mean, companies like Apple and Coca-Cola have marketing budgets into hundreds of millions if not billions.
And they have hundreds if not thousands of employees whose full-time jobs are to simply figure this out.
So, the reason that companies are reluctant to advertise on TikTok is not because they don't know how or can't figure it out, it's because they don't want to.
Why, you ask?
Well, for one, it's not a very lucrative audience.
41% of TikTok users are between the ages of 16 and 24, which means that most of them don't have any money.
For perspective, this is how YouTube's audience demographic looks.
As you can see, it's a lot more evenly dispersed.
This in itself is a big turnoff for advertisers, but the issue goes much deeper than just demographics.
Likely the biggest concern for most advertisers is brand optics.
It's no secret that the content on TikTok is, how should I say it, edgy.
You've got thirst traps, a bunch of cursing, and all this other stuff that YouTube tells you not to do.
This is actually what has made TikTok so popular in the first place, but there's a reason that YouTube does not lean into this content.
Advertisers simply do not want to be associated with this type of content.
I mean, if you were Apple, would you really want your ad to play after this?
I'm gonna guess no.
And this makes a far larger difference than you might think.
At this point, I think we can agree that TikTok is very much a worldwide platform.
In 2021, it was literally the world's most popular domain for crying out loud.
So clearly, it's extremely popular across the globe.
But guess what?
80% of TikTok's revenue still comes from China.
And if you didn't know, the TikTok that we use is actually banned in China.
You see, the CCP decided that mainstream TikTok is simply too vulgar and unproductive for the youth.
So instead, they have a healthy version of TikTok called Douyin.
Fundamentally speaking, it's the same app.
The difference is the type of content that is posted and promoted on the platform.
Douyin primarily promotes science, educational, and historical content instead of lip syncs and dancing.
Furthermore, younger generations are limited to just 40 minutes of Douyin per day, so no hours of mindless scrolling.
And Douyin is extremely popular in China, but it doesn't quite stack up to TikTok.
Douyin boasts 730 million monthly active users, while TikTok boasts 1.05 billion monthly active users.
So TikTok is not only more popular, but people tend to spend far more time on TikTok.
But despite this, China is able to account for 80% of TikTok's revenue because advertisers are actually interested in appearing next to Douyin videos.
So, until TikTok is able to address advertiser hesitation, TikTok will continue to face major monetization issues leading to more creators migrating away.
Advertisers no doubt play a massive role in how much is paid out to creators, but they're not the only issue plaguing TikTok.
You see, short-form content is simply fundamentally harder to monetize because views are worth substantially less.
On TikTok, for example, the average video is only 36 to 42 seconds long, depending on the size of the account.
Even if we assume that these videos have 75% audience retention on average, each view only translates to about 30 seconds of watch time.
Now, compare that to what we see on YouTube.
Using myself as an example, my average video gets just under 7 minutes of average watch time, which by the way, thank you.
This means that the average view on my channel is worth about 14 views on TikTok.
Why do I bring this up?
Well, monetization has more to do with watch time than views.
I tend to put an ad break once every 3 minutes, which means that the average view translates to 3 ad impressions.
For simplicity, let's say that TikTok also shows an ad once every 3 minutes.
Since each video is only watched for 30 seconds at best, a viewer would have to scroll through 6 TikToks before reaching an ad, and that's the best case scenario.
More likely, they'll have to scroll through 10 or 15 TikToks before seeing an ad, but we'll call it 6 to give them the benefit of the doubt.
This means that each view on TikTok only translates to 1 sixth of an ad impression.
Putting this next to YouTube, we'll see that each YouTube view translates to 18 times more ad impressions.
So, if we want to really create an accurate comparison between how much advertisers pay on YouTube versus how much they pay on TikTok, we can't compare views to revenue.
We have to compare ad impressions to revenue.
YouTube generally pays $3- $5 per thousand views in most niches.
And as we previously touched on, TikTok only pays $0.02- $4 per thousand views.
But if we normalize based on ad impressions, we'll see that TikTok is actually paying $0.36- $0.72 for the same number of ad impressions that you would get from 1,000 YouTube views.
Still about 7 to 8 times worse than YouTube, but also about 18 times better than what the upfront number suggested.
