The only way to work around this obstacle is to move towards longer form content, which is exactly what TikTok has been trying to do.
What started at a maximum video length of 7 seconds has grown all the way to 10 minutes.
TikTok has also been testing with landscape mode, but increasing the average view duration isn't as easy as just getting creators to post longer videos.
The algorithm highly values audience retention, so if TikTokers want their long-term videos to perform well, they have to increase video length without sacrificing audience retention.
Also, you know how we see all those articles about our ever-decreasing attention spans?
Well, if that's true anywhere, it's true on TikTok.
So, TikTok is very much fighting an uphill battle when it comes to monetization due to the fundamental nature of their content.
hearing all this you might be saying that this isn't just an issue on tiktok.
instagram and youtube have also been promoting short-form content so they should be facing the same issues right?
well you're right.
youtube and instagram are indeed facing the same issues.
with youtube shorts for example you can expect to earn five cents per thousand views.
but here's the thing YouTube and Instagram are not tied down by short-form content.
Short-form content is not their golden goose.
It's simply an expansion effort.
And they're already starting to decide that this expansion effort isn't worth it.
You see, platform monetization is a two-sided coin.
If creators aren't earning much money from ads, neither is the platform.
At least the creators can go out and get brand deals and sponsors and affiliates and all that.
For these platforms, their only revenue is ad revenue.
So if that's garbage, the entire revenue from the whole effort is garbage, and that's exactly what seems to be playing out.
In fact, according to Mark Zuckerberg, revenue from Reels is so garbage that Meta is losing $500 million per quarter because of users watching Reels instead of scrolling through pictures.
Yeah, I don't think you'd be surprised to hear that Meta has stopped offering Reels bonuses to creators.
So, while Instagram and YouTube are very much in the same position as TikTok with shorts, they're also not.
They have the luxury of pulling back and focusing on what they were already doing.
The same cannot be said about TikTok.
But then, what's the solution?
Well, unfortunately for TikTok, there is no clear solution to their monetization problem.
Again, this is literally why Vine shut down.
What TikTok really needs is time.
They need time for brands to become more open with the idea of advertising on TikTok.
In the meantime, their best bet is to tinker with the algorithm to push longer form content that's more advertiser friendly.
But this is also a pretty big gamble.
This can lead to a sort of ad apocalypse like we saw with YouTube back in 2017.
More edgy creators got pushed off the platform as family friendly content got pushed to the top.
But the thing to note is that YouTube always had a good mix of edgy and family friendly content, so the shift towards family-friendly content was more natural.
With TikTok, on the other hand, we're primarily dealing with edgy content, so the shift is a lot more jarring.
And it's not clear how many viewers TikTok would push off the platform by making such a change.
But with their peers already dropping out and pulling back, this might be the Hail Mary that TikTok needs to stay relevant over the long term.
As you can see, TikTok is very much facing a monetization crisis and there is no easy solution, but there is a silver lining for TikTok.
Unlike Vine which was backed by Twitter which in itself was not a profitable company, TikTok is backed by ByteDance which has been posting record profits.
In fact, they made $25 billion last year, so losses from TikTok are definitely something that they can sustain even over the long term.
Also, even if ByteDance can't pull it off on their own, they've got the backing of the CCP.
You can bet that as long as TikTok is popular, the CCP won't let them go under as TikTok is literally a goldmine for them.
So, from a financial perspective, they very much have time on their side, but they may not be able to say the same thing about their creators or viewers.
Their creators are naturally pivoting towards YouTube to build stronger businesses with more revenue.
And as for viewers, they could easily migrate back to YouTube with these creators.
Also, TikTok faces the risk of their viewers growing up kind of like what Snapchat is dealing with right now.
So, while TikTok may not be on the clock for financial reasons, they're very much on the clock due to trends amongst their viewers and creators.
Will they be able to beat the clock?
Well, only time will tell.

title: Schools Have Had It With Google
note: Trend explainer: states the decline first, flashes back to why Google won, then shows why the same traits now lose. Product-focused rather than person-focused.
sections: Why schools chose Google in the first place
lines: Schools are ditching Google from all fronts.
Up until the pandemic, Google Classroom interest was increasing year after year, but since 2020, interest in Google Classroom has struggled to even reach levels of 2015.
Instead, many schools are opting for third-party solutions like Schoology, Canvas, and Blackboard.
It's not just Google's virtual classrooms that schools are ditching either, schools are also ditching Gmail.
A quick Google search will bring up dozens of articles from school newspapers detailing the change, Here's a few examples.
If you look up the opposite, however, not only do you find fewer results, but the results that you do find are often from 2010.
And as for the oh-so-famous Chromebooks, these used to be the go-to devices for many school districts.
But more recently, schools have started to complain about them.
Apparently, Chromebooks have very short lifespans, making them a rather bad investment.
This is a very bad sign, not just for Google's educational business, but their office suite as a whole.
Here's the thing, everyday people virtually never pay for Google Drive or Google Docs or Gmail because the free tier is more than enough for most people.
So much of the money that Google and Microsoft makes from such products comes from corporations and schools.
Google was never really able to break into the corporate market with their office suite, but it did seem like they were breaking into the school market.
The collaboration features and online nature of Google's office suite made it perfect for team projects and presentations.
Combine this with the pandemic, and you would think that schools would be paying Google more than ever, and that was the case at the beginning.
When schools didn't know where to go, they turned to a familiar brand, leading to Chromebook sales rocketing by 87% between 2019 and 2020.
But now that schools have had time to become familiar with Google's shortcomings and research other solutions, it appears that a popular choice is to ditch Google, and here's why.

To understand why schools are suddenly ditching Google, we first have to take a look back at why Google became so popular among schools in the first place, as it was definitely not because it was the best option.
I mean, there was never really any comparison between Microsoft Office and G Suite.
Though G Suite had a few unique features like easy collaboration and autosaving onto the cloud, Microsoft Office was the clear winner.
And this is why corporations never really jumped on board with G Suite.
They were looking for the best tools available.
Not to mention, people were already familiar with the Microsoft Office suite, so going with Microsoft Office was a no-brainer.
For schools, however, the choice wasn't as clear.
Sure, Microsoft was better, but what real value would children, especially in elementary school, get from Excel or Word?
The reality was not much.
I remember back when I was in kindergarten and first grade, our class would go to the computer lab every week just to practice typing.
As we moved into fourth and fifth grade, we would still write and revise our essays on paper, but when we were ready for the final draft, we would switch over to computers.
But that was really the extent of all computer use, So, safe to say, Microsoft Office was quite overkill for most school applications.
But it wasn't just Office that was overkill, it was really the whole computer experience.
Most students had no use for a full-on Windows machine or Outlook email client.
In fact, this just made students harder to manage.
Instead of working on the final draft of an essay, students would just jump onto Armor Games or Miniclip.
So, giving children access to a computer was often more of a distraction than a tool.
Not to mention, Windows and Office were quite expensive.
Schools often had to shell out $100 plus to Microsoft alone with each computer.
Clearly, what schools needed was a cheaper, watered-down version of the whole computer experience.
This seems like the perfect opportunity for Google to step in with the G Suite, and that's what they tried doing in 2006, but it wasn't as successful as you might think.
While Google's offerings did mesh better with the needs of schools, it wasn't something that schools really paid much attention to.
After all, each school only had one or two computer labs, so paying a premium for 25 or 50 computers wasn't the biggest concern.
Not to mention, schools had full control of when they would incur these costs.
They could just stick around with Windows XP and Word 2003 as long as they wanted.
So, in the late 2000s, schools weren't exactly jumping up and down to switch to Google, but all of this would change with the 2010s.
Google's popularity within the educational space can really be summed up by one trend.
Schools aiming for a student-to-device ratio of 1 to 1.
Suddenly, buying Windows licenses wasn't just a matter of purchasing 25 or 50.
Elementary schools themselves had to buy several hundred.
Middle schools and high schools had to buy thousands, and colleges had to buy tens of thousands.
Some richer schools continued to shell out money for Microsoft licenses, but this didn't last for long as Microsoft would shoot themselves in the foot.
In 2010, Microsoft would introduce a subscription model for Office called Office 365, and this would eventually become the only option.
Really, the only reason for this move was that a subscription model was more lucrative for Microsoft than a licensing model.
Most corporations would just pony up the cash and jump onto the subscription because for professional use, the G Suite wasn't really a viable option.
For schools, however, Google's offerings started to seem a lot more attractive.
Google's offerings were not only cheap starting at just $3 per student per year, but you could even get it for free if your school met certain qualifications.
Around the same time, Google would also come out with the Chromebook, which was also perfect for schools.
Schools didn't have to worry about kids doing anything too crazy with Chromebooks because they couldn't do much to begin with.
It turned out that Chromebooks and the G Suite were the exact watered-down versions of computers that schools were looking for.
And before you knew it, schools were switching to Google left and right.
This isn't to say that they ditched Microsoft completely.
Schools might have still had a few dozen Windows and Office-based computers in computer labs.
But as for the hundreds and thousands of computers that were being issued to students, these were of course Chromebooks.
So when Google launched Classroom in 2014, it's no wonder why it became the go-to option for most schools.
But this heyday for Google education only lasted for a few years.
By the late 2010s, teachers and students started noticing quite a few shortcomings.
You see, Google Classroom was nothing more than a UI to share and manage Google Drive documents and presentations.
When a student turns in a document, literally the only thing that's happening is that the sharing permissions are being changed.
The document gets shared with the teacher and the student loses editing permissions.
That's pretty much it.
This in itself was a pretty crappy solution because students could no longer edit the document once it was turned in, which didn't really make sense in a lot of situations.
Also, there were no robust systems for self-grading assessments, announcements, gradebooks, online discussions, or meetings just to name a few.
These are all basic features that are available in every other e-learning solution.
But despite the shortcomings, most schools put up with Google throughout the late 2010s because it was cheap and was mostly sufficient for their needs.
But all of this would change with the pandemic.
When the pandemic hit, there was a massive influx of schools switching to Chromebooks and Google Classroom because that's what was popular.
But as the pandemic raged on, schools simply started investing in better solutions, and the reasoning isn't rocket science.
Virtual classrooms were no longer an extension to in-person classrooms.
For a period of time, they were a full-on replacement to in-person classrooms.
And even with the shift back to in-person classes, the utilization of these e-learning platforms is larger than ever.
In fact, in many schools, it seems that the in-person aspect is now the extension.
Every homework, every quiz, every test, and every project is completely online.
The instructions are posted online, the students work together online, and the project is turned in online.
Basically, everything other than the teacher's lecture itself can be found on Canvas or Schoology or whatever platform the school is using.
At universities, even the lectures are automatically recorded and uploaded onto these platforms.
In terms of cost, Canvas does have a free tier, but that's mostly for small-scale implementations.
For example, if you're running a yoga class or a math tutoring service, you might use the free tier.
For district-wide and university-wide implementations though, Canvas is not free.
It's actually quite expensive.
Canvas doesn't have any sort of set pricing and each school is handled on a case-by-case basis.
But here are some numbers that are floating around online.
It seems that on average, schools have to pay an upfront fee of several thousand dollars to set up the initial system, plus about $25 per user per month.
This could be higher or lower depending on what level of integration and the branding a given school's looking for, but that's a ballpark number.
As you can see, that's several times more than Google's $3 per month and free tiers, but systems like Canvas are also several times more effective than Google's tiers.
And given how heavily these systems are now utilized at schools, it simply doesn't make sense to go with a watered-down version from Google.
The same logic applies to Chromebooks as well.
Students no longer go to the computer lab once a week to practice typing.
They use computers the entire day at school and after school as well.
Also, they're doing increasingly complicated tasks.
Nowadays, students are 3D modeling in engineering classes and coding algorithms in computer science classes even in middle school.
Also, every job in the world uses Windows or Mac, so it really makes no sense to train students to use Chromebooks.
Some districts are even going as far as purchasing MacBooks and iPads for students.
But even those that aren't going that far are very much seeing a resurgence in Windows and Office and more professional tools in general, even though they're more expensive.
In the end, it seems that Google's greatest advantage within the educational space has also become their greatest weakness.

When tech adoption was still relatively early stage with schools, Google was able to make a big splash by offering tech for extremely cheap, whether that be Chromebooks, the G Suite, or Google Classroom.
While these options did have their shortcomings, when the virtual classroom was simply an addition to in-person learning, they held up alright.
But when virtual learning is front and center, the whole Google ecosystem starts to fall apart.
We should also mention that school districts are now being run by a newer generation that better understands tech.
They realize that investing in good tech for students is way more valuable than buying pencils and papers and desks or even building new buildings.
The ROI is simply incomparable, and that's why schools are giving up on Google.
They're simply leaning towards more professional solutions that make more sense in our increasingly tech-driven world.

title: The Demise of Big Tech - Is The End Near?
note: Argumentative essay with a three-stage monopoly lifecycle framework, opening on dated examples. No single protagonist; Google and Apple are recurring illustrations.
sections: Big Tech's current stage and buybacks
lines: Monopolies don't last.
1904, Rockefeller Standard Oil controls 91% of the US oil market.
2004, Standard Oil is just something that we read about in the history books.
2000, GE becomes the world's largest company.
2021, GE announces that they'll be divesting into three different companies.
2007, Nokia is synonymous with cell phones.
Nokia is the legacy company that's iconic for its ringtone.
2015, Apple, Google, Amazon, and Meta rule the world.
But 2045, 2060, when is their expiration?
These companies may seem unstoppable, unbreakable today, but there's only one thing for certain, each and every one of these companies will fail.
In fact, the bigger they get, the faster they'll fall.
You're probably asking how.
I mean, no one's ever gonna stop using smartphones or the internet, right?
Well, that's just because we don't yet know what's next.
Henry Ford once famously said, if I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses.
Today, horse-drawn carriages are virtually obsolete.
So, here's why all monopolies are doomed to fail and why big tech has already started their demise.
People love to hate on monopolies, but they often forget that it wasn't that long ago that the very same companies were cherished.
You see, companies don't just randomly become monopolies because they had better marketing or something.
Companies become monopolies because they offered something that was undeniably better than everything else.
Standard Oil offered an undeniably better way for energy production and transportation.
AT &T offered an undeniably better way to communicate.
And modern tech companies started off by offering an undeniably better way to navigate the internet.
Amazon mastered online shopping.
Apple mastered handheld devices.
Google mastered advertising, and Facebook mastered online communication.
So, ironically, the first stage of a monopoly is actually love.
All monopolies were loved by most of its user base at some point in time.
That's how they became a monopoly.
But this love also gives companies a lot of control, allowing them to do things that normal companies wouldn't be able to get away with.
Apple, for example, was able to drop the headphone jack, prevent consumers from repairing their devices, and even remove the power brick.
Yet, they're still the biggest company in the world because people love iPhones.
Such anti-consumer moves are usually what raise the first red flags that a given company is actually just a monopoly.
But by this point, the company already has control over the market, and they shift their focus to building an empire.
During this stage, companies can basically throw out anything they want and it'll stick.
Likely the best example of this was Microsoft back in the 90s and 2000s.
Windows and Office were actually phenomenal products that people loved.
Internet Explorer, on the other hand, was not.
But that didn't matter because Microsoft was able to push IE using Windows.
The same thing could be said about Hotmail, Outlook, and the MSN suite of products.
The same thing can also be said about Google and Apple throughout the 2010s.
People started using Google Drive because they already had Gmail accounts.
people started using Google Photos because they were already using Android.
Similarly, with Apple, people started using iCloud, Apple Music, Safari, and Apple Maps because it came along with iPhones.
This isn't to say that these products were bad, but they weren't especially stellar either.
I mean, let's just be honest, who's going to use Apple Maps or Safari or the Apple Mail client if it wasn't for iPhones?
The answer is no one, and this is really the trademark of an aged monopoly.
People used their newest products not because they were extraordinary, but because they were associated with something that was extraordinary.
Piggybacking mediocre products off of extraordinary products only works for so long though.
The beginning of the end for most monopolies is actually just themselves.
As monopolies grow more powerful, we start to see a clear disconnect between the company's original purpose and vision and the goals and visions of the company's employees.
I mean, just think about it.
What type of person joins a monopoly?
Well, it's usually someone with the mindset of, if you can't beat them, you might as well join them.
And I don't blame these people whatsoever.
They're simply looking out for themselves as they should be.
But this doesn't exactly play out well for the organization.
Suddenly, the primary goal of the average employee is no longer to serve the customer in the best way possible.
In fact, the average employee might not even know how their role impacts the customer as there's simply so many layers between them and the final product.
So, the primary goal of employees transitions to impressing their managers, getting promotions, and scoring bonuses.
This is how it becomes across the entire corporate ladder, and as for the top, well, the top isn't any better.
Most of the visionary executives have likely already retired, moved on to something else, or have just passed away.
So, the people who are left aren't visionaries, they're the ones who were able to play the corporate game the best.
They were able to handle office politics and the backstabbing and crappy managers and ineffective teams and whatever else.
These people aren't exactly leaders.
A better description would be survivors similar to winning the Hunger Games or something.
And given that this is what they've been used to their entire career, as executives, they're gonna focus on survival.
How do they survive at the top?
Well, it's not by serving the customers, it's by serving the shareholders.
The top two things that shareholders are looking for is growth and profit, and thus the priorities of the company also becomes growth and profit.
What's the easiest way to do this?
Well, the easiest ways are to cut costs and increase prices.
A perfect example of this is Google.
With Larry Page and Sergey Brin at the helm, the focus of the company was to push the boundaries and experiment.
In fact, Google was always super proud of all their failures, of which they had hundreds.
Their philosophy was always, you're gonna have a bunch of failures if you want to succeed.
But I'm not sure if we can say the same thing about Sundar's Google.
Over the past several months itself, Google has been pulling back on moonshot ideas substantially.
In fact, in some areas, they've canceled as many as half of their projects.
It's easy to say that they're pulling back because of the recession, but it's not like Google or Facebook or really any big tech company that's doing layoffs are actually at risk.
They're not even remotely close to being unprofitable.
For giants, recessions are simply a time to maximize efficiency so that they can become even more profitable for the next bull run.
But by the time the desire to maximize short-term profits becomes larger than the desire to create a long-term change, the end is already near.
Monopoly is really quite a fitting name for these companies because most modern monopolies are dependent on just one product.
It might seem like they're everywhere with hundreds of products and services, but really, the base of the company can usually be traced back to just one product.
To this day, Google search accounts for over 50% of all of Google's revenue.
iPhones account for over 50% of all of Apple's revenue.
AWS is the only reason Amazon is even profitable.
And the entire business of Meta can be summed up by Facebook, WhatsApp, and Instagram.
The only tech giant that breaks this trend is Microsoft.
They've become more of a tech holding company than an actual business, which seems to be working out great so far, but we'll have to see how it plays out over the long term.
As for everyone else though, their empires are actually extremely fragile.
The reality is that while they may have hundreds of microservices that generate a bunch of revenue, the only reason that any of these services are successful is because of the base product.
iCloud, for example, has nearly a billion users, but how many people would stick around after the iPhone is disrupted?
Similarly, how many people would even know about the metaverse if it wasn't for Facebook?
The harsh reality is that the only reason these extensions are successful or even relevant is because of the success of the original product.
Once that fades away, so does the entire company.
This isn't to say that the company goes bankrupt the day after or something.
Rather, they become a shell of their former self, similar to IBM or AT &T or GE.
They might be everywhere, but at the same time, they're nowhere because the brand no longer carries the same weight.
Take ChatGPT for example.
Let's say ChatGPT replaces Google search, which it might very well do.
As the masses flock over to ChatGPT, people will naturally start using the products that are associated with ChatGPT versus the products that are associated with Google.
Given that Microsoft is a major investor in ChatGPT, this means that a lot more people will start using Edge, Bing, Outlook, OneDrive, and Microsoft Office.
All of a sudden, Google's major product categories of Chrome, Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Office aren't nearly as popular despite nothing changing about them.
The bottom line is that the hero product changed and with that, all of the auxiliary products also changed.
So most of these big tech companies aren't as invincible as they may seem.
While they may have hundreds or even thousands of popular services, it's only a handful of products that really drive people to the ecosystem.
them.
Once those products fall out of favor, so does the entire company.
Looking at Feng today, it's clear that they're well past stage 1 of being a monopoly.
The days of people loving them were 15 to 20 years ago.
Nowadays, the sentiment that dominates for Feng is actually concerns.
Concerns about their power and influence, concerns about privacy, concerns about anti-consumer behavior.
These guys are also well past stage 2.
They've already leveraged their market share to push other products and services and to become omnipresent.
Their focus is no longer to improve the world, but to maximize stock growth.
This is why they spend so much money on stock buybacks.
Apple, for example, has spent $573 billion on buybacks over the past 10 years.
I've said this before, but that's literally enough money to buy out another fortune 10 company.
Such behavior is only evident in a late stage company.
If this was 2007, Apple would have been way too busy with scaling manufacturing, logistics, and R &D to be spending half a trillion on buybacks.
But all of this brings up the question, how much time do these companies have left?
Well, for that, we can just take it from the horse's mouth itself, Jeff Bezos.
Hearing that and looking around, big tech companies are rapidly approaching this milestone.
Amazon is 29 years old, Google is 25 years old, and Facebook is 19 years old.
Now, Apple is 47 years old, but they were completely reinvented with the iPod and iPhone, so the modern Apple is more like 20 years old.
So, it's likely that the utter dominance of these companies is already behind us.
In fact, the peak was probably the pandemic.
Again, this isn't to say that these companies will go bankrupt tomorrow.
tomorrow.
But what this does mean is that they've already started the transition into becoming the Cisco's and Intel's of the world.
And once they spend a good amount of time there, they'll become the Xerox's and Kodak's of the world, and that is the inevitable future of a thing.

title: The Reddit Protest Explained (From Reddit’s Perspective)
note: Event explainer told from the company's perspective: opens on the blackout, rewinds to business problems that caused the API pricing, then follows the protest and its collapse.
sections: API pricing announced; how APIs work
Apollo and the third-party app problem
RedDark protest and Huffman holds firm
lines: Blackout.
On June 12th, 2023, over 8,000 subreddits decided to go completely dark.
Users couldn't join, edit, or even view any of the content on these subreddits.
Instead, they were met with messages like this.
CFL has gone private and protested against Reddit's exorbitant new API pricing.
The community will not grant access requests during the protest.
Please do not message asking to be added to… Oh, oops, definitely did not do that.
Clearly, I was not aware of what was going on, but like hundreds of millions of other users, I became aware of the situation quite quickly as some of the biggest communities were going down.
This included r slash awe with 34 million members, r slash music with 32 million members, and r slash futurology with 18 million members just to name a few.

At first, this was seen as one of the most effective online protests we've seen, as it not only spread the word, but it also made Reddit feel the pain as they weren't earning ad revenue from the subreddits.
But almost as quickly as the protest gained steam, it disappeared.
What did Reddit do you ask?
Well, the answer is nothing.
They just stood their ground and waited, and things have somehow magically returned to normal.
So, join me as we take a deep dive dive into one of the biggest online protests we've seen and why it utterly failed.
Alright so what's the big deal anyway?
Why are hundreds of millions of users not able to see cat pics and memes?
Well it all boils down to the fact that reddit sucks, not as a platform though some would argue that as well, but as a business.
We've talked extensively on this channel about companies prioritizing growth and influence over profits, but Reddit is unlike anything else we've seen.
The company has been around for nearly 20 years and has 1.6 billion monthly active users.

Put another way, it's the 19th most visited website on the planet and the 12th most visited website in the US, but despite this, Reddit is somehow not only not profitable, but they don't pull in any money.
In fact, Reddit is estimated to only pull in a mere $510 million per year, which given their user count is absolute garbage.
I mean, they're literally making $0.25 per user per month.
For perspective, their own paid tier costs $6 per month, so we're talking about a revenue difference of nearly 200x between the average user and a paying user.
But not only do they pull in no money, they also spend a bunch of money.
Maintaining a platform with a billion plus users is not cheap by any means.
You need massive server rooms, databases, and a lot of tech infrastructure in general.
You also need a bunch of people to maintain all this.

And being headquartered in San Francisco, Reddit has become accustomed to insane compensation packages of half a million dollars for software engineers, which is great for the engineers, but once again, garbage for the business.
Virtually no money coming in, but exorbitant amounts going out.
To be honest, I have no idea how VCs have put up with Red's financials for so long, but it looks like they're finally pulling back.
In fact, Reddit is planning on IPO-ing later this year, likely hoping that the public markets are more tolerant of their losses.
But before doing that, they wanted to patch things up and make the business seem as viable as possible.
Likely the easiest way to do this would have been to crack down on Adblock.
I don't have any stats for this but I'd wager that the vast majority of redditors use adblock given that they tend to be more tech savvy and rebellious in general.
So, eliminating adblock itself might increase their revenue by multiple fold and I'm sure they consider that.
But it looks like they decided against it, likely fearing public backlash.
Another easy solution would've been to jack up prices on their premium subscriptions.
But then again, Netflix's brand favorability dropped to 11% after doing the same thing.
With the IPO coming up, Reddit really couldn't risk anything that would harm their brand image.
What they needed was a revenue stream that no one would bat an eye about, something that no one would even notice like API usage.
Surely price hikes for API usage would go completely unnoticed.
Oh how wrong they were.
In late April, Reddit announced that they would start charging for API usage for the first time.
The price?
24 cents per 1000 API calls.
Wait, hold up, what even are API calls?
Well, API calls are what you use to integrate various portions of Reddit into your own website or app.
API calls are not unique to Reddit, likely the most popular APIs are Google APIs.
For example, if you go onto a restaurant's website and see an interactive map showing you where the restaurant is located, that website is most likely using Google's Map API.
Similarly, if you're filling out a billing or shipping address and you see autocomplete results, that website is most likely using Google's Places API.
Every time a user interacts with a map or uses the autocomplete feature, an API call is being made to Google and these websites are charged based on how many API calls they make every month.
For dynamic maps, Google charges $7 per 1,000 requests, and for autocomplete, Google charges $2.83 per 1,000 requests.
Considering this, Reddit's $0.24 per 1,000 calls is really not out of the ordinary.
Not to mention, Reddit is offering an extremely generous free tier.
In fact, you can make up to 100 calls per minute completely for free.
So theoretically, you can make up to 4.3 million calls per month for absolutely no cost.
But then, what's the issue?
Well, the issue is that it used to be free regardless of scale, meaning that several substantial businesses have been built around this free idea.
One such business is Apollo.
Apollo is an iOS app that's basically a skin for Reddit.
Essentially, it uses a bunch of Reddit APIs to recreate the entire Reddit experience, but with a completely new UI which a lot of people prefer.
In fact, the app has nearly a million daily active users.
But here's the problem.
Apps like Apollo don't show Reddit ads because, I mean, what's in it for them?
This means that Reddit is essentially having to support all of these users completely for free.
Even worse, apps like Apollo are able to make money by charging users a premium subscription fee, none of which goes to Reddit.
So these businesses basically have no expenses.
All of the backend infrastructure is maintained and paid for by Reddit, and all of front-end runs on iPhones.
So, the only expense for these businesses is the cost of front-end development.
And given that most of these apps were built by a single developer or a small team, this is also a non-expense.
So, basically everything that people are willing to pay for these apps is pure profit, of course after the Apple tax.
But while this adds up to a lot of money on an individual basis, it's not allowed to run an actual business of their scale.
For example, let's assume that about 10% of Apollo's user base actually pays for the app.
This would translate to approximately $130,000 per month, which is again, great as an individual.
But as a business with 900,000 active users making 7 billion API calls per month, it's nothing, and that's the problem.
The core of the Reddit protest is that the API pricing is simply way too high, and on the surface, this indeed seems to be the case.
For Apollo to continue operations, they would have to pay Reddit $1.7 million per month or $20 million per year.
That's a crazy amount, right?
24 cents per 1,000 requests must be unreasonable.
But here's the deal.
Apollo was also making a crazy amount of requests.
They're literally making 7 billion requests per month.
That translates to nearly 8,000 requests per user per month.
That's why it's so expensive.
It's because the API is being used in a way that it's not meant to be used.
Here's an example of how APIs are normally used.
Maybe you can integrate a Twitter post into an article.
This would only cost a mere fifth of a penny per user according to Red's pricing, a super cheap fee.
But apps like Apollo aren't just importing one post.
They're trying to import the entire platform of Reddit and that's why it adds up to $2.50 per user per month.
And if you're still not convinced, think about this.
Even if Reddit decreased their pricing by 10x down to 2.4 cents per 1,000 calls, that would still cost $170,000 per month for Apollo, which would still likely be unsustainable.
So, is this a case of Reddit implementing pricing that's magnitudes higher than it should be, or is it a case of apps like Apollo only being viable if Reddit's APIs are virtually free?
I'll let you be the judge of that.
Feel free to post your thoughts down below.
But anyway, much of the userbases of Apollo, Red Planet, Sync, and Reddit is Fun naturally felt that it was Reddit's fault.
And given that this encompasses much of Reddit's most dedicated userbase, a lot of them knew mods and were mods themselves.
So, it didn't take long for them to join forces and stage one of the largest online protests we've seen, dubbed RedDark.
They would essentially make 8,000 of the most popular subreddits in the world private starting on June 12, 2023.
And let's just say, this definitely made a scene.
Almost overnight, all reddit users became aware of the protest against reddit.
And with how quickly drama spreads, it wasn't long until people who never even use reddit also knew about it.
And given that most people naturally have a tendency to side with the underdog, they immediately turned on reddit and especially reddit CEO Steve Hoffman.
Steve was under a lot of fire, but he didn't budge on reddit stance whatsoever.
The bottom line was, Reddit needs to be a self-sustaining business, and to do that, we can no longer subsidize commercial entities that require large-scale data use.
Reddit had made their position clear, but this only infuriated the community even more.
They were going to band together and protest for as long as it took.
Wait, never mind.
Just 48 hours later, most of the subreddits would be back up.
You're probably asking, what happened?
Why did the protests die down so quickly?
Well, a lot of people point to the limited blackout period of 48 hours.
You see, in order to get as many mods and subreddits on board, the organizers of Reddark only asked for a 48 hour blackout period.
Further protesting would be up to the discretion of the mods.
So, people say that if If the mods were more committed, the protest would have been more effective, which may have been true, but I don't think it would have changed the end result all that much.
The bottom line is that the average redditor simply did not care about the protest more than simply saying, oh wow, reddit is bad.
Now where are my cat memes and Mr.
Robot discussion threads?
I know that sounds stupid, but that's the reality.
Only 1 million people use Apollo.
Over a billion people use reddit.
So, we're talking about 0.1% of the user base.

So, while Reddark was able to spread awareness about their campaign and even get people to agree with the ideological effort, they were not able to get people to sacrifice for the cause, and that was really where it all fell apart.
The idea of any protest is that you sacrifice things in the short term to make things better over the long term.
The company Reddit clearly understood this as that was exactly what they were doing.
By protesting the protest, they were essentially sacrificing short term ad revenue and brand reputation for long term profitability.

Now I do want to mention that a good amount of subreddits are still protesting, but this is increasingly becoming the minority, especially with pressure mounting against mods both from the community and from reddit.
And unfortunately, it looks like services like Apollo will indeed be closing down at the end of June when the pricing changes go into effect after which protesting becomes virtually useless.

title: Are Layoffs Even Worth It?
note: Cost-benefit argument that debunks the layoff rationale step by step, then reveals investor pressure via one named person as the answer.
lines: Tech companies have laid off tens of thousands of employees, but they've also handed out hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of severance to each and every employee that was laid off.
Meta offered 16 weeks of base pay plus another 2 weeks of base pay for every year of tenure.
Google offered an identical package, but some companies took it even further.
Salesforce, for example, offered a minimum of 5 months worth of base pay, and that's just base pay itself.

Most severance packages also came along with stockvesting through the current quarter or more, 6 months of health insurance, the opportunity to cash out PTO, and compensation for the 60 day notification period.
So, most of the people who were laid off from big tech walked away with nearly 6 months worth of full compensation.
This is no doubt how severance should be handled if layoffs are required, but were these layoffs even worth it?
I mean, these companies are basically committing to paying these employees for the next 6 months.
A director for example would walk away with $400,000 to $500,000.
Not to mention, they never even stopped hiring.
Yes, we always see headlines about Google or Meta implementing a scary indefinite hiring freeze, but this isn't actually true.
While hiring is definitely slower and more selective, Google literally has over 1,900 job openings posted as we speak.
So if these companies are just hiring back new people as they lay off their existing staff, where exactly is the cost savings?
Sure, they can pay the newer people a marginally lower salary of 10 or 20%.
But for a company like Google or Microsoft, saving 10 or 20% on 10 or 20,000 employees is a rounding error.
Not to mention all of the terrible PR.
I mean, just look at Apple.
They're coming off as some sort of heroes for not doing layoffs, while Meta is presented as suffering from typhoid fever or something.
So, join me as we figure out just how much these companies are actually saving from layoffs and the real reason they're resorting to layoffs.
Let's start off by taking a look at the supposed benefit of layoffs, reduced operational expenses.
Given how much these companies pay, the apparent savings are actually quite large.
Google for instance has a median compensation of $295,000.
Facebook comes in just under that at $292,000.
These are already big numbers, but that's just direct compensation of base salary, stock, and bonus.

These companies also hand out extremely generous insurance plans, 401k plans, retirement plans, free food, smartphones, monitors, phone plans, software subscriptions, airline tickets, hotel rooms, and office spaces.
They also have to pay social security and Medicare tax on these salaries as well.
So, the indirect compensation itself easily adds up to another $50,000 to $100,000.
Let's call it a $100,000 to give these companies the benefit of the doubt.
This means that the average employee is costing Google and Facebook roughly $400,000.
So how much exactly are the layoffs saving?
Well, Google has thus far laid off 12,000 people and Facebook has laid off 21,000 people.
At 400k a pop, Google is saving $4.8 billion per year and Facebook is saving $8.4 billion per year.
This was the first time that I started thinking that maybe the layoffs were worth it.
I mean, we're talking about billions of dollars every single year.
That is until I faintly recalled that not a single one of these companies are losing money.
In fact, they're not even remotely close to losing money.
Some of them are straight up posting record profits.
And when you contextualize these savings with just how much these companies are pulling in, it just becomes even worse.
In terms of revenue, Google pulls in just under $300 billion per year, and Facebook pulls in just over $100 billion per year.
So, the savings only equate to 6 days worth of revenue for Google and 26 days worth of revenue for Facebook.
Obviously, they haven't hit the jackpot.
But with that being said, savings are savings.
Why make less money when you can just make more money?
Which brings us back to the idea of maybe the tech companies were right for doing layoffs until you consider natural attrition.
Here's a secret.
These big tech companies are actually really bad at employee retention.
And it's not because of bad pay or bad work culture, maybe with the exception of Amazon.
It's actually because most FANG level tech bros are simply not dependent on the company.
A lot of them have enough money to retire by the time they're 30, so it's not like they're held back by their job.
As such, they're constantly looking for better opportunities and leave as soon as they can find one.
This is why the average tenure at most tech companies is only 2 years.
For Google, this corresponds to an employee turnover rate of 13%.
Let me put that in another way.
Google has to hire 25,000 people every year just to maintain their headcount.
Meta has to hire 11,000, Microsoft has to hire 28,000, and Apple has to hire 21,000.
And all of that is just with a 13% turnover rate.
Some of these companies have turnovers that are way worse, which raises a rather interesting question.
Could these companies have just stopped hiring and waited it out?
Well, let's just say, the minute that the first big tech company announced mass layoffs, the strategy became a lot harder.
Suddenly, people are scared to join that new startup or even switch to another big tech company.
In fact, I bet natural attrition is the lowest it's been since like 2008.
And that's all thanks to Meta who kicked off the big tech layoff season back in November.
But this isn't to say that the strategy has become impossible.
I mean, Apple and Nvidia are literally leveraging the strategy as we speak.
But if all the big tech companies weathered out the storm together, the strategy would have simply been even more effective.
In fact, it would have negated the need for layoffs altogether for many companies.
Take Google for instance.
They have to hire 25,000 people every year just to keep up with the turnover.
over.

This means that instead of laying off 12,000 people and giving them ridiculous severance for 6 months, Google could have just implemented a real hiring freeze for 6 months and they would have ended up with the same headcount and the same cost savings.
This idea is simply even truer at Microsoft.
So far, they've laid off 10,000 people but they could have just frozen hiring for 4 and half months.
In fact, for Microsoft, it might have been cheaper to freeze hiring than do layoffs.
And don't even get me started on Amazon.
Their attrition is so dang high that they straight up measure it on a weekly basis.
They lose 3% of their warehouse workers every single week, and to be honest, I don't think their tech turnover is all that much better.
The reality is that for most companies, freezing hiring for 6 months would have accomplished the same goal as layoffs all with better PR.
The only notable exception to this would have been Meta, who would have had to freeze hiring for two years, which just goes to show how much they overhired.
But for everyone else, the situation wasn't that bad.
Also, freezing hiring isn't the only alternative.
There's plenty of other solutions like cutting bonuses.
Out of the average Googler's $300,000 salary, about $30,000 is just a bonus.
So, if Google had simply cut the bonus of all 190,000 employees, that itself would have saved $5.7 billion or $900 million more than layoffs.
Also, that's not even considering that directors and VPs and executives have exponentially larger bonuses.
But Google didn't even reduce bonuses, they simply delayed them.
Another solution would have been to offer early retirement and voluntary resignations.
This is usually what Southwest Airlines leans into whenever they're going through a turbulent period like the pandemic.
And newsflash, Southwest has never had layoffs despite having low single digit profit margins.
So if Southwest can get through without layoffs, tech companies definitely can with their 30-40% net margins.
The only argument against these alternatives would be that companies give up control as to who leaves.
With layoffs, companies can slash certain departments and titles.
But this can simply be corrected for with strategic hiring.
If you want get rid of recruiters, just stop hiring recruiters.
With time, things will level out how you want.
But then, if the savings from layoffs are marginal at best and there's little strategic benefit to doing layoffs, what's the real reason that everyone is doing layoffs?
To get to the root of why companies are really doing layoffs, we first have to identify who exactly wants layoffs.
It's obviously not the employees, but it's also not the employers either.
Do you really think that these companies want to be the bad guy?
They already have a bunch of bad rep regarding invasion of privacy, data collection, and monopolization.
Reputation wise, one of the only factors that are going in these companies favor nowadays is that they pay well and have happy employees.
So, it makes no sense to screw that up as well.
Not to mention all of the damage layoffs cause to company morale and ongoing projects.
Tech CEOs more than understand this and that's why most of them don't want to do layoffs.
Take Tim Cook for example, he's taken a pay cut from $265 million in 2020 to $49 million this year.
Similarly, Zoom CEO Eric Yuan has taken a 98% pay cut.
Now, I'm sure it's hard to sympathize with these billionaire CEOs.
Oh no, Tim is only making $50 million this year.
But bear with me.
The point is that these CEOs are doing their best to prevent layoffs themselves.
Hold on back up, what do I mean they're trying to prevent layoffs?
They're literally the ones approving them.
Well, as far as the public is concerned, that's true.
The CEOs are the ones who take all the blame and bad rep for layoffs, and they're definitely by no means saints, but they're also not the ones behind layoffs.
The ones who are really behind layoffs are people like this.
You probably have no idea who this guy is because people like this lurk in the shadows, but they pull all the strings.
This is Christopher Hahn, the founder of TCI Fund Management.
He's a multi-billionaire with a $6 billion stake in Google, and since last November, he has been constantly sending letters to Sundar and calling out Google amongst investor circles.
We are writing to express our view that the cost base alphabet is too high and management needs to take aggressive action.
The company has too many employees and the cost per employee is too high.
Within hours of this letter being sent, Google shares were already up 4.4%.
That doesn't sound like a lot, but for a company as big as Google, we're talking about a market cap increase of over $50 billion, making it crystal clear that this is what rich investors want.
The reality is that people like Christopher Hahn have no idea about tech.
They think it's like some sort of factory where you have to maximize output and minimize input.
That's not how tech works, and tech CEOs obviously know that, but that's completely irrelevant.
You get a dozen Christopher Hons together, and boom, and it's Sundar or Tim that's out of a job.
So naturally, they do as they're asked even though it's not all that effective.
Also, I don't want to understate the aggressiveness of these investors.
After the first round of layoffs at Google, the first thing Chris did was send in another letter asking for far more.
He wanted Google to cut a total of 40,000 jobs and reduce pay substantially, and Chris is just one example.
Most big investors do the exact same thing, just behind closed doors.
And that's why everyone is suddenly doing layoffs even though the effectiveness is questionable to say the least.

title: The 1.2 Billion Sub YouTuber That’s Losing It All
note: Rise-and-fall company story with a named protagonist introduced by hook; the propaganda claim is raised early, the 2016 theory is examined and rejected, and decline is blamed on algorithm shifts.
sections: Adme and the Soul Publishing origins
Election theory debunked; content farm rise
lines: This man has 1.2 billion subscribers.
What channel does he run?
Well, he runs our favorite channels, 5-Minute Crafts, 123Go, Brightside, Slick Slime Sam, La La Life, and BabyZoo, just to name a few.
All of these channels are owned by a corporation called The Soul Publishing, which is run by our protagonist, Pavel Radiv.
The company was only founded 7 years ago, but given that they post hundreds of videos per day across 21 languages, they've essentially been able to brute force their way to the top.
But while things look good on the surface, underneath the hood, things aren't going that great.
In fact, they're looking pretty bad.
Take 5 Minute Crafts for example.
The channel has a whopping 80 million subscribers, but a lot of their videos can't even break 100k views.
It's even worse at Brightside, a total of 45 million subscribers, but many of their videos can't even break 20k views.
Zooming out a bit, Brightside used to pull in 150 to 200 million views per month back in their heyday, but now the channel is down to 40 to 50 million views per month.
Not a bad amount, but given that they post three times a day, it's very possible that this operation is now unprofitable.
A similar story can be seen with their subscriber count as well.
Since last October, Brightside has had multiple months where their net subscriber gain was straight up zero.
Clearly, things aren't looking that great from a business perspective, but there's more to it than just that.
You see, it's easy to dismiss these whole publishing as just some soulless content farm that's looking to milk social media for views.
But when you take a deeper look, a much darker agenda becomes more evident.
Their quirky content is actually sometimes laced with politics and pro-Russian versions of history.
One of their now deleted videos for example claimed that Ukraine is part of Russia way back in 2019.
Another claimed that Alaska was a gift to the US from the Soviet Union.
And when you consider that the company is run by a bunch of Russian nationals, this all starts to make sense.
This means that this whole publishing may not just be the world's largest content farm, but also the world's largest propaganda machine.
So, here's the controversial rise and fall of the biggest YouTube empire of all time.
Taking a look back, the story of the Soul Publishing indeed only dates back to 2016, but the story of the company behind the company, Admi, dates back to the early 2000s to two men.
These men are Pavel Radiv and Merit Mukhamitov.
Admi started off as a media platform that seeked to offer serious informational content.
But over time, this evolved into being more lighthearted content focused on entertainment as this simply appealed to a far larger audience.

They basically became the Russian Buzzfeed and would eventually transition this style over to their dozens of YouTube channels which brings us into their first controversy, the timeline of the sole publishing.
After being a Russian-focused media organization for over a decade, Adme decided to launch the Soul Publishing in 2016.
This has prompted some to theorize that the Soul Publishing was created to influence the 2016 election.
At one point, even Forbes and the Business Insider explored the idea, but these claims don't hold up against further scrutiny.
For starters, many of the Soul Publishing's most popular channels were actually created after the election.
5-Minute Crafts, for example, was created a week after the election, and Brightside was created months after the election.
Also, even for channels that were created before the election, they simply didn't have much time to gain momentum and influence, even if that was their goal.
The reality was that the sole publishing was just putting out a bunch of corny videos like these, 35 unbelievable cooking hacks, 29 things we do wrong every day, and 5 minute crafts compilation.
To be honest, these videos carried no real value whatsoever, as most of the time, the hacks didn't even make sense.
I mean, like, what even is this?
The lack of functionality didn't really hurt the channel though.
They had some great titles and thumbnails that got people to click, and back in 2017 and 2018, that was really all you needed.
Also, they were posting dozens of videos every single day, so even if 99% of their videos went nowhere, as long as 1% went super viral, that was all they needed.
It didn't take long for reaction channels to start clowning on Brightside and 5 minute crafts, but this simply gave them even more publicity and exposure.
Before you knew it, each of their channels were racking up tens of millions of subscribers.
Brightside was able to reach over 30 million subscribers within a matter of 3 years, and 5-Minute Crafts was able to reach over 60 million subscribers within the same time period.
Also, it wasn't just YouTube that they were blowing up on.
They also had a massive presence on Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, and even Pinterest.
By the end of 2019, they were publishing 1,500 videos per month with the help of 550 employees.
This was literally the epitome of a content farm, but I mean, who could blame them?
They were making millions posting useless, but also harmless content, at least for the most part.
Unfortunately though, this heyday didn't last long as the company's first tribulations were just around the corner.
The company's first major challenge came from none other than YouTube's infamous algorithm.
them.
As we moved into the 2020s, YouTube started an internal campaign against clickbait.
For obvious reasons, YouTube was not exactly a fan of clickbait as it simply gave the entire platform a cheap tabloid vibe.
Not to mention, it likely led to people spending less time on the platform.
This wasn't originally a major concern as YouTube's user base was simply growing so much.
But as the platform started to mature, maximizing revenue from current users became a larger priority than trying to attract new users.
So, YouTube started focusing on a new metric, average view duration.
The longer people watched their videos, the more likely it was to be seen by more people.
So, naturally, videos that were based around stories and payoff started taking off and we saw creators lean towards longer and longer videos.
This, however, was terrible news for these whole publishing.
Virtually all of their content was centered around a gimmicky hook, similar to what we see on TikTok today.
So once viewers clicked on the video and saw the hack they came for, they clicked off.
They simply didn't care about the other 20 hacks in the video.
This meant that while channels like Brightside had a great click through rate, they had awful viewer retention.
As such, the soul would decide to change up their content with a new channel called Actually Happened.
Most of you have probably completely forgotten about this channel as it has since been deleted.
So, let me remind you about the cringe content they posted.
My BF has 74 GFs.
I date only psychos.
BFF broke her own leg so she can be the center of attention.
Now, these videos are actually from another channel called My Story Animated, but actually happened to post the same sort of stuff.
While this was no doubt cringe, it was once again effective at getting people to click.
People love hearing about drama and gossip.
Combine this with a storyline and characters and emotion, and boom, people are suddenly more invested in the videos than their own financial future.
This deadly combination of super high click-through rates and ridiculous watch time allowed it actually happened to basically blow up overnight, but it wasn't all sunshines and rainbows.
You see, the channel was so cringed that it was successful at creating a hate club also overnight.
People loved to clown on just how fake their stories were, and honestly, you can't even blame the critics.
I think I remember a video where the kid didn't want the dad to drop them off at school because the dad was gonna drop them off in a helicopter or some crap like that.
Yeah, it was really weird.
There were also complaints that the channel was a bad influence as it sometimes glorified abusive relationships and cheaters.
I mean, just listen to this.
I was going to marry my GF until I met my first love.
I'm a cheater.
Really quite a video, but out of nowhere, The Soul decided to wipe this entire channel completely off the face of the planet as they deleted literally every single video on the channel.
There was never an official explanation for this, but it was probably just because it got the company too much bad press.
Viewers quickly moved on and forgot about what actually happened, but The Soul was back to ground zero, and YouTube was about to evolve even more.
As YouTube started focusing on average view duration, creators naturally started trying to play this system as well.
They would artificially increase the length of videos to skew their watch time.
They would have gift cards throughout the video so that people watched it over and over again, even if the video sucked.
Again, this is not what YouTube had in mind when they started focusing on watch time.
If YouTube really wanted to maximize the time that people spent on YouTube, they had to focus on promoting videos that people actually liked, not just videos that people watched longer.
So, YouTube implemented yet another key metric into the algorithm, which was of course, viewer satisfaction.
